title: Falcons sign QB Andy Dalton and release Cooper Rush
summary: The Atlanta Falcons, fresh off a loss against the Chicago Bears, are signing veteran quarterback Andy Dalton. In a corresponding move, they’ve cut ties with fellow red-headed quarterback Cooper Rush. To say this is a bit of a curious move would be an understatement, given that Dalton will open up as the third quarterback on […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - JANUARY 3: Andy Dalton #14 of the Carolina Panthers warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Raymond James Stadium on January 3, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons, fresh off a loss against the Chicago Bears, are signing veteran quarterback Andy Dalton. In a corresponding move, they’ve cut ties with fellow red-headed quarterback Cooper Rush. To say this is a bit of a curious move would be an understatement, given that Dalton will open up as the third quarterback on the roster. Whether this is the Falcons covering themselves with Michael Penix Jr. getting banged up repeatedly and not wanting to chance Rush getting back into a game in case of a rash of injuries that takes down Penix and backup Tua Tagovailoa, or whether they view Dalton as a possible QB2 over Tua remains to be seen. Either way, Dalton’s a slam dunk upgrade on what the team had with Rush, at the very least. Veteran free-agent QB Andy Dalton is signing with the Atlanta Falcons, per sources. pic.twitter.com/fbRmoZlfx9 — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 19, 2026 It was recently reported that Dalton had turned down an offer to return to the Eagles , where he was Jalen Hurts’ backup until he threw an interception on his lone passing attempt in Week 3 against the Bears; the Eagles released him on October 9. With Hurts going on injured reserve and Tanner McKee, Cole Payton, and Joe Milton as the only quarterbacks in the mix, Philadelphia wanted him back, but he declined to return. The path to playing time would seem to be much clearer in Philadelphia, which is part of what makes this interesting. One would think for Dalton to sign on he’d have to be given a legitimate chance to compete with Tua to back up Penix, and that’s my operating assumption until I hear otherwise. Dalton has appeared in 180 games in his career with 139 starts, with his last more-or-less full-time role coming back in 2022 for the Saints. Originally a 2011 second round pick for the Bengals, Dalton finished his career second in passing yards and first in touchdowns in Cincinnati’s history. He has 254 career touchdown passes and 152 interceptions as his age 39 season rolls on and has typically been a solid backup at worst for the teams he’s played for, with a 66% completion percentage and 10 touchdowns against 7 interceptions in his last extended reserve stint with the Panthers from 2023 to 2025. It goes without saying that while his signing adds some intrigue to the backup competition here in Atlanta, my hope is that Penix is both healthy and effective enough that we never see him in 2026. Give Dalton a warm welcome, and we’ll see if he can overtake Tua for backup duties in the weeks ahead.
author: Dave Choate

title: Falcons – Bears Week 6 recap: A whole lot of stumbling
summary: The Atlanta Falcons turned in two glorious weeks where they beat down the Packers and Saints, giving us hope they were rounding into form and becoming something more than the mediocrity we had seen for nearly a decade running. Those hopes are not entirely dashed, but they are certainly dimmed by the past two games. […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - OCTOBER 18: Bijan Robinson #7 of the Atlanta Falcons rushes during the first quarter against the Chicago Bears at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons turned in two glorious weeks where they beat down the Packers and Saints, giving us hope they were rounding into form and becoming something more than the mediocrity we had seen for nearly a decade running. Those hopes are not entirely dashed, but they are certainly dimmed by the past two games. Facing good coaches and good teams, the Falcons have stumbled. Last week they played a close, solid game that fell apart late against the Ravens with a backup quarterback, and this week they managed to turn a 31-7 game into a 31-23 game late. Notably in both cases, they lost owing to excruciating special teams mishaps, defensive lapses spurred by injuries, and whatever the hell has been going on offensively. That has taken them from 2-2 to 2-4, hovering just above the dismal basement of the NFC South, and has effectively blown a hole in all the arguments for taking them seriously. Did you believe in the offense? They’ve been weirdly allergic to Bijan Robinson early in games and their quarterback, while capable of brilliance, is faltering under pressure. Do you love the defense? It’s down multiple cornerbacks, both starting linebackers, and is showing the cracks you’d expect when major injuries pile up. Did you have high hopes for special teams after an encouraging summer? They have a massive, persistent return game problem that has repeatedly put the offense in bad spots and given opposing teams life. And so on. Against a very good Bears that punched above its weight defensively for much of the afternoon, this team was only intermittently competitive. They were within one score early but kept dropping further and further behind until they were down 31-7, at which point the defense got a couple of stops, the offense kicked into high gear, and they climbed back within eight. After the team’s last ditch drive fell short, the defense couldn’t keep the Bears from running out the clock and they dropped their third game in three tries at home this year. There’s a wide swath of blame to go around here, and what makes efforts like these even more frustrating is that this team can pull together stretches of something approaching excellence, but has been unable to sustain them these past two weeks. Look, this is a team with a clear laundry list of needs, a massive amount of 2027 cap space, and enough picks to potentially go out and grab the high end players they need to fill those holes, and generally the decisions the front office has made to this point encourage us to feel hopeful about the future. If you came into this season expecting an up-and-down first season for Kevin Stefanski and company, the broad contours of this season to this point aren’t shocking. We probably need to retain the capacity to look at the future in a reasonable way to endure the roller coaster we are most assuredly riding now. We should also remember that outside of that dismal effort against the Panthers, the Falcons have been competitive in every game they’ve played despite the many rookies and one-year signings they’re relying on to get the job done in 2026, which is worth something . But! The here and now is deeply frustrating. It’s hard to explain why Bijan Robinson had one carry in the first two drives against a weak run defense and only nine carries overall when he’s so dynamic that he can change the flow of a game, even if you’re down by a lot. It’s hard to watch this team’s returners repeatedly elect to make a go at it with punts and kicks they have no business fielding and believe there’s not a ton of work to be done in that phase. And it’s hard to see such a game effort from a bruised and battered defense—please get well soon, Kendal Daniels—undone by injuries and other phases of the game, especially when they’re having to contend with Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams. It is just frustrating to be a Falcons fans right now, as it long has been, and difficult to see them reversing this skid against a 49ers team that ranks among the NFL’s best next week. Too long this team has been defined by what it can’t do rather than what it can do, and if the ceiling feels a bit higher this year with the glimpses of great play we’ve seen, the downside still seems destined to define their 2026. At 2-4, they’ll need to prove that sentiment wrong in a hurry if they’re able to do so. On to the full recap. The Good Michael Penix seems destined to be in both The Good and The Ugly every week with the way things are tracking. The good is not difficult to see—Penix got going against the blitz in the second half, he made some tremendous throws to Jahan Dotson, Kyle Pitts, and Drake London along the way—and I’m hopeful that him going out there and slinging three touchdowns after exiting last week with a rib injury will quiet some of the unjustified criticism of his toughness. When you can keep him clean or he knows where the pressure is coming from, Penix can do tremendous things. Bijan Robinson did well with his limited touches, with the only (very real) blemish on his day coming in the form of a rough holding call. The shame is that he didn’t get more work. It was another fine day from Drake London, who hoovered up every target he had a reasonable chance at, but this was the Kyle Pitts breakout game. He reeled in five of his seven targets for 60 yards and a pair of touchdowns, both excellent efforts and one of which saw him extend to make the score happen. After a three week drought to start the season that saw him with just two grabs for 20 yards on six targets, Pitts has 13 grabs for 149 yards and three touchdowns over the past three weeks. Tommy Rees appears to be figuring out how to utilize him, and if the team can just do so more consistently earlier in games, the offense should be in better shape. I’ve had Jahan Dotson in a dynasty league for a while now, so I’ve tracked his career with interest and have long felt he was better than his production has indicated. I was a fan of dropping him into this offense given his ability to win deep, and we saw that in Weeks 4 and 5. What we hadn’t seen necessarily was the ability to win contested catches, but Dotson did that on a great touchdown grab against the Bears where he was blanketed but reeled in a pretty ball from Michael Penix Jr. for the score, and Dotson finished as the team’s leading receiver with 87 yards and a score on three grabs. The one where he came back on an underthrown Penix deep ball and spun out of a tackle to pick up additional yardage afterwards was also worth calling out. The team needed a non-London receiving threat to step up, and Dotson is doing it in a major way. That Gervon Dexter/Brandon Dorlus duo is as good as it gets. They were one of the few consistent sources of pressure in this one and came up with two of Atlanta’s four sacks, with LaCale London and Za’Darius Smith also chipping in one each. All four have been assets this year, but Dorlus and Dexter simply blow up pockets week after week and even made a quarterback as elusive as Caleb Williams uncomfortable. Jessie Bates forced a fumble, the second straight week he’s been involved in a big turnover, with Harold Perkins Jr. scooping the ball up. After a quiet start to the year, Bates is heating up. I give Harold Perkins Jr. and Josh Woods a lot of credit for needing to come into this game and play major snaps with Divine Deablo and Kendal Daniels both out and holding their own, particularly Woods given that his role is typically exclusively on special teams. While special teams has been something of a disaster for Atlanta in 2026, it’s not because of Jake Bailey. The punter absolutely boomed multiple punts today despite unfavorable field position, giving Atlanta’s defense a fighting chance, and has been…
author: Dave Choate

title: Ravens discussion: should Eric DeCosta make a trade with the Colts?
summary: The Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday after a 2-4 start to the 2026 season, stirring speculation that the team could engage in a fire sale before the trade deadline. Baltimore Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta already made one blockbuster trade, sending a second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - NOVEMBER 23: Quenton Nelson #56 of the Indianapolis Colts runs onto the field before the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on November 23, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday after a 2-4 start to the 2026 season, stirring speculation that the team could engage in a fire sale before the trade deadline. Baltimore Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta already made one blockbuster trade, sending a second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for center Cam Jurgens. But the Colts have their own treasure trove of players to offer, particularly in the trenches where DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson can change games on their own. Should DeCosta call up Colts assistant GM Chris Dodds and make another deal? Nikhil Mehta If the Ravens want to move on from John Simpson as their starting left guard, they will have to stomach paying him $17.5 million for roughly half a season of work. Quenton Nelson would no doubt be a massive upgrade, but he is due for a substantial raise once his contract expires after the season. He would also cost premium draft capital – if Jurgens went for a second-round pick, Nelson is probably worth a first. It just does not make sense for Baltimore. Buckner, though, I have coveted for years. Officially, he already has four sacks and four tackles for loss through six games, and according to Pro Football Focus, he ranks ninth among interior defenders with 19 pressures. His pass rushing opportunities have also been somewhat limited by the Colts trailing for most of their games to open the year. This is another expiring contract in an expensive market, though, so a premium Day 3 pick would be the most I would offer for a half-season rental. Dustin Cox As much as I love the idea of adding Quinton Nelson to the Ravens, I simply do not think it is feasible given the combination of draft capitol required to pry him away from the Colts and the need to pay him a new contract. Nelson will surely demand another top-of-the-market deal and I am not sure if the Ravens are in a spot to hand one out, given their future cap situation and players such as Roger Rosengarten and Nate Wiggins who will be eligible for extensions next year. A player such as DeForest Buckner may make more sense, but Baltimore already has big-contract players on the defensive line in Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones. Already giving up a 2028 second-round pick for Cam Jurgens means Eric DeCosta may not be as willing to part with another Day 2 pick. If a trade is to be made before the deadline, I expect DeCosta to flip a mid-round pick for a solid player instead. Zach Canter The Ravens should absolutely be calling to see the asking price on Quinton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. Both are north of 30 and on expiring contracts that the Colts should be looking to offload. I could see the Ravens passing on Buckner cause they have both Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones signed long-term. Jesse Minter has struggled to get the most out of his pass rush, particularly with Trey Hendrickson and Mike Green failing to produce at the same time. Another disruptive interior would boost the pass rush and offer the flexibility for Madubuike to flex outside as a jumbo edge rusher. Nelson is a guy the Ravens shouldn’t be outbid for. There are a ton of resources now tied up in the offensive line: a first round pick in Ioane, the trade for Jurgens (and his contract), and veteran deals for John Simpson and Ronnie Stanley. Roger Rosengarten is eligible for an extension next spring and should be in line for a substantial raise. But with Stanley on an expiring contract and Vinson looking plausible as a future left tackle, there’s no reason for the Ravens to not go all in on building the wall this year and the future. There’s a very possible future that includes Nelson, Jurgens, Ioane, and Rosengarten the core of the OL for the next couple of years. Restructure a couple contracts, throw John Simpson in the deal, extend Lamar Jackson this offseason, and there’s a way to make the cap space for both Nelson and Rosengarten to get extensions. If the Ravens want to be a contender this year, it’s a move they should absolutely make. As the L.A. Rams say, F them picks. Kevin McNelis The Colts are in significant disarray at the moment, and Chris Ballard’s firing seems to signify that they’re ready to head in a new direction. With that in mind, I agree that Baltimore should see what the asking price is for Quenton Nelson and/or DeForest Buckner. The earlier acquisition of Cam Jurgens for a future second-rounder seems to signify that Baltimore is willing to deal at a high price to try to win now; the question is what kind of price they’re willing to pay for either of these guys, considering that they’d be short-term rentals under their current contracts. My gut says the Colts stand pat for at least a few more days while they try to figure out who is handling any trade considerations, especially given EDC’s track record of swooping in like a hawk to go after embattled franchises at moments of vulnerability. If I had to pick one target over the other, I’d see what the Colts want for Quenton Nelson since he would shore up the line basically everywhere barring another injury. Q is one of the most reliable guards in the league and has been for many years, so if you could line up LJ’s return with reinforcements along his line, this offense could get a huge, much-needed boost. I don’t know that I see the Ravens actually pulling the trigger to go after of these guys, but I’ve been surprised before (the Roquan acquisition comes to mind).
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 6: Rookie pass-catchers flash but offense struggles
summary: Offense Tyler Huntley drew his second consecutive start and played the entire game. Every offensive lineman also went the distance minus Ronnie Stanley, who was sidelined for just one play. Backup swing tackle Carson Vinson again saw a small handful of snaps as an extra blocker. The Ravens were out-snapped 57 to 63 overall after […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Ja'Kobi Lane #6 of the Baltimore Ravens catches a pass during the third quarter of a game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Offense QB: Tyler Huntley 57 RB: Derrick Henry 33, Justice Hill 24 WR: Zay Flowers 50, Devontez Walker 37, Ja’Kobi Lane 31, Rashod Bateman 17, LaJohntay Wester 3 TE: Mark Andrews 41, Josh Cuevas 23, Nick Vannett 23 OL: Emery Jones Jr. 57, John Simpson 57, Roger Rosengarten 57, Vega Ioane 57, Ronnie Stanley 56, Carson Vinson 4 Tyler Huntley drew his second consecutive start and played the entire game. Every offensive lineman also went the distance minus Ronnie Stanley, who was sidelined for just one play. Backup swing tackle Carson Vinson again saw a small handful of snaps as an extra blocker. The Ravens were out-snapped 57 to 63 overall after the Browns roughly doubled their snap total in the second half. In the backfield, Derrick Henry saw 33 snaps compared to Justice Hill’s 24. Hill did not receive a carry in this game and caught three passes for minimal gain. Henry ran 17 times but gained just 58 rushing yards and had a costly fourth-quarter fumble. Rashod Bateman exited the game after 17 snaps and did not return with a shoulder injury. That thrusted rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane, who was making his return from injured reserve, into a 31-snap role. Lane caught four passes for 40 yards with multiple first-down conversions. Zay Flowers played 50 of 57 (88%) snaps and Devontez Walker’s 37 snaps saw him targeted twice with no catches. Matthew Hibner’s absence at tight end opened the door for fellow rookie Josh Cuevas to shine. In 23 snaps, Cuevas caught a season-best four passes for 44 yards and a touchdown. Mark Andrews, despite playing 18 more snaps than both Cuevas and Nick Vannett, caught only one pass for a few years. Defense DL: Nnamdi Madubuike 49, Travis Jones 34, Calais Campbell 28, John Jenkins 14, Aeneas Peebles 6 EDGE: Trey Hendrickson 39, Tavius Robinson 31, Zion Young 25, Mike Green 24, Ethan Burke 7 ILB: Roquan Smith 63, Trenton Simpson 37, Teddye Buchanan 5 CB: Nate Wiggins 63, Marlon Humphrey 60, Keyon Martin 24, Chidobe Awuzie 3 S: Malaki Starks 63, Kyle Hamilton 63, Jaylinn Hawkins 55 On defense, the usual suspects played all 63 snaps: Roquan Smith, Nate Wiggins, Kyle Hamilton and Malaki Starks. Cornerback Marlon Humphrey gutted out 60 snaps despite nursing two lower-body injuries entering this game. Keyon Martin replaced Chandler Rivers as the primary slot corner, and he had a strong performance in 24 snaps. Rivers didn’t see the field after playing a lot since Week 1. Chidobe Awuzie played only 3 snaps and Jaylinn Hawkins’ snap share (87%) returned to a high level after he saw a dip in playing time last week. Trenton Simpson continues to maintain a strong hold on the starting weakside linebacker spot opposite Smith, with Teddye Buchanan’s snap count dropping from last week (19 to 5). Simpson tied with Hawkins for the team-lead in tackles (eight). The Ravens’ defensive front had an active day. Nnami Madubuike stuffed the stat sheet in 49 snaps with two quarterback hits and his first half-sack since returning from injury. Calais Campbell’s 28 snaps saw him record a sack, tackle for loss and two quarterback hits. Travis Jones, who suffered a knee injury in Week 5, played 34 snaps. Broderick Washington’s absence allowed Aeneas Peebles to play six snaps. On the edge, Trey Hendrickson returned from a two-game absence and led the group with 39 snaps. Tavius Robinson notably saw a big dip in playing time, as his snap share dropped below 50%. Mike Green’s snap count also decreased significantly in Hendrickson’s return to the lineup (24 snaps). Zion Young played 25 snaps while undrafted rookie Ethan Burke received seven defensive reps.
author: Frank Platko

title: State of the Ravens’ roster entering Week 7
summary: The Baltimore Ravens have been battered around in the first six weeks of the season. They’ve lost starters and depth players to both short-term and long-term injuries with several already on season-ending IR. With the Browns game now over, let’s check in on the current make up of the Ravens’ roster and practice squad. Quarterback […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Tyler Huntley #5 of the Baltimore Ravens looks to pass against the Cleveland Browns during the second quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens have been battered around in the first six weeks of the season. They’ve lost starters and depth players to both short-term and long-term injuries with several already on season-ending IR. With the Browns game now over, let’s check in on the current make up of the Ravens’ roster and practice squad. Quarterback (3) Active: Lamar Jackson, Tyler Huntley, Joe Fagnano Injured reserve: Skylar Thompson Lamar Jackson is expected back soon, potentially for next week’s game against the Cincinnati Bengals. He’s been phenomenal when healthy, and a 1-1 result in his two absences is not bad. Tyler Huntley did what a backup quarterback does: put together a solid game and then showed why he’s a backup and not a starter. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano remains on the roster as the third-string quarterback, though Jackson’s injury has elevated him to the No. 2 role for the last few weeks. Running back (3) Active: Derrick Henry, Justice Hill, Rasheen Ali Injured reserve: Adam Randall Practice squad: Jonathan Ward Many expected the Ravens to carry four running backs rookie Adam Randall mysteriously landed on IR during 53-man roster cuts. There have been zero updates on his health since then, and no word on when his 21-day practice window before activation will start. The run game has slowed down in recent weeks with the offensive line shuffling and the injury to Lamar Jackson, but Derrick Henry still has seven touchdowns in six games. Hill has been explosive in his role as the third-down back, throwing blocks, catching balls, and mixing in the occasional 20-yard carry. He’s averaging 7.4 yards per carry this season, albeit on a limited sample size. Ali hasn’t seen snaps on offense and was putting together a solid contract year on special teams before multiple gaffes on Sunday in Cleveland. Tight end (4) Active: Mark Andrews, Matt Hibner, Josh Cuevas, Nick Vannett IR: Durham Smythe (out for season) Practice squad: Ty Pezza, Lucas Scott (FB) The Ravens lost tight end Durham Smythe for the season to an Achilles injury in Week 4 against the Titans. In response, they signed veteran Nick Vannett off their practice squad to replace Smythe’s inline blocking. Matt Hibner also suffered a hand injury in Week 5 against the Falcons that has him out against the Browns and maybe longer, but head coach Jesse Minter said it won’t be an IR situation. Outside of that, the biggest problem in the room is Mark Andrew’s inability to transition from the YAC monster he once was to the possession tight end he is now. If he can transition into simply attacking the ball at the catch point and going down instead of trying to hit the button for the YAC option at the catch point, this room will be in better in great shape once Hibner and Josh Cuevas get involved as the explosive options. The latter had four catches for 44 yards and a touchdown in Cleveland. Wide receiver (6) Active: Zay Flowers, Rashod Bateman, Tez Walker, Ja’Kobi Lane, LaJohntay Wester, Elijah Sarratt Practice squad: Chris Moore, Gage Larvadain This might be the best wide receiver room in franchise history. Zay Flowers has been undeniably a top-5 pass-catcher this year and leads the league in several metrics. If you’re looking at a graph on social media, he is probably in the upper-right (very good) corner of it. Rashod Bateman looks very comfortable in his role, shining when Flowers was absent in Week 2 and led the team in yards in Week 5’s win. Tez Walker is still fighting for more playing time, but his ability as a deep threat is apparent in how often he can be seen flying by defensive backs on film. And now, Ja’Kobi Lane has returned to add a contested-catch element everyone has been excited for since he started balling in OTAs. In his first game back he had four catches for 40 yards as part of a clear effor to get him involved. Sarratt is best known for a costly holding penalty for now, but he was always going to face an uphill battle for snaps. This group can be truly special once Jackson returns at quarterback and the pass game takes over as the driving force for the offense. Offensive line (8) Active: Ronnie Stanley, John Simpson, Vega Ioane, Andrew Vorhees, Roger Rosengarten, Carson Vinson, Emery Jones Jr., Cam Jurgens Injured reserve: Danny Pinter (out for season), Jovaughn Gwyn, Ethan Pocic Practice squad: Chuma Edoga, Kyle Hergel, Gerad Lictenhan, Andre James, A.J. Arcuri This unit has been decimated. All three preseason starting center options are out long-term. Danny Pinter was declared out for the season in training camp; then both Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic were lost in Week 3 with IR placements shortly after. Their eventual return hasn’t been ruled out, but the Cam Jurgens trade seems to be signaling that the Ravens don’t expect those guys to contribute again this year. Rookie guard Vega Ioane has been admirably playing center in the meantime, with Andrew Vorhees and Emery Jones each starting one game at right guard. Ioane will slide back to his natural position once Jurgens clears concussion protocol and enters the starting lineup. The Ravens activated Kyle Hergel and Chuma Edoga this week against the Browns as depth with both Vorhees and Jones questionable. Hergel is out of elevations and could be added to the 53-man roster as the backup center moving forward. Defensive line (6) Active: Nnamdi Madubuike, Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, John Jenkins, Broderick Washington, Aeneas Peebles Practice squad: Rayshaun Benny, David Olajiga This group has been led by the resurgence of Nnamdi Madubuike, who has picked up where he left off pre-injury as a dominant 3-tech, and Calais Campbell’s continued excellence in his 19th NFL season. Travis Jones hasn’t been bad, but he has not lived up to post-extension expectations. He missed a large portion of camp with a pec injury, so hopefully he’ll continue to round into form. John Jenkins and Broderick Washington have disappeared at times as the unit’s designated run-stoppers, and I personally continue to question their activation over Aeneas Peebles – especially Washington. Speaking of which, Peebles has been a healthy scratch since Madubuike’s return, despite the pass-rush win rates he stacked in the early weeks beforehand. Washington was sidelined in Week 6, but Peebles only got a handful of snaps. His penetration ability may only come into play in specific game scripts. Outside linebacker (5) Active: Trey Hendrickson, Mike Green, Tavius Robinson, Zion Young, Ethan Burke Practice squad: Adisa Isaac, Kaimon Rucker Trey Hendrickson’s return to the lineup could take this group to new heights. He was fantastic in his first couple of games while playing with a broken finger. He may lack elite counting stats, but his pressure and win rates match his film of a disruptive, productive rusher. In Hendrickson’s absence in Weeks 4 and 5, Mike Green stepped up massively with eight pressures and a pass rush win rate over 20%. However, he and his All-Pro teammate cannot seem to get going when they are both on the field. Tavius Robinson’s pass rush metrics haven’t been great, but he leads the team in sacks and continues to be a menace against the run. He consistently makees plays and could be pricing himself out of Baltimore this coming offseason. Zion Young has a solidified role on run downs, and his play strength consistently shows up on tape, even if his pass rush impact has been up and down. UDFA Ethan Burke nabbed his first sack against the Titans, but his role on defense will likely be minimized with Hendrickson’s return. title: Ravens Report Card, Week 6: Sluggish offense falters in loss to Browns
summary: The Baltimore Ravens had their three-game win streak snapped by the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. The Ravens were shut out after the first quarter in a low-scoring affair and lost 13-10. Here are report card grades for the team’s offense and defense in the Week 6 defeat. Quarterback: C- After leading the Ravens to a […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - OCTOBER 18: Zay Flowers #4 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against Emmanuel McNeil-Warren #28 and Carson Schwesinger #49 of the Cleveland Browns during the second quarter of the game at Huntington Bank Field on October 18, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens had their three-game win streak snapped by the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. The Ravens were shut out after the first quarter in a low-scoring affair and lost 13-10. Here are report card grades for the team’s offense and defense in the Week 6 defeat. Quarterback: C- After leading the Ravens to a comeback victory in Week 6 with two touchdown drives, Tyler Huntley regressed against the Browns. He attempted 31 passes and only threw for 165 yards, as the Browns clamped down on short-yardage throws. Huntley had multiple pass attempts that were nearly intercepted. He finished with one touchdown pass, which was a fourth-down throw in the red zone. Running Back: D+ Derrick Henry found tough sledding on the ground, running 17 times for a season-low 58 yards (3.4 yards per carry). 17 of his yards came on one single carry. Henry did not score and had a costly lost fumble late in the fourth quarter, which the Browns recovered and quickly scored the game-tying touchdown a few minutes later. Justice Hill was not given any rushing attempts and only gained nine yards on three receptions out of the backfield. Wide Receiver: C+ Like last week, the Ravens didn’t do much damage in the downfield passing game. Zay Flowers led the team with 66 receiving yards but caught only six of his 11 targets. He did have a long 31-yard snag. Rookie Ja’Kobi Lane returned from injury and immediately made an impact. Lane caught four passes for 40 yards, showing some solid middle-of-the-field presence. Rashod Bateman exited the game early with a shoulder injury, and Devontez Walker did not catch any passes on two targets. Tight End: C+ The Ravens were undermanned again at tight end with Matthew Hibner sidelined due to a hand injury. Fellow rookie Josh Cuevas stepped up and delivered his best performance of the season, catching four passes for 44 yards and a touchdown. Cuevas’ 29-yard reception was his longest of the year as well. Mark Andrews had just one catch and four yards on three targets, dropping another pass for the second straight week. Offensive Line: D+ The Ravens did not regularly win at the line of scrimmage against the Browns’ defensive front. In the run game, the offensive line didn’t get consistent push and create rushing lanes for Henry. In pass protection, they surrendered nine quarterback hits and three sacks. The interior play from each of the offensive guard spots continues to leave much to be desired. Defensive Line: B+ On the flip side of the line of trenches, the Ravens’ defensive front was effective in this matchup. Nnamdi Madubuike had a great pass-rushing performance and finished with two quarterback hits along with a half-sack. Veteran Calais Campbell also had two quarterback hits, one sack and a tackle for loss. The Ravens didn’t allow a run longer than nine yards and held the Browns as a whole to 93 rushing yards (3.2 yards per carry). Edge Rusher: B+ The Ravens received good showings from their edge rusher group. Trey Hendrickson returned and was immediately effective, totaling eight charted pressures with a sack, quarterback hit and tackle for loss. Tavius Robinson also got after the quarterback with a half-sack and quarterback hit of his own. Mike Green had two tackles, and Zion Young likewise had a hit on Watson. Linebacker: B- Trenton Simpson tied for the team-lead in tackles with eight. He continues to make plays. Roquan Smith was active as a pass-rusher with one sack and two quarterback hits, which was tied for the most of any defender. The linebackers were party to some run stops at the line of scrimmage. Cornerback: B The Ravens didn’t allow a ton of damage from Cleveland’s wide receivers for most of the game. They particularly did a good job against rookie phenom Denzel Boston, who had just one catch on five targets. Keyon Martin replaced Chandler Rivers as the primary nickel corner and had a sack, tackle for loss, pass breakup and quarterback hit. Martin was flagged for a crucial defensive pass interference in the fourth quarter, but it was good coverage and a very questionable call. Marlon Humphrey had two passes defended and Nate Wiggins had one as well. Safety: B- Kyle Hamilton had another starring performance with three tackles for loss and seven tackles total. Hamilton was all over the field and regularly around the ball. Malaki Starks had five tackles with a pass defended. No. 3 safety Jaylinn Hawkins had a team-high eight tackles. On a long third-down completion to Jerry Jeudy late in the fourth quarter, which moved the Browns in position to kick a game-winning field goal, Hawkins appeared to be out of position in zone coverage. Special Teams: C Tyler Loop is evidently not out of the woods yet, as he continues to be inconsistent. Loop missed a 49-yard field goal attempt early in the fourth quarter that would have given the Ravens a 13-3 lead. In a game where the Ravens ended up losing by three points, a missed field goal is all the more harmful. Ryan Eckley was busy with seven punts and had a long boom of 62 yards. Three of his punts landed inside the 20 yard line.

title: Christian Benford’s play has returned to normal in Jim Leonhard’s defense
summary: Christian Benford remains one of the most underrated cornerbacks in the NFL, and he’s started to round into form for the Buffalo Bills the past two weeks. And his spike in performance has ironically occurred after he missed a game with a turf toe injury. Let’s track Benford’s 2026 season thus far. In Week 1, […]
full_text: Christian Benford remains one of the most underrated cornerbacks in the NFL, and he’s started to round into form for the Buffalo Bills the past two weeks. And his spike in performance has ironically occurred after he missed a game with a turf toe injury. Let’s track Benford’s 2026 season thus far. In Week 1, he followed Nico Collins. Shadowed him, really. He was the primary coverage defender on 91.4% of the Texans receiver’s routes, and the results weren’t fantastic but were far from brutal for Benford. He allowed six catches for 66 yards and a touchdown on 32 routes in coverage on Collins. Then, in Week 2, Benford covered the super-slippery, mostly-slot specialist Amon-Ra St. Brown on 13 routes. He yielded two grabs for 23 yards and a score. Better. The predominant coverage assignment for Benford in that game, Isaac TeSlaa, whom the Bills cornerback followed on 60.6% of his routes, only had one catch for 20 yards in those matchups. In Week 3, Benford did not shadow anyone. He moved around throughout the game and surrendered three catches for 40 yards to Quentin Johnston and just one snag for 11 yards to Ladd McConkey on 14 total coverage snaps. He missed Week 4’s game with that turf toe injury. In Week 5, Benford covered Puka Nacua and Davante Adams on more than 67% of those receivers’ routes. On those 30 routes, the Bills top cornerback allowed six catches for a mere 44 yards without a score. In Week 6, Benford really settled into a groove. He covered Raiders phenom tight end Brock Bowers on 18 of his routes and gave up two catches for 23 yards. Bowers first catch in the game didn’t happen until there was less than five minutes to go in the third quarter. Altogether, Benford has five pass breakups and 28 tackles in five contests to date this season. The former sixth-round pick is back to playing his normal brand of football. And although he doesn’t have the blue-blood college pedigree or a freaky combine performance on his resume, he’s acclimated well to Jim Leonhard’s scheme. All stats courtesy of Fantasy Points Data*

title: Buffalo Bills HC Joe Brady voices support for S C.J. Gardner-Johnson
summary: Without question, it’s been a tough start to the season for Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson. His frustration boiled over in Week 6 during Buffalo’s road game at the Las Vegas Raiders, which led to his being flagged for a personal foul and ejected from the game for spitting in the direction of tight end […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 12: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 of the Buffalo Bills lines up before the snap during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on October 12, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Without question, it’s been a tough start to the season for Buffalo Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson. His frustration boiled over in Week 6 during Buffalo’s road game at the Las Vegas Raiders, which led to his being flagged for a personal foul and ejected from the game for spitting in the direction of tight end Brock Bowers. On the heels of that incident, Gardner-Johnson has been handed a one-game suspension . Despite all that, head coach Joe Brady isn’t blinking in the face of adversity and the court of public opinion. During his most recent media availability on Monday following the team’s win in Vegas, Brady explained that Gardner-Johnson “knows that can’t happen, that’s inexcusable, that’s not the standard that we’re gonna have and play with,” and that despite their intent to “toe the line, we can’t cross the line.” Brady then also gave a vote of confidence in Gardner-Johnson, saying that no additional discipline or action will happen beyond the league punishment. He also acknowledged there’s plenty of room for improvement as a player and member of the locker room. When asked point-blank if Gardner-Johnson has a starting job when he returns, Brady said: “Yeah, I mean, look, C.J.’s a member of the Buffalo Bills. We brought him here for a reason and we know that he — he knows that he has to play better. He knows he has to be better for this team. You know, just like, like everybody else. Right? We gotta learn from this stuff, and we have to improve, and find ways to get better as the season goes. You know, no different than — it’s different , right? — Jimbo fumblin’, you know. We have to continue to find ways to get better, and he (Gardner-Johnson) knows that he has to be better. And, you know, it’s just an opportunity for him — look, it’d be an opportunity for someone else to, you know, play in the week and step up — but it’s an opportunity for him grow and be better as a better teammate and a better football player, you know, when his opportunity comes up again.” Gardner-Johnson’s actions will cost him an opportunity to suit up and play in the team’s Week 8 matchup against the Baltimore Ravens, their first game back following the bye week. Bills Mafia will have to wait to find out what Brady meant by stating “when his opportunity comes up again.” For his part, Gardner-Johnson owned his mistake and expressed a willingness to “ take my consequence as it is, my fine, whatever it may be .” Here's C.J. Gardner-Johnson's full postgame comments after being ejected from today's game. #Bills safety says he let emotions get the best of him. title: Buffalo Bills defense not better, but certainly different, in 2026
summary: The Bills were always going to look different on defense in 2026. From the time the firing of former head coach Sean McDermott was announced in the early parts of 2026, we all knew that Buffalo Bills owner Terry Pegula was pointing to coaching for a reason, and it wasn’t the performance of the team’s […]
full_text: The Bills were always going to look different on defense in 2026. From the time the firing of former head coach Sean McDermott was announced in the early parts of 2026, we all knew that Buffalo Bills owner Terry Pegula was pointing to coaching for a reason, and it wasn’t the performance of the team’s offense. So when new head coach and former offensive coordinator Joe Brady hired Jim Leonhard to be his defensive coordinator, everyone knew that qualitatively, what the Bills looked like on defense in 2026 would be very different than what the fans had been used to seeing from that unit for the previous nine years. Through six weeks of the 2026 regular season, the Bills defense has absolutely looked different than it has in previous years. It’s also objectively been worse (data from Fantasy Points Data Suite). The Buffalo defense thus far in 2026 is: 30th in EPA per play allowed 28th in EPA per drop back 25th in EPA per rush 28th in success rate against 28th in explosive play rate against To put this in perspective, in 2025 in the same categories, the Bills were: 14th in EPA per play allowed 8th in EPA per drop back 31st in EPA per rush 11th in success rate against 25th in explosive play rate against When your eyes tell you that the team has been a little better against the run than in 2025, your eyes are right. Everything else in terms of resultant defensive metrics is not just worse, but bad. How did we get here? What’s different stylistically in 2026 versus previous years? The biggest and most glaring departure for the 2026 is that the Bills, for a decade one of the most nickel-stubborn teams in the National Football League, are now running base personnel 36.2% of their defensive snaps (9th in the NFL), up from single digit base defense percentages in most years of the Sean McDermott era. The increased base defensive percentage also leads to the Bills having an average box count of 7.13 (5th in the NFL), compared to 6.87 in 2025 (19th in the league) and 6.52 in 2024 (27th in the league). This heavier phenomenon is a contributing factor to the slightly increased effectiveness against the run, but it’s also a factor in the decreased effectiveness against the pass. the McDermott Bills were well-noted to be a team that refused to be dictated to in terms of defensive personnel, and former nickel defender Taron Johnson was the centerpiece of that philosophy that has changed under Jim Leonhard. The next defensive characteristic that has changed significantly in 2026 on defense is the Bills coverage splits on defense. We live in a cover 3 league meta right now (current league average for cover 3 usage is 32.7%, the largest plurality of all coverage groups), but the Bills play cover 4 an astounding 26% of the time in 2026 (#1 in the league) while also being above league average in cover 3 usage (34.4% for Buffalo), which means over 60% of the time, the Bills are running either cover 3 or cover 4. Compare this to 2025, when the Bills ran cover 3 at a mark below the league average with cover 4 right at the league average and cover 2 and cover 1 above the league average. This shows that coverage diversity was far more present in 2025 versus 2026. So the Bills are running a lot more base defense with heavier boxes and a lot more cover 3 and cover 4 (the most cover 4 in the league, even). You may think this is a more aggressive lean, but the Bills are pressing at least one receiver less in 2026 (14.1%, 28th in the league) than the “maligned for ‘soft coverage’” Sean McDermott’s defense in 2025 (30.2%, 7th in the NFL). “Maybe they’re blitzing more”, you say. I mean, a little bit. Buffalo is 20th in the NFL in blitz rate in 2026 (27.9%) and was 23rd in 2025 (24.3%), so not a statistically significantly difference. If you have a team that is: running heavier defensive personnel running heavier boxes running the most cover 4 in the league running a less diverse selection of coverages pressing a lot less still not blitzing much You have the 2026 Bills defense compared to the previous and most recent versions of it. And the results make sense: they’ve seen a slight uptick in run defense due to heavier boxes and heavier personnel, but they’re running a lot of cover 4 to prevent explosives, which might get them there if the communication in the back seven wasn’t leading to blown coverages, allowing explosive plays in the pass game despite the cover 4 calls. They’re not blitzing, they’re not pressing, they’re not diversifying, and they’re not disguising (26.3% disguise rate, 28th in the NFL), so quarterbacks aren’t holding the ball (2.68 average time to throw against, 11th in the NFL). Being able to stop the run from two high is the holy grail of NFL defenses (the Bills are top 12 in both two-high and base personnel usage), so you can see the outcome the Bills are trying to generate, but it’s not happening for them through six weeks. The Bills were trying to get over the hump when they fired Sean McDermott, and they elected to hire a rookie head coach and a rookie defensive coordinator. You can’t do that and then logically not provide any grace for rookie mistakes from your rookie coaches, but the Bills are fortunate to be 5-1 going into their bye week with the defensive generating results this poor. Let’s hope we come out of the bye with a clear identity of how Jim Leonhard and the defense will get where we all want them to go. …and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

title: Buffalo Bills records and milestones from Week 6
summary: Well, that one was a little closer than we would have liked, but the Buffalo Bills get to head into the bye with a win. That’s definitely going to make the next two weeks a little more enjoyable while we wait to see them back on the field.  There’s been plenty of criticism of the […]
full_text: Well, that one was a little closer than we would have liked, but the Buffalo Bills get to head into the bye with a win. That’s definitely going to make the next two weeks a little more enjoyable while we wait to see them back on the field. There’s been plenty of criticism of the Bills’ play — and rightfully so — but not everything has been a cause for concern. So, let’s take a look at a few Shout!outs for the things that went right this week. _____________________________________________________________________________ Josh Allen just passed Russell Wilson. Allen’s 9-yard touchdown pass to Khalil Shakir was the 317th total touchdown of his career, moving him past Russell Wilson for the second-most touchdowns by a player in his first 10 NFL seasons. Allen, of course, is only six games into season No. 9. Josh Allen’s 9-yard TD pass to Khalil Shakir marked Allen’s 317th total TD. Allen (playing in his 6th game of his 9th season) has now passed Russell Wilson (316) for the second-most total TDs in a player’s first 10 seasons. pic.twitter.com/boWs38DKT5 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 18, 2026 Of course, we know that in the third quarter of the game, Allen tied Hall of Famer Jim Kelly atop the Bills’ franchise record as well. You can read about that here. With that 12-yard TD pass to Keon Coleman, Josh Allen now has 258 passing TDs (including playoffs). Allen is now tied with Jim Kelly for the most in team history. pic.twitter.com/zh6CefDawU — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 18, 2026 Joe Brady is in some pretty good company. Through his first six games as a head coach, Brady’s Bills are averaging 32.8 points per game. That’s the second-highest average in the Super Bowl era for a coach’s first six career games. The only man ahead of him? Mike Martz, whose 2000 Rams averaged an absurd 43.7 points. The Bills 32.8 points per game under Joe Brady mark the second-most in the Super Bowl era through a head coach’s first 6 career games. Only Mike Martz (Rams – 43.7 in 2000) averaged more points. https://t.co/5DPssggUKp — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 19, 2026 Tyler Bass has found his groove. Remember when every field goal attempt felt like an adventure? Bass has now made 18 straight dating back to 2024, tying Rian Lindell for the longest streak by a Bills kicker since Lindell put together 18 consecutive makes in 2007. Tyler Bass has made 18 straight field goals dating back to 2024. He is tied for the longest streak by a Bills kicker since Rian Lindell with 18 (10/21/2007-12/09/2007). pic.twitter.com/sxfoQYH5c0 — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 18, 2026 Keon Coleman is making a habit of finding the end zone. Coleman has caught a touchdown pass in three straight games, becoming the first Bills wide receiver to do that since Gabe Davis scored in four consecutive games back in 2023. All four of Keon Coleman's catches today have been for first downs (including TDs). 15 of his 19 catches this year have gone for first downs. https://t.co/P38jXFxxqH — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 19, 2026 And one more for the defense. Dorian Williams picked off Kirk Cousins for the first interception of his NFL career. It might not be history-making, but your first career interception deserves a Shout! James Cook is up to 627 rushing yards this season. Only O.J. Simpson has had more in their first 6 games of a season in Bills history (868 yds in 1973 and 911 yds in 1975). pic.twitter.com/jPzKUo0KeL — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) October 18, 2026 _____________________________________________________________________________ The Bills have plenty to work on, but there are some pretty good things happening in between the things that make us yell at our televisions. And with Allen rewriting record books, Brady collecting wins (whether they’re pretty or not is not for us to judge here), and Bass doing his job without giving us a collective heart attack, we’ve got plenty of reasons to keep Shout! ing.

full_text: The Buffalo Bills are bringing back a familiar name in fan-favorite cornerback Tre’Davious White. ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter reports that White is signing to the Bills’ practice squad, “where he will acclimate before joining their active roster .” Making is third stint with One Bills Drive, the 31-year-old White was the first player selected by former head coach Sean McDermott — going 27th overall in the 2017 NFL Draft following a blockbuster trade involving the Kansas City Chiefs. White has played in 98 games across eight seasons for Buffalo, making 19 interceptions, 78 pass defenses, five forced fumbles, five fumble recoveries, one fumble return for a touchdown, three sacks, six quarterback hits, 351 tackles (271 solo), and 18 tackles for loss (per Pro Football Reference ). The timing of White’s signing make sense with the Bills headed into their bye week. It remains to be seen how and where White will slot in once signed to the active roster. One could envision White initially serving as a depth cornerback in a key mentorship role for rookie cornerback Davison Igbinosun. We’ll find out in time how White’s signing impacts second-year cornerback Maxwell Hairston. Here’s the report from NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport: While the suspension isn’t a stunner, there is some […]
full_text: To the surprise of no one, the NFL has levied a suspension on Buffalo Bills safety CJ Gardner-Johnson for spitting in the direction of Brock Bowers in the second quarter of the Week 6 game in Las Vegas. Here’s the report from NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport: From the NFL: Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson has been suspended without pay for one game for an act of unsportsmanlike conduct during Sunday’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders. During the second quarter, Gardner-Johnson spit at an opponent, violating Rule 12, Section 3,… — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) October 19, 2026 While the suspension isn’t a stunner, there is some precedent here for Garnder-Johnson to appeal the fine. At the start of the 2025 campaign, before the first snap of the season began, Eagles defensive tackle Jalen Carter spit in the face of Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott and was promptly ejected from the NFC East contest. Carter was not suspended in the aftermath, and the speculation for the reason centered around the fact that Carter had missed the entire Week 1 contest. While certainly a despicable act, Garnder-Johnson spit toward Bowers, not directly on him. And it happened with under 20 seconds remaining in the first half. So he’s already missed an entire half of football. I wouldn’t necessarily bank Gardner-Johnson winning his appeal, given his reputation as an agitator. He’s racked up a decent amount of fines for said agitation on the field and was ejected from a game in 2024 against the Commanders while he played safety for the Eagles. If he is suspended, this is the financial impact: CJ Gardner-Johnson will forfeit $109,166 per his 1-game suspension for unsportsmanlike conduct against the #Raiders . CJGJ signed a 1-year, $3.5M contract with the #Bills this past March that includes another $2.5M via playing time & INT incentives. — Spotrac (@spotrac) October 19, 2026 We’ll see what happens. Maybe Gardner-Johnson doesn’t even appeal. Most players do. As of now the Bills will be without one of their starting safeties for the November 1 home game against the Ravens.

Allen getting extraordinarily good at evading sacks coincided with his ascension to elite […]
full_text: The hidden superpower of Josh Allen is his ability to avoid sacks. He’s a magician who regularly conjures magnificent elusiveness inside and outside the pocket behind the line of scrimmage to make something out of what appears to be a dire situation. Allen getting extraordinarily good at evading sacks coincided with his ascension to elite status in the NFL. While the sharpening of that skill is certainly not the sole reason the Bills quarterback has been so good for so long now, the alignment of those timelines is both fascinating and telling. A season ago, when Allen took a career-high 40 sacks during the regular season, that superpower faded. The best way to quantifiably measure a quarterback’s elusiveness in the pocket is with the advanced metric pressure-to-sack rate, which is precisely what it sounds like — the frequency at which a quarterback pressure becomes a quarterback sack. For all intents and purposes, the line of demarcation for pressure-to-sack rate is 20% in the NFL. If a quarterback is near, at, or above a pressure-to-sack rate of 20%, he’s really struggling in this regard. If he’s closer to 15%, he’s doing fine work. If he’s hovering near 10% in pressure-to-sack rate, he’s probably the NFL’s most elusive quarterback in these scenarios. During the 40-sack 2025 campaign, Allen’s pressure-to-sack rate was 18.6%, his highest rate since 2019. It ranked 28th out of 45 qualifiers. Before that, here’s how Allen fared, by season, in this metric and where he ranked among qualifying quarterbacks (lower is better): 2024: 8.0% (1st/44) 2023: 10.3% (2nd/45) 2022: 14.7% (9th/41) 2021: 10.6% (1st/39) 2020: 10.7% (3rd/42) As you can see, I wasn’t exaggerating in the first few paragraphs. Allen has been a wizard in this area, and he’s been excellent avoiding sacks while pressured for a long time now. But many speculated the 18.6% pressure-to-sack rate during his Age 29 season in 2025 was the first sign of Allen’s decline. In the first three games of the 2026 campaign, he was sacked eight times and had pressure-to-sack rates of 16.7%, 11.8%, and a whopping 33.3% in the games leading into Week 4. I’ll give this next sentence a little Mark Twain twist — the reports of the death of Allen’s ability to evade sacks were greatly exaggerated. In the last three outings, Allen has once again, summoned the sack-eluding magic. He’s been sacked three times and has pressure-to-sack rates of 7.1% against the Patriots, 9.1% against the Rams, and 7.7% in Las Vegas against the Raiders. And those incredibly low pressure-to-sack rate contests came after all the speculation about a potential knee injury following a hit to his leg in the second half against the Chargers in Week 3. Even with the shaky-ish start, Allen’s 2026 pressure-to-sack rate entering the bye week is 13.9%, almost identical to his career average of 13.7%. In the 2020s, when it has come to dodging sacks in the face of pressure, no quarterback has been better than Allen. After a down 2025 and a somewhat concerning start to the 2026 campaign, Allen’s enchanting sack-avoiding ways have returned.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Deone Walker wrecked Tyler Linderbaum in Buffalo Bills win over Raiders
summary: Deone Walker is probably going to be the antagonist in Tyler Linderbaum’s nightmares for a while. The Raiders made Linderbaum the NFL’s highest-paid center this offseason, inking him to a three-year, $81 million deal with $60M guaranteed at signing, and the Bills disruptive nose tackle demolished him for a large portion of Buffalo’s 33-30 win […]
full_text: Deone Walker is probably going to be the antagonist in Tyler Linderbaum’s nightmares for a while. The Raiders made Linderbaum the NFL’s highest-paid center this offseason, inking him to a three-year, $81 million deal with $60M guaranteed at signing, and the Bills disruptive nose tackle demolished him for a large portion of Buffalo’s 33-30 win over Las Vegas in Week 6. Now, Walker was only credited with one pressure on 30 pass-rush snaps, but he “won” his one-on-one reps with Linderbaum far more frequently than that, and he wreaked havoc against the Raiders run game, a ground attack that only averaged 3.3 yards per rush. With this film session, let’s start there, and I’ll begin with the most emphatic display of Walker’s dominance in this game: pic.twitter.com/d9NFwgQajG — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 19, 2026 What’s the appropriate response to that rep? Linderbaum had become an elite-level center during his time in Baltimore, before he signed the monster free-agent deal in Las Vegas. He routinely won with a tremendous combination of balance, agility, and power. Remember too, Linderbaum was an All-State wrestler in high school who famously pinned Tristan Wirfs back in a 2017 match between the future NFL offensive linemen. Walker tossed the 6’2”, 305-pound Linderbaum aside like he was a practice-squad long-snapper on that rep then wrapped up Mike Washington for a short gain. All-Pro level highlight there. At Iowa and early in his career with the Ravens, Linderbaum was a menace in the run game because of how rapidly he erupted out of his stance when either climbing the second level or getting to reach blocks across a gap. He regularly carried out those duties with ease. The movement element to his game is why Linderbaum was a first-round pick and a big reason why he signed such a lucrative deal in March. Linderbaum’s speciality was irrelevant here against Walker: pic.twitter.com/JudDp2cBMK — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 19, 2026 And that is the exact type of block on which the smaller but more explosive Linderbaum should get the better of Walker. The clear win for Buffalo’s second-year defensive tackle wasn’t a fluke. He had managed an even cleaner victory later in the game on a similar blocking concept that amounted to a tackle for loss: pic.twitter.com/zOVFpHskYr — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 19, 2026 I’m telling you — 6’6” and 345 should not be physically capable of shooting a gap like that on Linderbaum.No way, no how. But Walker did. The majority of his pass-rushing opportunities featured double teams. Yet when Walker was given a chance to rush man-on-man, he either freed himself from the block or caved the pocket in front of Kirk Cousins. This was the Raiders first offensive play of the game. Walker initially bull rushed Linderbaum, but take note of how he countered off it late it get a hand up near the throwing motion of Cousins: pic.twitter.com/6Ls3I0MsV0 — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 19, 2026 That’s a reasonably high-caliber rep for a defensive tackle who probably wasn’t credited with a pressure on the play. He has regularly still impacted the pocket even when he’s been technically blocked. And check this rep from Walker going full Swim Diesel on Linderbaum to force a hurried throw and incompletion from the Raiders veteran quarterback: pic.twitter.com/zUPijGwLRv — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) October 19, 2026 Through six games — before Monday Night Football — there are only three defensive tackles with more pressures than Walker’s 22. He’s been a stalwart against the run too. At 22 years old, while playing 70.9% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps, Walker is playing like one of the best interior defensive linemen in football. His performance against the league’s highest-paid center should remind everyone of that.

title: Spitting and holding create setbacks for Buffalo Bills in win over Raiders
summary: Let’s address the elephant in the room; C.J. Gardner-Johnson’s disqualification. Both the DQ and suspension are completely warranted in my opinion, and for all the people who are saying we should cut they guy loose; I’m not opposed to that in the least (though I would defer to the locker room in his case). A […]
full_text: Let’s address the elephant in the room; C.J. Gardner-Johnson’s disqualification. Both the DQ and suspension are completely warranted in my opinion, and for all the people who are saying we should cut they guy loose; I’m not opposed to that in the least (though I would defer to the locker room in his case). A lot of penalties are problematic behavior, but this stands out to me if you care about my soapbox for a moment (if not, check out the charts and fun stuff below). Most penalties are truly “crap happens” events. High speed sport with a lot of complexities. Things happen. Throwing a punch, getting in a person’s face, and similar flags between the whistles are inherently more intentional. That applies to spitting as well. Perhaps doubly so. I don’t want to dismiss throwing a punch, but on some level in a sport as violent as football, it’s almost understandable that there’s an instinct to throw a punch or shove someone. I just don’t see that same instinctual aspect for spitting. It could be if you’ve done it a lot I suppose, but that isn’t exactly any better is it? There’s also the cultural aspect, with just about everyone agreeing how revolting it is. Put differently, it’s an act known to be shocking. That’s the whole point of it. Gardner-Johnson isn’t the worst person to ever wear the Bills uni, but this action was pretty bad. Now for your regularly scheduled penalty recap! Standard and Advanced Metrics Penalty Counts After the data-entry fest from last week, I’ll take average in a heartbeat. Both teams were right at the mark and from this chart, there’s really no significant separation between Buffalo and Las Vegas. I haven’t done a league average update in awhile and this might be a good time. Through six weeks, per team per game, the officials are tossing 1.35 more flags and assessing 1.25 more than last season. Now this should come down some, but I’m not super confident they’ll get back down to 2025 levels. Penalty Yards Similarly, there’s about ten more yards per team each game this season too. I’ll reiterate this gap should close some, but maybe not 10 yards worth. As for this game, The Bills are a little elevated compared to the league and the raiders, but nothing too crazy. Penalty Harm Las Vegas Raiders The Raiders just inched over the bad line with their seven flags, accumulating 11.0 Harm during the game. Looking at just the classifications, it makes some sense. You have the face mask call which starts at 1.5 for the 15 yards. Defensive pass interference can escalate quickly. In this case, Hezekiah Masses was called for a 13-yarder which also gave up a free down. Most of the stories here are pretty similar, with nothing too extravagant. Caleb Rogers was called for holding. That was ten yards assessed, an eight-yard pass to Bowers negated, and one down lost. Treydan Stukes was called for defensive holding, which starts with a five-yard assessment. Stukes’ flag came on third down and gave Buffalo two free chances. There’s one last fun thing which is more of a quirk. The false start on Linderbaum was not half the distance to the goal. They were on the Buffalo 13-yard line. Once in awhile, a flag has a rounding error on the play by play due to the spot being not quite exactly on the indicated yard-line. This may have prevented more points for the Raiders. Now faced with 4th & 5 instead of 4th & 1, the Raiders kicked a field goal rather than go for it and potentially convert for a fresh set of downs. Buffalo Bills Despite having quite a few more flags last week, the Bills exceeded the Harm rating in this game largely off the back of an offensive holding call from O’Cyrus Torrence. We’ll get back to that in a moment with my only remaining note on it for the moment being that it’s always fun to see a single flag really screw up the chart’s scale. That one flag is SOOOO out of whack, it’s hard to realize that Davison Igbinosun’s defensive holding flag is right up there with the worst of what was called on the Raiders. Igbinosun’s holding call was five yards and gave up two free downs. The defensive pass interference from Dee Alford was called for 22 yards and one down and was higher than any flag Las Vegas had on them all day. But it’s nothing compared to the one on O’Cyrus Torrence. For the formula lovers: 1.0 Harm for the ten assessed yards. 1.8 Harm for wiping out an 18-yard gain from Dawson Knox. The play scored a touchdown, and that’s treated as 7.0 Harm. The play was on fourth down and there was room to gain the first without the TD so I hold them accountable for that too. That’s 3.0 Harm for the downs they lost. Is it fair to Torrence accountable for all that? I think so. This literally took points off the board, which are never guaranteed to come back onto it. The Bills settled for a field which means this flag literally wiped four points out, never to be seen again…

title: Panthers vs Eagles game review: Milestones
summary: They can’t all be pretty. In fact, almost every game the Carolina Panthers have participated in this season has had a certain quality that only their fans can love. While the product on the field may have been ugly, there’s a certain aesthetic that having more wins than losses has that I think we can […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Bryce Young #9 of the Carolina Panthers looks to pass against the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images They can’t all be pretty. In fact, almost every game the Carolina Panthers have participated in this season has had a certain quality that only their fans can love. While the product on the field may have been ugly, there’s a certain aesthetic that having more wins than losses has that I think we can all appreciate. While taking down the Philadelphia Eagles in their own building was the main goal, the Panthers set some personal records while a handful of players also made some history. For this weeks game review, let’s take a look at some of the records, milestones, and other notable marks that were reached. Prior to kickoff, the Panthers social team put out a few things to watch with most coming to fruition. Some @Panthers notes and milestones to watch for in Week 6 at the Eagles. #KeepPounding pic.twitter.com/F4p2YsuibD — Carolina Panthers Football Communications (@PanthersFBComms) October 16, 2026 Bryce Young became the first quarterback in team history to have at least 250 passing yards and a touchdown pass in seven consecutive games and the first player in the NFL since 2013 to throw for at least 280 yards and a touchdown in the first five games of the season. The last two of three quarterbacks to accomplish the same feat won MVP – Aaron Rodgers in 2011 and Peyton Manning in 2013. Bryce Young in rarified air pic.twitter.com/XvFmHHeSxW — PFF (@PFF) October 19, 2026 On that note, the Young-led offense has score 146 points so far this season. This is the highest total through 5 games in team history, surpassing the old record of 135 set by Cam Newton and the 2015 Panthers on route to an MVP season and SB 50. Tetairoa McMillan’s six receptions has him tied with Kelvin Benjamin as the second fastest player in team history to reach 100 career receptions. While not my favorite career-trajectory comparison, it is impressive nonetheless. Speaking of great stats with frightening names tied to them, Ryan Fitzgerald’s first field goal of the afternoon made him the first kicker since big-legged Joey Slye to make the first 10 attempts in a season. Also, yes, Slye did also miss two extra points in that time. Of course, there was also JJ Jansen setting the record for most games played by a long snapper in NFL history. Only another 100 more games to go until breaking the record for most games played in NFL history . J.J. Jansen is now the all-time leader in games played for a long snapper! (282 games) 👏 @Panthers | #KeepPounding pic.twitter.com/wzwXEvR0ZC — NFL+ (@NFLPlus) October 18, 2026 Of course, it can’t all be positive. The Panthers also set the team record for most penalty yardage given up in a single game. A worrying trend as the team has been near the top in penalties for the entire season and after a bye week they decided that wasn’t enough. The #Panthers have set a new franchise for penalty yards in a game (144). Previous high was 120 against the Bucs in Week 2 of 2003. — Mike Kaye (@mike_e_kaye) October 18, 2026 One last one to close out the fun. For the schadenfreude enjoyers: by beating the Eagles, the Panthers contributed to the NFC East being the first division in NFL history to have all their teams go winless in back-to-back weeks. NFC East made history, going two straight weeks without a win. https://t.co/xMtbduIJio — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) October 20, 2026 It’s hard to ignore the positive vibes permeating the team and their performance. A history of disappointment is sure to keep a sliver of nagging doubt in the back of the mind, but when the team is making history – the good kind, not the tragic kind – it’s bound to get people excited. Let’s see how things play out when the Panthers take on the division rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers next week. Until then, keep pounding.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Jamari Johnson
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 26: Tight end Jamari Johnson (9) of the Oregon Ducks makes a one handed catch of the football in action during a game between the Oregon Ducks and the USC Trojans at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on September 26, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. (Photo by Robin Alam/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Oregon Ducks tight end Jamari Johnson. Bio Johnson (6’5”, 257 lbs.) was originally a high school quarterback who showed the versatility to play other positions, including receiver, running back, and defensive end. A fairly highly touted four star recruit, he originally joined the Louisville Cardinals for a couple years before transferring to Oregon. Despite sharing the spotlight with fellow tight end and eventual first round pick Kenyon Sadiq, Johnson managed to put up some solid numbers while providing good run blocking as an inline and slot option. He missed a couple games due to injury so far this season, but has still managed 17 catches for 224 yards and a couple scores in just four games played for the Ducks. Strengths/Weaknesses Johnson has elite size and enough athleticism to be a problem in the passing game. He has the speed and wiggle to average 16 yards per catch in 2025, making him one of the best downfield threats at tight end in the Draft. He is a willing and able run blocker and even showed reliability as a pass protector when called upon. Johnson has some versatility, lining up inline or flexed and consistently moving around the offense. While he does give good effort in the run blocking game, Johnson doesn’t get a whole lot of push. He’s mostly able to hold his ground, but he’ll need to improve his strength and technique at the point of attack in order to be a true three down, inline tight end at the next level. Johnson also benefits from Oregon’s offensive scheme, with almost none of his targets being classified as “contested” or “in traffic.” NFL defenders are able to make those windows smaller, so he’ll have to show he can make those types of plays with defenders in his personal space. Projection Jamari Johnson has the size, speed, and catch radius to be a problem over the middle of the field, especially in the intermediate and deep ranges. He’s not especially twitchy, but manages to get open and is a massive target. His blocking needs to improve, and his route tree is a bit limited, but the potential for a three down move tight end is definitely there. The Carolina Panthers have truly run a tight end by committee so far this season, with both Darren Waller and Tommy Tremble notching multi touchdown games. With Waller being on a one year deal and turning 34 last month, the Panthers could look to add to that room with another massive weapon for Bryce Young to target over the middle and in the redzone. Right now, Johnson is seen as a late first/early second round prospect by most outlets, though he could obviously shoot up boards with some big games and a good showing at the Combine in February. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Jamari Johnson is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
