title: Cowboys at Packers: Joey Porter Jr. makes his presence felt in tough loss
summary: Week 6 was seen as a turning point for the 2026 Dallas Cowboys. After an embarrassing home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 10 days earlier, Dallas discussed plenty of big-picture questions during its mini bye week. From the coaches and players, we heard this team was ready to turn the page and not let […]
full_text: (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Week 6 was seen as a turning point for the 2026 Dallas Cowboys. After an embarrassing home loss to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 10 days earlier, Dallas discussed plenty of big-picture questions during its mini bye week. From the coaches and players, we heard this team was ready to turn the page and not let their abysmal performance in Week 5 be a sign of things to come. There was some optimism heading into their matchup against the Green Bay Packers, but after a 23-13 loss in which the score was not indicative of how close the teams were on the field, that optimism seems to be all but gone. Dallas got both outperformed and outcoached in a big way on Sunday night. While their defense did perform a bit better, it still didn’t resemble anything close to even a league-average unit. To the shock of many, Dallas’ offense was even worse than the defense. Dak Prescott and company looked out of sync all night long as the Packers’ defense dominated the matchup. There weren’t many positives to take away from this game, but one lone bright spot was cornerback Joey Porter Jr. In his second game as a Cowboy, the former Steeler performed very well, earning him this week’s game ball award. In 28 coverage snaps, Porter did not allow a single reception, while posting an excellent 39.6 Passer Rating against. Porter also recorded an impressive PBU on a deep ball to Packers wideout Matthew Golden, saving Dallas’ defense from allowing another touchdown. Joey Porter Jr. was with him step-for-step DALvsGB on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/8AgCGjPZPp — NFL (@NFL) October 19, 2026 Joey Porter Jr is having a night! #SFSP pic.twitter.com/xcl0NEqKwc — Oliver Davis II (@I_Am_OD3) October 19, 2026 If there is one positive to come out of the Green Bay matchup, it’s that Joey Porter Jr. looks like a true number one lockdown corner. If he can stay healthy and help slow down teams’ number-one offensive targets week in and week out, it will greatly help Daron Bland, Shavon Revel, and other members of Dallas’ secondary who have been struggling to this point in the season.

For Mike McCarthy (2020), Jason Garrett […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have only two wins through their first six games for just the 16th time in franchise history. Amazingly, and unfortunately, this has now been the case for them in back-to-back seasons. Brian Schottenheimer’s direct predecessors each oversaw only one start to a season of this variety. For Mike McCarthy (2020), Jason Garrett (2015), and Wade Phillips (2010) mid-October saw them lead the Cowboys to at least a hat trick’s worth of wins more often than not. Schottenheimer is the subject of great focus for the Cowboys right now and as a result some on the internet are wondering if the Cowboys could look to make a move. You will of course be shocked to learn that the team’s brass said that is in no way on their minds at the moment. Cowboys EVP Stephen Jones on @1053thefan said they “absolutely” believe in Brian Schottenheimer. “There’s not any question in Jerry and my mind. He has the team. There’s no question they want to go out there and execute and make things happen. Feel really good about our coaching… — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) October 19, 2026 You can file this under “what else are they supposed to say” as the Cowboys know that they are in a bad NFC East and could wind up winning it when this calendar year wraps. Even if that happens, it is hard to see how the critics will cool on Brian Schottenheimer. Winning does cure all, though. If you are curious what would happen if the wheels continued to fall off, it isn’t exactly the Cowboys’ style to fire coaches midseason. Heck, it isn’t even their style (relative to modern times) to fire them at all. Wade Phillips was the last head coach who the Cowboys paid to not work for them, and they infamously fired him after a Sunday Night Football loss to the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field. Sound familiar? As many have said over the last decade and a half, the Cowboys were clearly comfortable doing that then because they had what they saw to be as an obvious replacement on staff already in Jason Garrett. Garrett did become the next head coach, and he was never fired by the team. The Cowboys saw his contract through twice. It was after that second one came to an end that Dallas chose to simply not bring him back. They, as you know, brought in Mike McCarthy (who coincidentally delivered the final blow to Wade Phillips that fateful night at Lambeau) and he also saw his contract run through before he and the team went their separate ways. This leads us to our present time. Schottenheimer signed a four-year deal with the Cowboys when they brought him on in 2025. This means that he isn’t even halfway done which is why the historical context is necessary here. History says the Cowboys will hold. What do you think, though? Do you think it’s possible this is the time that they buck that trend? Or do you expect more of the same in that capacity?
author: RJ Ochoa

title: Cowboys news: Stephen Jones gives full support to Brian Schottenheimer
summary: The Dallas Cowboys came out against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday night needing a win in the worst way. Instead, the defense spent the first half looking like they didn’t learn anything from their previous loss, putting the team in a 17-0 hole. The offense never really fully woke up to respond, and anything […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Jerome Miron-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Dallas Cowboys came out against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday night needing a win in the worst way. Instead, the defense spent the first half looking like they didn’t learn anything from their previous loss, putting the team in a 17-0 hole. The offense never really fully woke up to respond, and anything they did do well was far too late, especially after two turnovers. This team being 2-4 as a result has called into question every single aspect of the coaching that’s supposed to have them prepared for gamedays, but isn’t right now. Stephen Jones says Brian Schottenheimer has full support of Cowboys’ ownership – Todd Archer, ESPN Brian Schottenheimer is on the hot seat as far as fans are concerned, but the Joneses say it isn’t so. Twenty-three games into his tenure as the Dallas Cowboys head coach, Brian Schottenheimer has a 9-13-1 record and the full support of ownership. “Absolutely. There’s not any question in Jerry’s and I’s mind,” executive vice president Stephen Jones said Monday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas. “He has the team. There’s no question they want to go out there and execute and make things happen. We feel really good … about our coaching staff. We just have to continue to evolve and get to a point where we can win these football games.” Cowboys’ Christian Parker hire looks worse than ever after Jonathan Gannon revenge game – Jerry Trotta, The Landry Hat Jonathan Gannon continues to dominate the Cowboys offense every time he gets a chance to coach against it. Gannon had already built a long track record of coaching successful defenses, most notably in Philadelphia. The Eagles fielded one of the NFL’s best defenses during their run to the Super Bowl in 2022, and he had Arizona punching above its weight class for most of his tenure. One variable the Cowboys clearly overlooked was Gannon’s history against Dak Prescott. There’s a misconception that Vic Fangio gives Prescott the most fits of any defensive play-caller, when Gannon is actually the Prescott Stopper. Sunday night hammered that home . Pro Bowl WR blames ‘mid OC’ Schottenheimer for Cowboys’ struggles – Todd Brock, The Cowboys Wire The evidence is building that HC Brian Schottenheimer is simply in over his head right now. Much of the focus is starting to land on Schottenheimer as the offensive play-caller. Now 9-13-1 since taking the head coaching job in Dallas, many within Cowboys Nation are now openly calling for a change and wondering if Schottenheimer was ever the offensive mastermind he was marketed to be. Former NFL wide receiver Braylon Edwards pulled back the curtain in a social media post on Monday, leveling a shot directly at his onetime offensive coordinator: Watching the @dallascowboys struggle two weeks in a row reminded me of why we as a Jets offense were terrible in back to back afc championship games in '09' and '10'….mid OC by the name of Brian Schottenheimer. — Braylon Edwards (@OfficialBraylon) October 19, 2026 Brian Schottenheimer: Cowboys offense ‘a little bit one-sided,’ needs balance – Todd Archer, ESPN.com Getting the ball to George Pickens and CeeDee Lamb shouldn’t be as hard as it is right now. Prescott averaged just 4.8 yards per attempt (34-of-54, 258 yards) with two interceptions. It was the first time he averaged fewer than 5 yards per attempt and had multiple interceptions since Week 3 of the 2018 season against the Seattle Seahawks . The normally reliable connections with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens were off. Prescott completed only 15 of 29 throws to the duo, and both of the turnovers were on throws to Lamb, who slipped on his route leading to the second pick. Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Cowboys offensive game plan has become predictable – Shane Taylor, Inside The Star The Cowboys should expect to see a heavy dose of blitzes until they show they have an answer for it. Over the last two weeks, against the Buccaneers (43.9% blitz rate, the third-highest in the NFL) and the Packers (33.9%, tied for the 10th-highest in the NFL), he got completely out classes the last two weeks by a defensive play caller. This coaching staff had 10 days to prepare for this game, and you saw no adjustments to free blitzes, pressure on every drop back, launching the ball off the back foot. Dee Winters to miss time, DeMarvion Overshown gets major update from Cowboys – Patrik Walker, DallasCowboys.com The Cowboys will likely have a revolving door at linebacker, with Dee Winters missing time and DeMarvion Overshown ready to return. n return, for the first time since going down with a hamstring injury in Week 1 against the New York Giants, linebacker DeMarvion Overshown has “a great chance” at taking the field after rehabbing over the past five games. Furthermore, to answer the riddle of if he’d return to the green dot/middle linebacker/MIKE role, Jones made it known that will not be the case. Overshown is expected to take the spot vacated by Winters alongside rookie third-round pick Jaishawn Barham, the owner of the green dot and MIKE LB role since Overshown’s injury in mid-September.

title: The Cowboys completely abandoned the run in Green Bay
summary: The Dallas Cowboys were quite pass heavy as things wore on in the second half on Sunday night. To be clear, the Cowboys appeared rather outmatched in an overall sense. Based on how they played it feels fair to say that they were always going to lose that game, but their decision-making as it wore […]
full_text: Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys were quite pass heavy as things wore on in the second half on Sunday night. To be clear, the Cowboys appeared rather outmatched in an overall sense. Based on how they played it feels fair to say that they were always going to lose that game, but their decision-making as it wore on was certainly a bit suspect. Consider that the Cowboys did make it close, though. They scored by way of Javonte Williams with 9:24 left in the third quarter and trailed 17-7. Plenty of time left. At this point the Cowboys offense became incredibly one-dimensional, though. Below are their final 40 plays on offense. You will notice a common theme. Possession: Pass Pass Pass Pass (Punt after) Possession: Bad snap Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass (Turnover on Downs) Possession: Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Sack Pass Pass Pass (Turnover on Downs) Possession: Pass Pass Run Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass Pass (TD) Pass (Failed 2-Point) To be very clear, diluting what happened down to “pass” or “run” is a silly concept as football is more complicated than that. But the purpose here was to show that across their final 40 plays the Cowboys threw the ball 39 times. That isn’t sustainable. It was a horrible plan. The Packers entered this game with the league’s 17th-ranked defense in rushing efficiency, courtesy of NFL Pro. Look at their key advantages graphic and breakdown of how the Cowboys offense fared (theoretically) against the Packers defense from a rushing perspective. Obviously the context of the game matters and things were not exactly working out for the Cowboys offense at the time in question that they abandoned the run. But the argument here isn’t that things should have been 39-1 flipped the other way. The argument is that 39-1 is not practical in any amalgamation. The Cowboys seemed to panic and tried to hope that something would hit in the air. That was not the case, and they wound up losing in tough fashion.

title: Cowboys at Packers Stock Report: Brian Schottenheimer leads latest downward trend
summary: The Dallas Cowboys were never really competitive on Sunday night at Lambeau Field. Sure, they technically were close at one point in time. The scoreboard says they “only” lost by 10 points. But anybody who watched that game knows that Dallas was getting beat soundly from start to finish. In a matter of serious frustration, […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys were never really competitive on Sunday night at Lambeau Field. Sure, they technically were close at one point in time. The scoreboard says they “only” lost by 10 points. But anybody who watched that game knows that Dallas was getting beat soundly from start to finish. In a matter of serious frustration, this is the second week in a row where this was the case. The Cowboys are at a crossroads right now. Are they going to continue to be the lifeless version that we are seeing on a week to week basis? I suppose that since they keep offering it they are choosing to answer that way. Whatever the case, here is our Stock Report following Sunday’s loss. It is, shocker here, not fun. Stock Down: Brian Schottenheimer What is unique about this moment is that the Cowboys had the mini-bye to prepare for this game. Obviously the goal was to win, but if they had shown fight then at least you could make an argument that they were prepared and simply fell short. That was not the case. This team looks flat and like it lacks leadership, so the leadership is in serious question. Stock Down: Dak Prescott This was certainly one of the worst games of Dak Prescott’s career. What happened to the version of Dak that excelled against the blitz? Maybe defenses have figured out a way to neutralize what he took advantage of, but right now it has seriously become the quarterback’s kryptonite. A lot went wrong. But the franchise quarterback being a part of that is never a good thing. Stock Down: Klayton Adams It feels like Klayton Adams has seen others around him take more heat given that he is the offensive coordinator who doesn’t call plays. Well, what does he do then? I ask this respectfully. Before, Adams was helpful in coordinating the run game and setting things up in that fashion. The run game is a serious problem. So what is it that he is overseeing right now? That question needs answering. Stock Down: Terence Steele We are again stating the obvious, but the Cowboys have a serious problem on the right side of their offensive line. Terence Steele is actively limiting the potential of the offense as a whole. This is where it would be nice to see Klayton Adams help out. Stock Down: Christian Parker After the game it seemed like a lot of people “felt like” the Cowboys defense did a better job in the second half. The bar is low here, but I kind of agreed with that in the moment. With some time to reflect it seems this really wasn’t the case. Even if it was, the Cowboys defense hardly had a good night. Look how they were obliterated on money downs specifically. The Cowboys' defense on first and second down vs. third and fourth down last night: pic.twitter.com/kEQZZXL5xP — Bobby Belt (@BobbyBeltTX) October 19, 2026 What’s more is that the Packers kept seeing their star receivers drop what would have been huge gains or touchdowns. The point here is that things could/should have been much worse for the Cowboys defense and that is Christian Parker’s territory. Parker’s public approval rating is as low as it can get these days. The Cowboys are in a spot where they need consistency on that side of the ball. But this is so bad. Stock Down: Caleb Downs Early in this game the Cowboys saw their rookie getting picked on. On one hand it feels unfair to expect Downs to be elite right away, but on the other, that was sort of the expectation based on who he was in college. It can’t be both ways. Downs has to find a way to catch up to the NFL level. Right now that has yet to fully take. Stock Down: Jaishawn Barham Similarly, it is hard to say that a rookie, third-round pick should be tasked with saving the Cowboys defense. This becomes even more true when you remember that Barham had his hand in the ground a lot in college. But what we are seeing now is so far from the progress that Barham showed against Baltimore. He is another liability out there. Stock Down: Von Miller When the Cowboys signed Von Miller it was an awesome story. He is a legend of the state and it seemed like he had enough corporate knowledge to pass down to the young players across the roster. Has any of that happened? Right now Von Miller just looks like a shell of himself, and it’s not like the rest of the defense is looking incredible in the process. Stock Down: Donovan Ezeiruaku So much of this season’s hopes rested on Donovan Ezeiruaku taking a step in his second season. He actually saw his playtime diminished in this game in favor of rookie Malachi Lawrence for any indication on how that process is going. The Cowboys are in the worst need for pass rush help. Ezeiruaku has to provide it. Some of it. Any kind of it. Stock Up: Brevyn Spann-Ford At the very least the Cowboys appeared to get some stable and solid production out of Spann-Ford. This was one of their “we are going to make some changes!” moves that seemed to produce legitimate fruit. Maybe the others will someday, too.
author: RJ Ochoa

title: New problems surface as the Cowboys offense buckles under pressure
summary: The Dallas Cowboys provided another disappointing showing on Sunday night, losing to the Green Bay Packers, 23-13. The difficult part of this loss comes from the fact that the defense actually played okay. They struggled at times, which almost feels inevitable at this point, but they also gave their offense a fighting chance. The problem […]
full_text: Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys provided another disappointing showing on Sunday night, losing to the Green Bay Packers, 23-13. The difficult part of this loss comes from the fact that the defense actually played okay. They struggled at times, which almost feels inevitable at this point, but they also gave their offense a fighting chance. The problem is that the Cowboys’ offense had no fight in them. What went wrong? To get a better sense of the issues in this game, let’s take a closer look at what happened in this game. The game started well with an eight-yard gain from Javonte Williams after Tyler Booker pushed into the second level with a great block. But a second-and-short became a third-and-long when Terence Steele completely whiffed on a block, and Williams was taken down in the backfield for a two-yard loss. This set up the first of what we would see all night, a Packers blitz getting in the face of Dak Prescott. Fortunately, Prescott read it quickly and fired a perfect pass to Ryan Flournoy to convert on third down. It was a good conversion. Things looked promising, but little did we know that those moments faded quickly. A minimal gain bootleg and running play set them up with another 3rd-and-4. The Packers again showed blitz, only this time the defenders dropped back into coverage. Prescott panicked and quickly swung it out to Williams, who had absolutely no chance. Just like that, the Cowboys’ first drive had stalled. After the Packers strolled 90 yards to take an early 7-0 lead, the offense needed to answer back, but what did they do instead? False start. Illegal man downfield. Right away, they are in a 1st-and-20 hole thanks to two penalties by the offensive line. After a couple of short checkdowns, the Cowboys came up short on third-and-long after facing yet another Packers blitz. The game had just started, and already we saw a big problem. The Packers’ defense had a good game plan. The Cowboys offense did not. In an unexpected turn, the defense came up with a huge takeaway, giving the ball back to Dallas in Packers territory. This was the break the team needed. Quickly, another tackle-for-loss running play puts them in another third down, but they convert. But after a first-down run went nowhere, the offense is forced to pass, and Prescott again came under fire. A linebacker blitz shook him after Prescott took a shot to the ribs. Then, a panicked Prescott didn’t see the defender drop back into coverage to jump a pass intended for CeeDee Lamb near the goal line. A chance for a game-tying touchdown turned into no points. After the pick, the Packers offense drove all the way down the field, however, the defense made a great goal line stand thanks to clutch defensive plays by Quinnen Williams and Malik Hooker. The Cowboys defense picked a great time to make their first stop on third down, and Green Bay had to settle for a field goal. The game was still within reason. The Cowboys offense then put together their best drive so far with a couple of decent runs and Dak throwing on the move. The best play from this series came when Prescott evaded a pass rusher and found George Pickens downfield. Finally, something good was about to happen. But no sooner did that feeling enter our souls than did it immediately escape when Lamb slipped coming out of his break, causing a perfectly thrown ball to go into the hands of a Packers defender. Once again, a red zone opportunity turns into a whole lotta nada for the Cowboys. The Packers offense again marched down the field with a well-executed two-minute drive finished off by a Jordan Love quarterback sneak. An entire half of football was played, and the Cowboys did not score a single point. It was 17-0, and the Packers got the ball to open the second half. The game was slipping away. In a surprise twist, the second half started fantastically. The Cowboys defense forced a quick three-and-out, and even sent the Packers backwards thanks to a Kenny Clark sack near the goal line. After a nice return from Jonathan Mingo, the Cowboys started their first possession of the second half inside Packers territory. The offense finally capitalized on an opportunity. It took a fourth-down conversion to Lamb, who had wisely changed his cleats, and some physical plays by Williams and Brevyn Spann-Ford, but the Cowboys punched it in, and suddenly they had life again. The mood started to shift, but we have seen this before. In fact, we have seen this quite a lot lately. The team starts slowly, falls into despair, and then finally shows some life and starts to climb back into the game. Was the stage set for another one of these dramatic comeback attempts? Could the defense honestly make enough stops to give their offense a chance? What happened next is hard to explain. The defense did give them a chance. The Packers never scored another touchdown. They kicked two field goals, putting them at 23 total points, but shockingly, that was more than enough to easily secure the victory for Green Bay. What had happened to the Cowboys’ offense? Their ensuing possessions looked eerily similar to what we saw early in the game. Can’t run the ball. Repeatedly throwing way short of the sticks. Blitz coming. Dak’s in trouble. It was a recurring nightmare. Prescott had to take what the defense gave up, constantly pulling up short. When he did go deeper, a defender was right in the hip pocket of the receiver, ready to come away with more interceptions. The running game had completely vanished, and the Cowboys always found themselves in third-and-long situations, allowing the Packers’ defense to pin their ears back and come after Dak. The Cowboys struggled to pick up where the Packers’ blitz was coming from as they disguised it very well. This caused us to repeatedly hear the announcer say, “Dak hit as he throws.” It felt like the Cowboys’ biggest gains came when Green Bay was tagged for roughing the passer, which happened three times. Dak was a sitting duck back there. It was really difficult to watch. Despite having two great receivers and a talented quarterback, the offense could not come up with anything. They did score a garbage-time touchdown with 44 seconds left in the game, but they could not land the two-point conversion, basically ending the game. The Cowboys need to figure out how to attack better in space. Based on what we have seen over the past two games, opposing defenses have picked up on tendencies and are exploiting areas that Dak and the offense are struggling with. And that is not going to end until the Cowboys offensive coaches come up with an effective counter. It is very unfortunate that the Cowboys wasted the best performance by the defense and gave away a very winnable game. Failing to execute when it is clear they have talent is a huge indicator that the coaching staff is failing them, and now it is no longer limited to just the defensive side of the ball.
author: Dan Rogers

title: Cowboys at Packers: The good, the bad, and the ugly from Week 6
summary: The Dallas Cowboys disappointing 2026 season continues after the 23-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers in Week 6. The offense could never get anything going and defensively things continue to look bad. This team is performing well below expectations this year, and sadly, that could just be who they are. Only time will tell. […]
full_text: Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys disappointing 2026 season continues after the 23-13 loss to the Green Bay Packers in Week 6. The offense could never get anything going and defensively things continue to look bad. This team is performing well below expectations this year, and sadly, that could just be who they are. Only time will tell. This Week 6 matchup with the Packers was yet another example that talent doesn’t always equate to success. The Cowboys were outcoached and outplayed Sunday night, which is starting to become a reoccurring theme. This game was chock-full with more bad and ugly than good, but there’s still a chance to turn things around. Right!? THE GOOD – NFC East division still wide open Depending on the outcome of tonight’s game between the Washington Commanders and San Francisco 49ers on Monday Night Football, it’s looking as if the entire NFC East division will lose this week. That puts the Giants still first in the division at 3-2-1 with the Cowboys and Eagles right behind them at 2-4. This division is still wide open and up for grabs. There’s still a lot of football to play, but the Cowboys playoff hopes are still somehow alive despite how poorly they played. Maybe they can still turn this around and get on a hot streak at the right time. THE BAD – Christian Parker’s defense The Cowboys defense was victimized yet again Sunday night by Packers QB Jordan Love and Company, despite being much more aggressive than we’ve seen from them at any other point this season, Dallas’ defense still couldn’t make the plays needed to get off the field, especially on third down . Anytime Green Bay needed to convert on third at any distance, they seemed to do so easily to extend the drives. All we can do is hope that the return of Cobie Durant and Jalen Thompson to the lineup will help, otherwise this could be a problem the rest of the season. THE UGLY – Dak Prescott and Company For the second week in a row the Cowboys offense couldn’t get anything going on the ground or through the air. The Packers defense, much like Tampa Bay’s last week, continuously blitzed/applied pressure throughout the game making things difficult for Dak Prescott to find any of his weapons in the passing game. Brian Schottenheimer deserves some blame as well. His questionable playcalling isn’t helping things either. He didn’t adjust to the Packers pressure making No. 4 pretty much a fixed target. This is unacceptable considering the talent they have.
author: Brian Martin

title: Cowboys leave points on field at Packers, leave Lambeau on 2-game skid
summary: The notion that the Dallas Cowboys can never have all three phases of the game playing at least average football at the same time has never been more true. In their last two games, they’ve gone to the fourth quarter with ten points or less, and failed to pull out either game. Their latest loss […]
full_text: Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images | Getty Images The notion that the Dallas Cowboys can never have all three phases of the game playing at least average football at the same time has never been more true. In their last two games, they’ve gone to the fourth quarter with ten points or less, and failed to pull out either game. Their latest loss came at the Green Bay Packers on Sunday night, 23-13. The Cowboys turned the ball over twice in the second quarter, and the Packers scored ten points off of them to create the winning margin. These drives also saw the Packers hold the ball for over nine and a half minutes of the second quarter, and this came after Green Bay’s first offensive drive following a Dallas punt lasted 14 plays over six and a half minutes of game time and ended with a touchdown. The Cowboys found a way to even out the final time of possession battle in this game, but the early favor for the home team again made Brian Schottenheimer’s offense one-dimensional. This set up far too many situations where the game came down to Schotty’s play calling in the pass game versus Packers defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon’s scheming. Cowboys fans have already seen in these first two months of the season how such matchups have gone, against John Harbaugh to start the season, Jesse Minter, and before this game Todd Bowles. The only hope was that the extra time off after the embarrassing home loss to Bowles’ Tampa Bay Buccaneers last Thursday night would be the motivation needed for the coaching on offense to improve. Not only did this not happen, but the same woes against the blitz were evident all night from the Cowboys offense, something that used to be a strength of the passing game led by Dak Prescott. Let’s get to some notes on the loss. Over Packing For the second week in a row, the Cowboys made f ar too many things difficult on themselves and had to battle against their own mistakes in addition to the opponent. The Cowboys did well to give themselves life in this game out of the locker room, but by the fourth quarter felt like a desperately worn out team with not even close to enough juice to pull out a win. One of the most glaring areas the Cowboys are putting this on display is with the amount of plays they seemingly waste on offense. It’s gotten so bad that every highlight play is hardly a reason to cheer, and more so a chance to simply ask “why can’t we do that more often?”. The Cowboys chose to start the game on offense, and faced an immediate third and short. Going to a formation they had success with against the Bucs with running back Javonte Williams in to protect, they hit Ryan Flournoy over the middle to convert. This first down helped the Cowboys overcome a negative Williams run on second down the play prior. When faced with another third down right after Flournoy’s catch though, they used a play that we’ve highlighted time and time again as a drive killer, a pass behind the line of scrimmage to Williams. The Cowboys punted before either CeeDee Lamb or George Pickens ever got a target in this game, and although it wasn’t known yet, truly never connected with the game for the entire rest of the night from this point on – digging themselves a 17-0 hole by halftime. The closest Dallas came to showing life in this game was when Williams scored the first points of the night in the third quarter to make the score 17-7. Schottenheimer called Williams’ number to carry the ball exactly one time from this point on until the end of the game. This drive even featured Lamb moving the chains on fourth down with the stack release alongside Flournoy, but it was a Cowboys opponent that yet again put on a masterclass of dictating matchups and playing a game on their terms compared to how few and far between these types of plays were for the Cowboys. The late-game 4th-and-2 rollout to the left to cut the field in half for Prescott and throw a broken up pass intended for Lamb was also a headscratcher, and came after a third down where Dak and Lamb couldn’t beat the blitz with a short pass yet again. It took just one game for the Cowboys to go from their worst run/pass split of the entire Schottenheimer era against the Bucs for them to reset this with an even more dramatic split of 54 throws to 15 runs on Sunday night. Their offensive line is not built to be going backwards in pass protection this often without reps to flex their muscle in run blocking, and the Cowboys paid for it at both tackle spots against the Packers. Third Down & Dusted We came into this matchup highlighting the need for the Cowboys to win on third down, and they did not. The Cowboys defense was the perfect ‘get right’ defense for the Packers offense to go from the worst third-down offense to 11-18 on Sunday night. The Packers converted a 3rd-and-5, 3rd-and-13, and 3rd-and-13 again before scoring on 3rd-and-6 on Matthew Golden’s touchdown to jump ahead 7-0. Malik Hooker would make a 3rd-and-goal stop to hold the Packers to a field goal after this, which was a nice play from the veteran safety for a defense that again paid for it’s inexperience and youth in too many other spots this game (more on that later). Green Bay went right back to picking up 3rd-and-8 on a Joey Porter Jr. pass interference penalty and a 3rd-and-6 on a long scramble drill from Jordan Love running away from Donovan Ezeiruaku, capping this drive with the score that put them up 17-0. The other area the Cowboys failed yet again to help themselves in against an opponent that projected to give them a chance to do so was penalties, matching the Packers’ 11 penalties and having more penalty yards against. The Cowboys couldn’t even score late in the game on a drive extended with an illegal contact penalty on the defense on 3rd-and-20, interception called back by roughing the passer, and even a second roughing the passer call – all before a fourth down throwaway through the back of the endzone. Rookie Defenders It certainly wasn’t all bad for the Cowboys defense in this game, as they found their spots yet again to compete and try to keep an offense that was wasting one opportunity after another in the game. The Cowboys had Joey Porter Jr. back in the lineup at cornerback, and this made a difference in their coverage schemes being a lot tighter. They saw both Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark get a sack, with Clark’s forcing a very quick three and out to start the second half. Some of these positives felt like early returns on the Mike Pettine hire, but sticking with the theme we started this whole recap with, not enough good things can be true for the Cowboys all at one time. What cost the Cowboys defensively too much in this game was the play of three of their rookies, Jaishawn Barham, Caleb Downs, and Malachi Lawrence. Lawrence had the opportunity to start over Ezeiruaku, but as the game wore on there was plenty of both Ezeiruaku and Von Miller on the field, and no impact being felt from Lawrence to capitalize on this opportunity. Downs was forced into a coverage role much more than he should be in this game, and saw a volume of throws that comes with Porter forcing quarterbacks to often throw elsewhere. It was Downs that didn’t plaster to Golden on the scramble drill to set up Jordan Love’s rushing touchdown at the end of the first half. Finally, Barham didn’t get out to the flat route against TE Tucker Kraft on a key third down after the Cowboys cut the score to 17-7, extending a Packers drive that saw them build the lead to 20-7. He also whiffed on a tackle early in the game on third down that extended the Packers scoring drive. There was so much talk leading into this game about the Cowboys paying for inexperience in their coaching staff led by defensive coordinator Christian Parker, just to see some slight improvement here, but pay a price for starting rookie defenders. With Clark, Williams, and Porter making plays this game, at least the Cowboys shouldn’t be able to use their struggles this season as a…

title: Horse Tracks: Stop blaming Bo
summary: Good morning, Broncos Country! Everyone, just freakin’ relax on the QB play, will you? The second question at yesterday’s presser with Sean Payton was wondering if the head coach had considered replacing Bo Nix. What are you even talking about? I’m a big fan of Jarrett Stidham as our backup. If Nix goes down, he’s […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos walks off the field after winning in overtime against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field At Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images Good morning, Broncos Country! Everyone, just freakin’ relax on the QB play, will you? The second question at yesterday’s presser with Sean Payton was wondering if the head coach had considered replacing Bo Nix. What are you even talking about? I’m a big fan of Jarrett Stidham as our backup. If Nix goes down, he’s a very capable QB who knows Payton’s system (and that’s something!) and has enough experience to not be completely overwhelmed. But come on. Benching your starter when the entire offense (and the offensive coaching staff, mind you) is underperforming, is as close to knee-jerk as you can get. Nix is the starter, and struggling against a top-ranked defense is no reason to put in a backup who will likely fare no better, will probably fare worse, and will kill whatever morale is left with an offense that knows it has to do better and that one player is not the problem. Not the only problem anyway. Bo Nix may not be living up to his potential, but neither is Sean Payton or the entire offense. Don't blame Bo (only). But instead, enjoy this #Broncos ' defense AND 4-2! https://t.co/qZl83EQthQ — Doctor of Words (@docllv) October 18, 2026 Payton had a lot more patience than I would have with the benching question. “To answer your question, no. He’s going to become the byproduct of all the finer things that get improved,” Payton said, noting that better play from the O-line, better run-pass balance and better run game performance overall will go a long way in helping Nix. “That’s our jobs as coaches here. We talked after the game about we’re excited to get that win, and yet at the same time find that improvement we need in all areas. So, it starts with all of us.” Payton also played down that Nix was suffering from any mental hurdles after coming back from injury. “This is a tough league. We hit every aspect, and I think that’s one of the things that attracted us to Bo in the beginning is we had seen his ability to climb through adversity,” Payton added. “It’s not just Bo that feels that. Right now, offensively, I feel that, our players feel that and we’ll improve.” Immediately following the Broncos’ win over the Seahawks — and the ensuing meltdown from Ryan Fitzpatrick that provided great TV drama for a day — Tim Jenkins spoke the real truth. If anything, Broncos Country should be encouraged that this team is winning in spite of its underperforming offense. And he also pointed out several instances where just because the play didn’t develop as planned or designed, it didn’t mean it was due to poor QB play. And in response to Fitzpatrick’s primary criticism that Nix wasn’t “playing competitive football” because he didn’t get a first down one-on-one versus a 250-pound linebacker, Jenkins was all over it. “Would I love to see Nix make the linebacker miss one-on-one and get a first down? Sure. Who wouldn’t? Do I think that’s a fair criticism in the National Football League that a quarterback didn’t make a linebacker miss one-on-one? No,” he said. “That’s potentially the dumbest thing I’ve heard all day. And I have five kids 9 and under, so I hear dumb stuff all day long.” Ease up, Broncos Country. There’s a lot to fix, but they’ll get it done. Reminder what our QB can do… https://t.co/Tf6nt1ycWQ — Doctor of Words (@docllv) October 19, 2026

title: Broncos’ run game is terrible: who is to blame?
summary: With one game remaining in week six of the 2026 NFL season the Denver Broncos’ run game has been one of the worst in the NFL. The Broncos are 30th in yards per carry at 3.4. Only the Raiders (3.0) and the Packers (2.9) are worse. The Chiefs lead the league at 5.5. The Bronco […]
full_text: With one game remaining in week six of the 2026 NFL season the Denver Broncos’ run game has been one of the worst in the NFL. The Broncos are 30th in yards per carry at 3.4. Only the Raiders (3.0) and the Packers (2.9) are worse. The Chiefs lead the league at 5.5. The Bronco run game is tied for last (with four other teams) in terms of explosive runs (runs that gain 10 or more) at nine. The Bills lead the league with 31 . The only area where the Broncos have been moderately successful in the run game is converting on 3rd or 4th down and short (one or two yards needed). They have converted on ten of thirteen (77 percent). The Steelers lead the league at 100 percent (9 for 9), while the Seahawks have been worst (25 percent, 2 for 8). So where does the blame lie – with the running backs, or with the offensive line? We will look at three measures of how well the offensive line is run blocking and then a couple of advanced metrics on running back performance. Offensive Line SISdatahub.com has a stat called blown blocks and another called stuffs. A blown block is any time a blocker does not successfully block the defender they attempted to engage with and, as a result, gives the defender an opportunity to negatively affect the play. A stuff is when that blown block leads to a TFL for the defender that the blocker was supposed to block. A blown block can lead to a stuff, but does not have to if the ballcarrier avoids the tackler in the backfield. The Bronco OL has been doing a good job of not blowing blocks or getting stuffed according to SISdatahub.com. They have only 10 blown blocks in the run game and they have only have two stuffs. After six games, 15.5 percent of runs for the Broncos this season have gained 0 yards or lost yards. That is the 11th best value in the league. The Rams have been best at 11.9 percent and the Packers have been worst at 24.6 percent. So this tracks with what SIS is saying about the OL not getting abused, but how do we tell if they are getting any push in the run game (moving defenders off the LOS). That can be seen be average yards before RB contact on run plays which will be discussed after we see ESPN’s run block win rate. None of the Bronco OL guys are in the top 10 individually, and the team is average in both run block win rate and pass block win rate. If the OL is blocking well, running backs will get 2.5+ yards past the LOS before they are contacted by a defender. Currently the two leaders in yards before contact per attempt (YBC/Att) are James Cook at 3.92 and Kenneth Walker at 3.64. Among qualifiers, Quinshon Judkins has the lowest at 1.53. JK Dobbins is fifth lowest at 1.69. Correlation between YBC/att and success rate is high for sports stats at +0.54. It stands to reason, if you are getting good blocking (YBC/att will be higher with good blocking) you will have more successful runs. Runners at the top are getting hit at the or behind LOS often pic.twitter.com/DWB21gYaiO — Joe Mahoney (@ndjomo76) October 19, 2026 YBC is a function of the blocking of the OL and the elusiveness of running back. Yards after contact is all on the RB. Dobbins is currently getting 1.64 yards after contact per attempt. That is 16th of 41 qualifiers, so that is above average. The best RBs in the NFL are getting 2.5 or more yards after contact per carry. Those are Jaylen Warren (2.68), Walker (2.63), and Kyle Monangai (2.55). The four worst qualifiers are getting less than one yard after contact per carry. Those are Woody Marks (0.98), Tyler Allgeier (0.98), Marshawn Lloyd (0.81), and Kendre Miller (0.69). Success rate is another stat that can be used to compare running backs, although it can be hard to decouple it from blocking. A successful run on first down gains 40% of the needed yards, on second down it gains 60% of the needed yards, and on third or fourth down it converts. JK Dobbins has a success rate of 38.3 this season, which is tied for second to last among 41 runners (two QBs have enough carries to qualify – Josh Allen and Deshaun Watson). Only Lloyd has a lower success rate at 37.5 percent. Kyren Williams has the best success rate among RBs with a 60 percent – Josh Allen’s 62.5 percent leads all runners. For comparison, RJ Harvey has a 57.1 percent success rate (admittedly on only 21 carriers). Tyler Badie has a 66.7 percent on only six carries. Jonah Coleman has a 40 percent success rate on his ten runs. So all of the RBs who have carried the ball (omitting Adam Prentice’s one carry) have a better success rate than Dobbins, but he has more carries than the other three combined – 81 to 37. Dobbins 81 carriers have gained 270 yards – 3.33 yards per carry. The other RBs have gained 142 yards on their 37 carries – 3.84 yards per carry. While that is not great, it is still half a yard per carry better than Dobbins. Dobbins does have the only broken tackle in the running game among the running backs. However, one broken tackle on 81 carries is poor. Kenneth Walker has 12 broken tackles (not all against Denver) on 106 carries – one broken tackle every 8.9 carries . Only Blake Corum and TreVeyon Henderson have zero broken tackles in the run game among qualifying RBs. Conclusion Looking at all the data, I would put the majority of the blame for the feckless Bronco run game on JK Dobbins. The OL has not been great by any stretch, but they appear to be average in run blocking. So a competent running back should be getting better results behind them. Dobbins has been one of the worst primary ballcarriers in the NFL so far this season. The fact that Harvey, Coleman and Badie have all gotten better results than he has points the finger at JK and not at the OL. I should also mention that the play calling could be having an effect, but the defense is not. Dobbins is facing an 8-man box on only 17.3 percent of his runs according to NFL nextgen stats. That is one of the lower values in the league. So he (and the OL) are failing to run the ball effectively against light boxes. Defenses are daring the Broncos to run because they know they can stop the run game without committing a safety to the run. Kendre Miller is facing a heavy box at twice the rate that Dobbins is. Dobbins is also taking 2.98s per run to get to the LOS (TLOS). This is the sixth highest TLOS in the league, but this is not necessarily a bad thing as Kyren Williams, Jeremiyah Love and Saquon Barkley all take about the same amount of time to get to the LOS. Keaton Mitchell’s 3.18 is the highest while Chris Rodriguez Jr.‘s 2.44 seconds is the lowest. For what it’s worth, there is no correlation between TLOS and YPC or between TLOS and RYOE/att. RYOE is rushing yards over expected.

title: Broncos vs. Seahawks: The No Bull Review
summary: We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love.  Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - OCTOBER 15: Kris Abrams-Draine #31 celebrates with Ja'Quan McMillian #29 of the Denver Broncos after securing an interception during the fourth quarter of an NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Empower Field at Mile High on October 15, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re a finicky bunch here in Broncos Country. Also, the media is always a fickle bunch of knee-jerk creatures with little to no nuance for this game that we love. Let me lay some No Bull truth down for you all that can hopefully talk some of you back from the ledge into wading into the abyss about Bo Nix and the offensive woes that Fitz-ception and the rest of the talking heads are freaking out about. Credit where it is due The #1 thing that everyone who’s trying to dump on Bo Nix right now is forgetting is that the Seattle Seahawks have an absolutely fierce defense that matches up VERY well against our offense. Their front is one of the best in the game. They schematically crush average run games (and let’s be honest, ours is not average: it is poor). They also make it extremely hard on the back end to complete deep passes. Everyone wants to talk about how bad Nix is, but has absolutely no clue about what happened on the film. I do not have access to All-22, but I can tell you there were NOT people open against that defense. When the broadcast did show us the better angles, our receivers were smothered outside of one singular play. Dial back the perspective a little wider. We just played 6 of the toughest defenses in the NFL, and our two losses came to two of the undefeated teams as it stands today: the 49ers and Chiefs. This game was never going to be pretty offensively. This 6-game stretch was never going to be roses and touchdowns. Perspective is needed Let’s be better fans and think a little deeper. We’ve seen so much of this story before. Bo Nix struggled just as badly last season, the same way early in the season. We looked terrible in a Thursday night game last season. This run game is a stinking hot one and a half-foot-wide cow patty, and our wide receivers are very much overrated and inconsistent. Thinking back a little further, I saw this same story back in the 2015 season. I think a lot of you have forgotten just how pathetic the offense was under Peyton Manning and Brock Osweiler that season. That team got dragged by the defense all the way to the Super Bowl. Take a deep breath, Broncos Country. Uncle Sadaraine is here to tell you this season is not in danger…it is actually just getting started. More on that when we wrap up. For now, let’s dig into reviewing this game. Offense While I love to see a coach dedicated to the run game, I am getting quite uncomfortable with how much we lean into a part of the game that performs so poorly. We ran into 8 and 9-man boxes (loosely…you could say the safety was out of the box, but he was only out by one friggin step) multiple times. I do not understand how this offense wasn’t dialing up a quick slant / out or a play-action audible more often. Either the players aren’t capable of adjusting on the field for whatever strange reason, or Payton doesn’t trust them to execute (or both). But we had many 2 and less yard gains because of running into stacked boxes with a back who looks completely washed and a line that is inconsistent at executing their blocks. Yes, we made 2 drives work with a run game that churned out production. But when that dried up, they just kept hitting the same buttons hoping for it to finally work. It was absolute insanity through the 3rd and 4th quarters. One problem I saw was a problem with design. In the 4th quarter on 3rd and 10, the play design was absolutely mind-boggling to the side Nix was reading. Both outside routes Nix was looking at were in-breaking next to each other with a safety over the top. There was no space for him to find a play to throw to. Just have those guys scissor and give your quarterback a read to throw to one-on-one. They can’t keep a safety over both if you do that. Quarterbacks Bo Nix is not broken. He has regressed this season at some level, but I do expect that at some level when his offseason was spent recovering from a broken ankle and 2nd surgery. I know Broncos Country is absolutely coo coo for Cocoa Puffs when it comes to quarterback play, but you all need to ease up. This is only his 3rd year, and he did NOT have a full offseason to sharpen his skill set. I’m not saying he’s a great quarterback. I think he’s looking average at best. But when we think about how many good defenses he’s been facing, I have to think there’s a really great opportunity in front of him to start rounding into form as the season wears on. I do get frustrated on 3rd down after 3rd down with him not producing something, but I’d love someone to show me all the opportunities he missed because they sure as hell didn’t look to me to be there when we did get coverage angles. Line This line had a good half with really well-executed blocks for two touchdown drives. As the game wore on, they wore down, and the play got choppy up front (especially in the run plays). They ran power a few times that were as good as you will see in the NFL this weekend. I was rather disappointed with Luke Wattenburgh’s bad snap. At what point will he play like a long-term starting center? Running Backs RJ Harvey is the one guy on the offense that is playing inspired football. He’s only getting a couple of handfuls of touches each game, but he’s making them count. He executed a great screen play with a great block from Wattenburg out in space for a 16-yard gain. Later on the same drive, he pulled off another to get the ball inside the 10. He also converted a 3rd and 1 out of shotgun by shooting to the outside. He took a wild cat snap to the house for the 2nd touchdown of the game. He finished with 6 runs for 25 yards (4.2 ypc) and 3 catches on 4 targets for 31 yards. We’re going to go way back with JK Dobbins to spit some No Bull truth this week. JK Dobbins is Lance Ball. He’s a guy we’re feeding who knows the offense but just doesn’t bring anything worthwhile to the table. His touchdown run was a credit to the line (one of their best blocked plays of the game). He had one good run for 16 yards where he actually jump-stepped to avoid a tackle for 16 yards. But he only created 41 yards on 17 carries (2.4 ypc). Without that one 16-yard run, he was 16 for 25, which is 1.57 ypc. This is honestly dog shit production from a running back. The SECOND that Jonah Coleman gets back, he should get a start over Dobbins or Tyler Badie. Dobbins is a detriment to this offense and should be treated as such. He’s supposed to be a power back who can power through tackles, and I just don’t see that in his game this year. Let’s throw in some credit to Tyler Badie for his big conversion on 4th and 3 behind Meinerz and McGlinchey. It was a shame he got injured and was out of the game, as I think he deserves more opportunities given what we’ve seen in front of him so far this season. Receivers None of our receivers are worthy of anything positive this week. They got owned by and large the whole game and did not create separation to give Nix options. Cortland Sutton dropped a pass that hit him in the hands. Jaylen Waddle got dinged up and finished the game, but was only 4 out of 7 targets for 24 yards. The receivers and tight ends were smothered by the Seahawks defense and did not find a way to fight that got them openings. Defense Vance Joseph and this defense deserve all the credit in the world for this win. They were a salient force that does not get enough credit for how well they have been playing. JSN is the Seahawks’ offense. He got his 134 yards on 12 receptions. I will take that all day, and I’m not even kidding. Vance had his guys play a mix of off coverage or press with a safety over the top and set things up so that JSN was never allowed to get a ton of space to work…

title: Detroit Lions bye week evaluation: Is the team really on the rise?
summary: One of the more interesting comments from Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell on Monday was his level of optimism at the bye week compared to last year. Even though Detroit had come off a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to move to 5-2 last year, Campbell said he feels better about this season […]
full_text: Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff leads the team onto the field from the tunnel for the first half against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Arizona on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co One of the more interesting comments from Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell on Monday was his level of optimism at the bye week compared to last year. Even though Detroit had come off a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers to move to 5-2 last year, Campbell said he feels better about this season because of the youth and growth already shown through five games. “In some regards I feel better going into this bye than even I did last year because I know we’re ascending and we’re young and we’re growing and that’s exciting,” Campbell said. “Sometimes you feel like you’re topped off and maybe you’re beginning to deteriorate because of issues worn down, age, whatever it is. “So that’s exciting. I do feel like we’re on the rise here a little bit. We’ve just got to keep getting better. We’ve got to keep testing ourselves. And look, we’re in for the long haul now and it’s really about to get geared up and the competition is about to really raise up another level, and it starts with Green Bay.” But is that optimism actually warranted? Is this team’s future far more bright than the one that finished 9-8 and out of the playoffs last year? On this week’s PODcast, we re-evaluate how the team has played through five games. What have they done well? What have they struggled with? What successes are likely to continue through January, and which struggles could actually improve in the back half of the season? Last year, John Morton led the highest-scoring offense in the league through the first couple months. What is different about this season that could keep the offense efficient throughout the entire year? And what hope is there that the Lions defense can turn things around? In the last portion of the PODcast, we discuss the outlook of the NFC North and the overall NFC, and where the Lions fall in the clutter. title: Film study: Packers’ deep passing attack is a paper tiger
summary: The Detroit Lions (3-2) will take on their first divisional opponent in Week 7 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) come to Ford Field Sunday afternoon fresh off two big wins. Let’s just get straight to the point and talk about the elephant in the room. All eyes will be on the Lions defense—and particularly […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions cornerback Keith Abney II (6) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Detroit Lions (3-2) will take on their first divisional opponent in Week 7 as the Green Bay Packers (4-2) come to Ford Field Sunday afternoon fresh off two big wins. Let’s just get straight to the point and talk about the elephant in the room. All eyes will be on the Lions defense—and particularly the secondary—as it takes on the Packers’ passing attack. Headed into Week 6, the Packers boasted the fourth-highest explosive play rate in passing offense while the Lions defense checked in at 17th, despite giving up a league-high 297.4 passing yards per game. Offensive and defensive explosive play rates: The Bills offense is very good pic.twitter.com/Dr7YFUrYSn — Sam Hoppen (@SamHoppen) October 13, 2026 The mission of this film study is to generate a scouting report aimed at diagnosing what patterns and tendencies, if any, the Packers have shown in their deep passing game and what that means for the Lions defense. So I watched all 32 of the Packers’ pass attempts of 20+ air yards and came away with some interesting insights. Packers’ aggression comes overwhelmingly in comfortable game scripts The first and most critical tendency to take note of is that, per NFL Pro , of the 32 passes of 20+ air yards or more attempted this season, only four have come while trailing their opponent. In fact, all four of these passes came in a single game: Week 3 against the Atlanta Falcons. Digging even deeper, two of the four occurred after the two-minute warning in the fourth quarter, when the Packers were down by a score of 35-14. Further, all four pass attempts were incomplete. Okay, but surely this could be misleading, and the Packers have just played with either a tie or lead in many games, much like we say on “Sunday Night Football” against the Dallas Cowboys? Not really. Quarterback Jordan Love has attempted 60 passes this season while the team has been behind in score. I’ll do the math for you. That is only a 6.67% deep pass rate while trailing. Compare that to 16 deep passes attempted while the Packers are playing with the lead on 103 total passing attempts with a lead. That’s 15.5%. Okay, but surely this is just a small sample size trend, right? Not really. To further magnify the situational shift in play calling, the Packers have attempted short passes of under 10 air yards 64 times on 103 pass plays (62.2%) with the lead compared to 44 times on 60 pass plays (73.3%) while trailing. Head coach Matt LaFleur clearly has a tendency toward paradoxical aggression. He tends to take risks when he’s living in advantageous game scripts, but his focus shifts to a low-risk approach when the game script pressure turns up. This creates a perception of the deep passing game being a strength, but the reality is it’s more of a “kill shot” tool, and when it rains, it pours. Compare that to Lions offensive coordinator and Drew Petzing and Jared Goff, who have executed the same number of deep passes of 20+ air yards or more (6) when trailing in score as when leading in score, showing no situational tendency so far in 2026’s early sample size. For the Lions to avoid falling victim in the explosive passing game, the key to winning here is to score early and play with a lead. Packers’ aggression comes overwhelmingly in certain down-and-distances The second critical tendency to take note of is that, per NFL Pro , the Packers rarely throw the deep ball in short-to-medium yards-to-go situations, especially on second down. Of the 32 passes of 20+ air yards or more, they break down in the following downs and distances: first-and-10 (11) third-and-long (7+ yards) (9) second-and-long (7+ yards) (6) third-and-medium/short (0-6 yards) (4) second-and-medium (4-6 yards) (2) second-and-short (0-3 yards) (0) The key insight here is that LaFleur’s play calling tends not to take advantage of “waste” downs, which I would categorize as the second-and-short/medium range to take shots down the field. Of the two deep passes noted in second-and-medium situations, both were against Dallas in Week 6 and were second-and-6s from inside the Dallas 26-yard line. It is interesting that LaFleur likes to take risks predominantly with the lead, but does not feel comfortable taking the same risks in advantageous down-and-distance situations. Packers’ deep ball success is feast or famine The third critical insight in the Packers’ deep passing game is that its success is remarkably feast or famine. Overall, Jordan Love has completed 10-of-32 (31%) deep passes of 20+ air yards. But six of those 10 completions came in a single game: Week 5 against the Chicago Bears, where Love went 6-for-8 on deep passes. In three games, Love did not complete a single deep pass (0-for-3 vs the New York Jets, 0-for-7 vs the Atlanta Falcons, and 0-for-6 vs the Dallas Cowboys). Without the Week 5 explosion week, the Packers are just 4-for-26 (15.8%) on deep passes on the season. So what happened against the Bears? Five of the eight deep passes against Chicago came on first-and-10 situations, four of which were play-action passes. Below is the first. This is a simple two-man fade-out combination route. If the quarterback sees Cover-3, the out is opened under the outside fade. But in this case, the Bears are in Cover-2, where the deep, field-side safety is responsible for the outside fade. The Bears safety is caught with dirty eyes in the backfield and flat-footed, a huge missed execution play leading to the Green Bay touchdown that should not have been so easy. If the Lions rookie Keith Abney gets more snaps at the free safety spot this week, expect the Packers to test his eyes. A key point in the above clip is that the play design is also a simple single read for Jordan Love. On the two-man route concept, it’s not a strenuous progression with both routes to the same side of the field. Similarly, below is another simple single read concept with the core routes all to the field-side of the formation. LaFleur is not asking a lot of Love with either of these concepts. To his credit, Love executes this with great timing and ball placement before Bears’ rookie safety Dillon Theineman (31) can close the gap in the zone. Overall thoughts The Lions’ passing defense has not been great against deep passes this year, giving up 12 completions on 22 attempts. But outside of the Bears game, the Packers are not an unstoppable force in this area either. In addition to the tendencies discussed already, it’s clear that Love has his favorites, with 14-of-32 deep targets going to Matthew Golden and 10-of-32 going to Christian Watson. It will be interesting to see if defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard deploys any similarly unique coverages against the Packers as he did against the Arizona Cardinals . Lastly, Love does not seem to be impacted one way or the other when it comes to handling pressure in his deep passing ability, as he is 4-of-16 while under pressure and 6-of-16 while kept clean. Score early. Play with a lead. Don’t play with dirty eyes.

title: Discussion: How should the Detroit Lions handle Cade Mays’ return?
summary: On Monday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell announced the impending return of two key players. Barring some unforeseen setback, starting center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch will make their 2026 debuts on Sunday afternoon against the Green Bay Packers. For Branch, his return is pretty simple. While it sounds like the Lions will limit […]
full_text: Jun 17, 2026; Detroit, MI, USA; Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) gets ready to take a snap from center Cade Mays (64) during the Detroit Lions veteran’s minicamp at the Allen Park Training Facility. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect On Monday, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell announced the impending return of two key players. Barring some unforeseen setback, starting center Cade Mays and safety Brian Branch will make their 2026 debuts on Sunday afternoon against the Green Bay Packers. For Branch, his return is pretty simple. While it sounds like the Lions will limit his reps a bit, Campbell seemed confident the Pro Bowl safety can take on a significant role, and his presence will be welcomed in a secondary that has struggled through five games. Mays’ situation is far more complicated. For one, unlike safety, it’s hard to just give a center a situational role to ease him back in. A team wants to keep their center the same throughout the game for a ton of reasons, but none more important than keeping that exchange between center and quarterback consistent. “We’re still back-and-forth on what do we do with him,” Campbell said of Mays. “Do we work him and Juice (Scruggs) in and out? Do we—the center position, it’s a little different than a guard. That’s somebody that’s constantly touching the football.” Making the transition even tougher is the fact that current Lions starting center Juice Scruggs is playing very good football in Mays’ absence. It’s unlikely that Scruggs takes the starting job from Mays, but I’m sure it does bring up thoughts of, “Why mess with something that’s working?” So today’s Question of the Day is: How should the Lions handle Cade Mays’ return? My answer: Let’s establish what the Lions should do once they believe Mays is fully healthy and ready for a full share of snaps. At that point, I don’t think there should be any question that Mays should be the starting center. Scruggs may be playing well, but Mays is better. There’s a reason Mays was a costly free agent, and Scruggs was part of a trade for a starting running back. I don’t think the perception of these players should change based on a five-game sample size that includes a very rough game from Scruggs vs. the Bills. But what’s a good way to ease Mays in this week? Do you actually give him a few drives at center? Do you have him simulate making protection calls from the sideline? Do you get him out there as an extra lineman in some formations? Or do you just relegate him to some special teams snaps to get him on the field, get used to contact, and re-evaluate next week? I’m leaning toward that last option. I really don’t like the idea of rotating Mays in at center for a drive or two or three. It just seems like too much of a risk. Either make him your starting center or find another way to get him out there. The best way to do that is to give him some special teams reps or jumbo package responsibilities, and then make him the starting center in Week 8 against the Vikings’ tough defense. It’s not an ideal spot to throw him in, but I don’t think there is an ideal option out there. What do you think? How would you handle Cade Mays’ return? Share your ideas in the comment section below. title: Why Dan Campbell is more optimistic at the bye week than he was in 2025
summary: Last year, the Detroit Lions entered the bye week with a solid 5-2 record coming off of a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. This year, the Lions are 3-2 at the bye with a couple of narrow victories over the Jets and Saints and a couple of decisive losses to the Bills and […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Last year, the Detroit Lions entered the bye week with a solid 5-2 record coming off of a big win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. This year, the Lions are 3-2 at the bye with a couple of narrow victories over the Jets and Saints and a couple of decisive losses to the Bills and Panthers. Despite what it looks like on the surface, Campbell said that he actually feels more optimistic about this year’s team. “We went in (last year), and I don’t remember what we were, but we had just won, and it seems pretty good, but there were some things that you could feel a little bit,” Campbell said. “In some regards, I feel better going into this bye than I even I did last year, because I know we’re ascending and we’re young and we’re growing, and that’s exciting.” Last year, there were plenty of warning signs with Detroit’s 5-2 start that would ultimately result in a 4-6 finish. None were clearer than a running game that wasn’t nearly as efficient as it looked on the surface. At the bye week, the Lions averaged 4.5 yards per carry (13th) and had 10 touchdowns (second), but posted just a 40.3% success rate (19th). In short, a handful of huge runs were boosting their numbers. This year, it’s the opposite. They’re lacking the huge, explosive runs, but they’re much more efficient on a down-to-down basis. They’re averaging a very similar 4.4 yards per carry (12th) and have eight touchdowns (t-fifth), but the Lions’ 46.2% rushing success rate ranks fourth-best. Detroit made a ton of investments in their offensive line this offseason, moving on from older players like Taylor Decker and Graham Glasgow. That mantle has been handed to Penei Sewell (26 years old), Christian Mahogany (26), Juice Scruggs (26), Tate Ratledge (25), and rookie Blake Miller (22). When free agent addition Cade Mays returns to the lineup this week , he’ll be the oldest starter on the front at 27 years old. It’s not just the offensive line, either. Detroit is now leaning more heavily on other key, young players like running back Jahmyr Gibbs (24), defensive tackle Tyleik Williams (23), rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard (24), and linebacker Jack Campbell (26). It’s only a matter of time before rookie defenders Derrick Moore and Jimmy Rolder get an increased role. And don’t forget the return of Brian Branch, who will turn 25 this week. With that youth comes potential. These players are not just still growing into their NFL careers, but they’re building chemistry together. The key for Detroit is to keep their trajectory headed in the right direction. “Sometimes you feel like you’re topped off and maybe you’re beginning to deteriorate because of issues, worn down, age, whatever it is,” Campbell said of last year. “So [this year] is exciting. I do feel like we’re on the rise here a little bit. We’ve just got to keep getting better. We’ve got to keep testing ourselves. And, look, we’re in for the long haul now, and it’s really about to get geared up. The competition is about to really raise up another level, and it starts with Green Bay.”

title: Brian Branch, Cade Mays to play vs. Packers, but workload undecided
summary: Out of the bye week, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell confirmed that both Brian Branch and Cade Mays will make their 2026 debuts against the Green Bay Packers this week. Branch will see the field for the first time since suffering a torn Achilles in early December. Mays will make his Lions debut after suffering […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Thursday, August 21, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Out of the bye week, Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell confirmed that both Brian Branch and Cade Mays will make their 2026 debuts against the Green Bay Packers this week. Branch will see the field for the first time since suffering a torn Achilles in early December. Mays will make his Lions debut after suffering a wrist fracture early in training camp. While both are expected to suit up on Sunday, Campbell said they were still evaluating how much each player will play on Sunday. The Lions coach made it clear that he doesn’t intend to give Branch a full-time load, but he will probably still play a significant amount of snaps. “I think that’d be asking a lot to say he’s going to play 70 plays, but we feel like there’s—we do feel like he can handle quite a bit here,” Campbell said. “We’re going to push him in practice early. That’s one of the reasons we’re practicing tomorrow and not Wednesday. So we can push some of these guys a little bit knowing they’re going into a day off. I think that’ll help a little bit. Then we’ll have a really good idea by the time we hit the game. We already kind of have a range of what we’re looking at for him.” It’s a little more complicated for Mays. Campbell noted that while it’s not uncommon for guards to play in a rotational role during a game, that’s not how centers are typically treated. “We’re still back-and-forth on what do we do with him,” Campbell said. “Do we work him and Juice (Scruggs) in and out? Do we—the center position, it’s a little different than a guard. That’s somebody that’s constantly touching the football. But either way, barring anything negatively happening between now and the game, we plan on playing both of those guys.” Complicating things further with Mays is also the strong play of backup center Juice Scruggs. Not only is he currently the No. 2 graded center per PFF, but Campbell says he’s been very impressed with how he’s played and grown at the position. “That’s the hard thing, Juice is playing pretty good football for us right now,” Campbell said. “He’s done a good job, he’s gotten better every week, and Juice is a freakin’ team guy. Doesn’t mean that if it comes to that (benching him), that he doesn’t like that. Because there’s definitely an argument to keep him rolling, because he’s playing good football. But he’s a team guy; he’s all-in; he’ll do whatever we ask him to do. And the good news is, one way or another, we get Cade worked back in with Juice playing pretty good, (Christian) Mahogany’s had a couple of good weeks—well, now we’ve got some guys. We’ve got a pretty good crew there to go with and get better as the season goes.” Campbell has already mentioned that by the time Mays is settled back into the starting role, Scruggs could re-enter the starting competition at left guard . But in the meantime, they like having him continue to grow at center to give the Lions some depth and insurance at one of the more important offensive line positions. “Some of it will need to be dependent on how much Cade can play, as we keep Juice ready to play center, because he’s really plug-and-play in that regard—the IDs, all of those things,” Campbell said. “And then the more comfortable we get, then Juice is working the guard position a little bit with those guys. So now you’re getting some really good competition; you’ve got depth; you’ve got guys that can play.”
