title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: There are always small picture and big picture takeaways from these things. The big picture takeaway is simply that the universe has a way of balancing things out. It seemed like the Texans were on the wrong side of the bounce of the ball, blow of the whistle, and clutch performance in the first five […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 18: Dalton Schultz of the Houston Texans is tackled by Dennis Gardeck of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the NFL London Series match between Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on October 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Julian Finney/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are always small picture and big picture takeaways from these things. The big picture takeaway is simply that the universe has a way of balancing things out. It seemed like the Texans were on the wrong side of the bounce of the ball, blow of the whistle, and clutch performance in the first five games. Those things rarely ever go one direction for a whole season. So, the Texans finally benefitted from some positive fortune on all of those counts on Sunday. The good news is that it means the Texans aren’t as bad as their 2-4 record suggests. In fact, if we were to follow Pythagorean theory, they should be 3-3 as they have scored one more point on the season than they have allowed. Of course, the bad news would be that they are still not as good as what we anticipated they would be coming into the season. Of course, we will get to that when we get to the great, good, and bad. The Numbers Total Yards: Texans 59/426, Jaguars 68/412 Rushing Yards: Texans 25/114, Jaguars 27/106 Passing Yards: Texans 34/312, Jaguars 41/306 Third Down: Texans 5/11, Jaguars 7/12 Fourth Down: Texans 0/0, Jaguars 0/1 Sacks: Texans 0, Jaguars 0 Turnovers: Texans 1, Jaguars 1 Penalties: Texans 6/40, Jaguars 6/66 Time of Possession: Texans 29:37, Jaguars 30:23 The numbers look like it was an even football game and that would be a good description of it. Both offenses moved the ball easily and both were equally effective in the red zone. Both had red zone turnovers that hurt. It was as even as even can get and when you win those games you have to come out feeling pretty good. This is especially true since this was technically a road game. The Texans have three home games in the division in the second half of the season. You have to feel pretty good about that. The Great We have to remember these moments when the opposite comes up. DeMeco Ryans overwhelming instinct is to turtle when he is up in a game. He trusts his defense. In most of his tenure that has been a good bet. It hasn’t been a good bet in this one and he recognized that for the most part. The hardest thing for a head coach and playcaller to do is to get a feel for what the moment calls for. They did turtle when up 24-14, but instinct is what it is. Otherwise, Ryans overcame his instincts and kept the pedal to the metal because that is what the game called for. In particular, Ryans handled the end of the game very well with balancing the desire to give his kicker a chance to ice the game with guarding against disaster in case it didn’t work out. He also handled the clock at the end of the first half very well. That was a criticism in the Indianapolis game, so he showed a ton of growth in this one and we should mark it down because we would certainly mention it if the opposite were true. The Good This was the best rushing performance of the season. Make no mistake, this is still a passing football team and should be going forward. However, you don’t win football games unless you can gain yards on the ground when you need to. It wasn’t always pretty. For much of the first three quarters we were yelling at the screen whenever any rushing attempt came. However, they came alive in the fourth quarter and did just enough to keep the Jaguars honest. Obviously, we will get to the majority of the passing game in our dedicated segment, but here is another hat tip to Jaylin Noel. He has gotten better in each of the past three weeks and is now a fully integrated part of the offense. Add in a clutch three catch performance from Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. and the shape of this passing attack is intact. The tight ends may be the story of this one though as they combined for more than 100 yards and two touchdowns. We will get to the ramifications on the wide receiver room down the line. The Bad It doesn’t matter who is calling plays. This is not the 2024-2025 defense. Heck, it isn’t even the 2023 defense. For whatever reason, they just aren’t good enough. Perhaps it was missing Jalen Pitre in the middle. Perhaps they whiffed on Reed Blankenship. Perhaps Kamari Lassiter and Derek Stingley Jr, just aren’t as good this year as they were a year ago. Maybe all of those things are true in addition to the injury troubles in the linebacking core. Whatever the case may be, the time for simply thinking this group will snap out of it is over. They still have some players (Will Anderson cough) playing at a very high level, but it isn’t enough to simply throw out a vanilla defense and think you can outalent everyone. Either adjustments in the lineup or adjustments in the scheme will be needed to turn this around. Focus on Stroud The numbers will say that Stroud threw for 312 yards, three touchdowns, and a pick. The rating says it was a 116.3 as Stroud had his best game of the season. However, that doesn’t tell the whole story. For the first three quarters, the Jaguars knew the pass was coming because that is all the Texans had. He beat the blitz consistently and had the only one bad play. Otherwise, it was a perfect performance. When the dust settles, he will have nine touchdowns and one interception on the season, will be near the league lead in passing yards, and a quarterback rating at almost 100. There is a stat called “expected completion percentage” that rates the difficulty of throws based on how open receivers are and how far down the field the attempts come. Stroud is second in the NFL in that department. Ultimately, the events of the past month indicate that the team is turning over the reigns to him to save their season. So far so good. The revisionists will claim that Nick Caserio made a mistake by not paying him. It certainly looks that way now, but most of us were saying no before the season. We wanted to see it first. Well, we have seen it. This guy is earning his bag one game at a time. It will be exciting to see what happens with Harrison Jr. added to the receiving group. Plus, Tank Dell is almost ready to return. Let’s go.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: How much is DeForest Buckner worth on the trade market?
summary: This is the second part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. This one is about DeForest Buckner. You can click here to read the previous one on Jonathan Taylor. As with Taylor, this is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade Buckner. The Colts […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 11: DeForest Buckner #99 of the Indianapolis Colts celebrates during the third quarter of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images This is the second part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. This one is about DeForest Buckner. You can click here to read the previous one on Jonathan Taylor . As with Taylor, this is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade Buckner. The Colts probably should not be looking to move any of these players unless the season falls apart or another team comes calling with an offer that is too good to ignore. The point of the series is simply to determine what these players would realistically be worth if serious trade interest developed around the deadline. Buckner is an interesting case because the player is still very good, but almost everything surrounding him works against his value. He is 32 years old. His contract voids after this season. Any team acquiring him would be doing so primarily for the stretch run and playoffs, with no guarantee he would remain there beyond February. That makes this much more complicated than simply asking how good DeForest Buckner is. Buckner is still really good The easiest part of this evaluation is determining whether Buckner can still play. He definitely can. Through six games, Buckner has four sacks, eight quarterback hits and 18 pressures. He consistently ranks amongst the highest interior defensive linemen in these categories. That is especially important considering the state of the Colts’ defensive front. Indianapolis has struggled badly to consistently pressure quarterbacks this season, yet Buckner continues to create problems from the interior. At 32 years old, he is still arguably the most dependable pass rusher on the roster. There has been no dramatic falloff where we are evaluating Buckner based on what he used to be. He is still collapsing pockets, still winning inside against the top interior offensive linemen and still capable of ruining a drive. That puts him in a different category from the typical veteran defensive lineman available at the deadline. The two trades that make sense as comparisons There have been plenty of defensive tackles traded over the last decade, but very few are particularly useful here. The best comparison is Leonard Williams. Seattle acquired Williams from the Giants at the 2023 trade deadline for a second-round pick in 2024 and a fifth-round pick in 2025. Williams was 29 and in the final year of his contract. Through eight games with the Giants that season, he had only 1.5 sacks. The Seahawks were 5-2, believed they could make a run and paid a significant price for a high-end interior defender. The other useful comparison goes back to 2017, when Seattle acquired Sheldon Richardson from the Jets. The Seahawks sent a second-round pick and Jermaine Kearse while the teams also swapped seventh-round selections. Richardson was 26 at the time and coming off a season with 1.5 sacks, although he had already made a Pro Bowl and had an eight-sack season earlier in his career. Both trades tell us that teams will pay substantial draft capital for an impact interior defensive lineman when they believe they are close to winning. From a performance standpoint, Buckner belongs in that conversation. He has already doubled Williams’ pre-trade sack total in three fewer games this season, and Richardson was coming off one of the quieter statistical seasons of his career when Seattle acquired him. The problem is that Williams was 29 and Richardson was 26. Buckner is 32. That is an enormous difference when assigning trade value, even if Buckner is playing just as well or better than either player was at the time. The contract makes him a potential rental This is probably the biggest factor dragging Buckner’s value down. His contract voids in February, which means a team trading for him would only control him for the remainder of the 2026 season unless it negotiated another deal. That could be eight or nine regular-season games plus the playoffs. The financial cost for this season would not be particularly difficult to handle. Buckner has a $13 million base salary in 2026. The Colts already paid his $10 million roster bonus, and the prorated signing-bonus money would remain Indianapolis’ responsibility. A team acquiring him around the halfway point of the season would therefore be taking on roughly half of that $13 million salary, somewhere around $6.5 million depending on the exact date of the trade. Most contenders can find a way to absorb that, but the larger issue is what happens afterward. There is no cheap year of team control waiting in 2027. There is no franchise-friendly contract that makes him a multi-year asset. The team either lets him reach free agency or has to negotiate a new contract with a player who will turn 33 next season. That has to significantly reduce the return compared with Williams and Richardson. How much does Buckner have left? Age is a legitimate concern, but I would not assume Buckner is approaching the end. Defensive tackle is one of the positions where elite players can remain productive well into their 30s. Cameron Heyward might be the most obvious example. He is 37 years old and was still one of the best defensive linemen in football last season. At age 36, PFF gave him the highest grade of any interior defender in the league at 90.4, and he earned another All-Pro selection. Heyward is obviously an extreme example, not the standard everyone should be expected to follow. Calais Campbell is still playing the position at 40! Defensive tackle is a position that relies a lot on strength, technique and instincts and those 3 things don’t age. All of this shows that 32 is hardly ancient for a great defensive tackle. Buckner’s game also lends itself to aging relatively well. He is 6-foot-7, incredibly long and wins with power, technique and an ability to use his frame inside. He does not need to rely entirely on explosive athleticism to remain effective. I would be comfortable saying Buckner has at least a few quality seasons left if he remains healthy and if he decides he wants to play that long. There have been rumours about him retiring the last couple of seasons, so that also plays a factor into things. A contender acquiring him would be doing so for the current playoff run first, but there is a legitimate possibility that the relationship could continue beyond that. If Buckner finishes the year playing at his current level, it would not be surprising at all to see him sign another multi-year contract. The uncertainty simply means a team cannot value those future seasons as part of the trade itself. Who could use Buckner? Unlike Taylor, where only certain contenders have an obvious need at running back, the market for Buckner could be fairly broad. Almost every playoff team could use another interior defender who can rush the quarterback, but 4 stand out to me. Detroit would probably be the most interesting fit. The Lions are 3-2 and clearly still view themselves as a championship contender. Aidan Hutchinson gives them a premier edge rusher, while Alim McNeill is a good interior player, but Detroit lost veteran nose tackle D.J. Reader during the offseason. Adding Buckner would give the Lions another proven interior pass rusher and allow them to build a defensive front capable of creating pressure without constantly blitzing. For a team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations, Buckner is exactly the type of veteran addition that makes sense in October. San Francisco would be the funniest destination for obvious reasons. The 49ers traded Buckner to Indianapolis in 2020 because they did not want to give him the enormous contract he eventually received. Six years later, they could theoretically bring him back for…
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Evaluating Colts veteran trade chips who could be on the move soon to jumpstart rebuild
summary: After longtime general manager Chris Ballard was fired Monday, it’s a reasonable expectation right now that the Indianapolis Colts (at 2-4) may look to trade off some of their veteran players to recoup lost draft compensation. As you may recall, the Colts currently do not have a 2027 first round pick, as theirs went to […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 12: Indianapolis Colts guard Quenton Nelson (56) congratulates Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) on his nice run during and NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and the Arizona Cardinals on October 12, 2025 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images After longtime general manager Chris Ballard was fired Monday, it’s a reasonable expectation right now that the Indianapolis Colts (at 2-4) may look to trade off some of their veteran players to recoup lost draft compensation. As you may recall, the Colts currently do not have a 2027 first round pick, as theirs went to the New York Jets, along with other pieces, in last year’s trade deadline deal for shutdown cornerback Sauce Gardner. Newly appointed interim general manager Ed Dodds may be tasked with trying to trade some sought after Colts veterans ahead of this year’s trade deadline in early November. Let’s look at some of the Colts top trade candidates, that have value to other teams and could realistically be on the move for a clearly rebuilding team: DeForest Buckner Look, no one wants to trade Buckner, who’s consistently embodied what it means to be a member of the Horseshoe about as well as anyone during his entire tenure in Indianapolis. However, Buckner is 32-years-old coming off neck surgery, entering the last year of his current contract, and was publicly frustrated after Sunday’s brutal loss. If the price is right, it makes sense to trade him to a title contender for the last stretch of his standout playing career, perhaps back to the San Francisco Bay where it all started for him. It makes sense to me that a contender could be interested in the still highly productive veteran pass rushing defensive tackle, similarly to when the Colts traded a 2nd round pick for Anthony ’Booger’ McFarland of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers which helped galvanize their interior run defense for a Super Bowl run—along with the return of starting safety Bob Sanders of course. Buckner has 26 tackles (9 solo), 4.0 sacks, 18 QB pressures, 3 passes defensed, and a fumble recovery during all 6 starts in 2026. Trade Compensation: 2027 2nd round pick Possible Trade Suitors: Buffalo Bills, Los Angeles Rams, and San Francisco 49ers Quenton Nelson Unless the future Hall of Famer goes to interim Colts management or ownership and explicitly states, “I want out,” the pending free agent should remain in Indianapolis for the remainder of his playing career prime through a new lucrative contract extension, regardless of who the next general manager is calling the shots—and that should come from a mandate above by team ownership. Simply put, “Lock up Nelson for life!” Since being selected by the Colts with the 6th overall pick of the 2018 NFL Draft, Nelson has been a perennial NFL All-Pro and one of the best offensive guards in all of football. He’s still playing at a very high Pro Bowl level again, and at age 30 is still young enough to outlast a short rebuild with productive football still left in him—as great offensive guards can still age pretty gracefully until at least their mid-thirties. Particularly one with great technique and fundamentals like Big Q, who should be a future Ring of Honor player for the Colts franchise, when his Canton-bound career is all said and done. Nelson has started all 6 games for the Colts and has a +84.3 overall grade via PFF, having allowed 0 sacks and just 7 total QB pressures during his 248 total pass blocking snaps. Trade Compensation: 2027 first round pick Possible Trade Suitors: Detroit Lions, Minnesota Vikings, Seattle Seahawks Grover Stewart Buckner’s longtime running mate at defensive tackle, Grover Stewart, has been a consistent run stopping force in the middle of the Indianapolis defensive line and like Buckner, another longtime veteran leader of their defense. At 32-years-old, he’s also starting to get a bit long in the tooth at defensive tackle for Indianapolis and while his play has dipped a bit this season, perhaps a change of scenery and playing for a contender could motivate ‘Big Grove’ to find his vintage run stuffing self again during a serious playoff push. There has to be a legit playoff hopeful, who’s looking to shore up their run defense, and Stewart could be that guy for them in the short-term as another pending free agent. On the 2026 campaign, Stewart has 20 tackles (5 solo), 0.5 sacks, and a pass defensed during all 6 starts. Trade Compensation: 2027 4th Round Pick Possible Trade Suitors: Dallas Cowboys, Green Bay Packers, Las Vegas Raiders. Jonathan Taylor Look, I can certainly understand the rationale for trading Taylor at this time, he’s 27-years-old with a lot of mileage on his tires, and NFL running backs typically do not age all that gracefully into their early thirties, unless apparently you’re freak of nature Derrick Henry. To me, this is similar to Nelson though, where unless Taylor asks out via a trade, I think the Colts would look to keep the star workhorse for the remainder of his playing career prime here—as another future Ring of Honor guy and NFL Hall of Famer, when it’s all said and done. Plus, you still want to give fans a reason to go to Colts games and have stars they can be proud of and root for on Sundays, if the expected trade return isn’t going to be all that worth the while. On the season, Taylor has 122 carries for 492 total rushing yards (4.0 ypc avg.) and 7 rushing touchdowns during all 6 starts in the 2026 season. Trade Compensation: 2027 2nd round pick Possible Trade Suitors: Denver Broncos, Green Bay Packers, Minnesota Vikings Charvarius ‘Mooney’ Ward With a myriad of injuries, including multiple concussions, since joining Indianapolis in the 2025 offseason, it’s hard to see much of a robust market for the 30-year-old cornerback, who’s had some up-and-down play this year. While Ward clearly hasn’t played up to his current Colts lucrative contract, he has no guaranteed money for next year, meaning a contending team with a clear need for a proven veteran cornerback could potentially kick the tires on Mooney Ward finding his familiar self down the season’s stretch as a rental to shore up their secondary. Ward has 18 tackles (12 solo) and 4 passes defensed during all 6 starts, with a +64.7 overall grade via PFF—including a +62.8 coverage grade. Trade Compensation: 2027 5th round pick Possible Trade Suitors: Detroit Lions, Kansas City Chiefs, Pittsburgh Steelers, San Francisco 49ers
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts ‘first call’ was reportedly to Peyton Manning for GM job, which isn’t first time franchise made strong push for reunion
summary: According to host Dan Patrick of ‘The Dan Patrick Show’ and his sourcing, one of the first calls that the Indianapolis Colts team ownership made on Monday, following the firing of longtime general manager Chris Ballard, was to the franchise’s former legendary (and Hall of Fame) quarterback Peyton Manning: While this could be the Colts […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 30: Former Indianapolis Colts Peyton Manning looks on during the Indianapolis Colts Ring of Honor ceremony for Tarik Glenn during halftime of a game against the Washington Commanders at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 30, 2022 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to host Dan Patrick of ‘The Dan Patrick Show’ and his sourcing, one of the first calls that the Indianapolis Colts team ownership made on Monday, following the firing of longtime general manager Chris Ballard, was to the franchise’s former legendary (and Hall of Fame) quarterback Peyton Manning: "The Colts' first call will be/has been to Peyton Manning." — DP shares what his source has told him. pic.twitter.com/MgTbuJIxhW — Dan Patrick Show (@dpshow) October 19, 2026 While this could be the Colts simply performing their due diligence and leaving no stone unturned regarding their latest GM search, it’s not the first time that that the Colts reportedly approached Manning about rejoining the franchise—as it was previously for the franchise’s potential Team President role. Specifically, the last go around was back in early 2017 ( via 1075 the Fan’s JMV ) under late team owner Jim Irsay, before Ballard was hired later in that offseason as their new general manager. This latest reported attempt, if it indeed transpires, will go to his daughters, and namely, team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon. In early 2017, multiple sources reported that Jim Irsay made a strong “secret” push in Houston with his private jet to pair Manning, as his new team president, with former Oakland Raiders and Tampa Bay Buccaneers Super Bowl winning head coach Jon Gruden leading along the sidelines: Colts owner Jim Irsay in fact made strong push for Peyton Manning as head of football w Gruden as coach. Still hopeful to get Peyton — Jay Glazer (@JayGlazer) January 14, 2017 WTHR can confirm that the Colts have spoken to Peyton Manning about a front office job with team. Told it's still a fluid situation. — Bob Kravitz (@bkravitz) January 14, 2017 While there were initial reports (from 1075 The Fan’s JMV) that Manning privately felt he wasn’t ready for an NFL GM job at that time, there was also speculation that Manning would have to receive a ‘minor’ team ownership stake to seriously consider any top NFL football leadership position as an employee: “The question is whether Manning, whom many thinks has ownership aspirations, would do anything without equity,” wrote PFT’s Mike Florio back in early January of 2017. “Which then makes the question whether Irsay would shave off a few percentage points to ensure that the value of the franchise will be enhanced by the tireless efforts Peyton Manning would bring to the annual quest for football supremacy.” That’s still a question that remains unclear regarding the transitioning ownership from the late Jim Irsay to his three daughters, and as Dan Patrick alluded to on Monday, Jim Irsay never considered it when posed privately previously. We’ve since seen other organizations open to this such as the Las Vegas Raiders with Tom Brady, as their new limited partner and minority team owner. In my honest opinion, Manning makes more sense as the Colts’ new President of Football Operations, like the role fellow Hall of Fame quarterback John Elway previously served with the Denver Broncos and former Colts starting quarterback (and perhaps future Hall of Famer) Matt Ryan currently serves with the Atlanta Falcons. In Atlanta, under Ryan, Ian Cunningham serves as the team’s general manager, performing the day-to-day football ops. For Manning and the Colts, this would be the ideal arrangement, especially given Manning’s off-the-field interests and endeavors with Omaha Productions, etc., as well as most notably, family commitments and time with his wife and twins. Manning oversees the football department as the new face of the Colts organization’s operations collectively, bringing in leadership, accountability, and football expertise at a higher-level—with a savvy new general manager working under him performing the heavy-lifting in football ops and working that daily grind from a player personnel evaluation, roster management, and scouting standpoint. In fact, it’s not all that dissimilar to when Larry Bird previously served as the Indiana Pacers President of Basketball Operations, with Kevin Pritchard as general manager and VP of basketball operations way-back-when. At any rate, whether the Colts are engaging Manning from a potential President of Football Ops, General Manager, or even as an informal consultant on “who to hire next” standpoint, it makes sense to pick the brain of one of the most brilliant football minds to have played for the franchise, when they achieved their peak success.

title: Colts fire Chris Ballard after mounting 10 seasons of mediocrity
summary: The Indianapolis Colts fired General Manager Chris Ballard, ending his 10-year tenure after a humiliating loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans inside Lucas Oil Stadium.  It’s about time to light the match. The final year for Ballard produced way more frustration than any success. Ballard took over as general manager in 2017 and will […]
full_text: Chris Ballard, Indianapolis Colts general manager, talks Friday, July 25, 2025, with Colts owner Carlie Irsay-Gordon during training camp held at Grand Park in Westfield. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Indianapolis Colts fired General Manager Chris Ballard, ending his 10-year tenure after a humiliating loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans inside Lucas Oil Stadium. It’s about time to light the match. The final year for Ballard produced way more frustration than any success. Ballard took over as general manager in 2017 and will leave Indianapolis posting a 72-82-1 regular-season record and a 1-2 playoff record. Despite being given multiple opportunities to build a consistent contender, the Colts never won an AFC South title under his leadership and currently are in a five-year playoff drought. That final defeat forced fans to file out early, while leaving a roar of boos to echo throughout Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday. Tennessee was 0-5 and had 11 consecutive divisional losses, which proves that loss was the final straw for an organization that has spent the last decade searching for answers. Indianapolis has lost four of its first six games to start this season and has been defeated in 12 of its last 15 contests dating to last season’s collapse. For a Stampede Blue community that once believed it was possible to restore the franchise back to prominence, that patience had all but disappeared. Ballard’s tenure featured stretches of promise, but the organization never established the sustained success necessary to compete with the perennial AFC contenders. The biggest issue over his tenure is the endless quarterback carousel. Daniel Jones is struggling as the eighth different season opener starter over the last 10 seasons. Choosing to start the campaign with this awful linebacker unit, while drafting two linebackers that can’t seem to find playing time is another mark on personnel decisions. The constant lack of a pass rush is another stain that can’t just be wiped away. Alec Pierce signed the largest deal for a free agent receiver in NFL history, but has played just 41% of the offensive snaps. The trade for cornerback Sauce Gardner has backfired as Indianapolis could’ve used those two first-round picks, especially since the 2027 pick may wind up inside the top 10. This decision also marks a reversal for Principal Owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon, who elected to retain Ballard following last season’s falloff. Instead, the Colts have continued to struggle and the intensified questions about the direction of the organization have started to fall on her shoulders. Ballard, whose contract was set to expire after the season, acknowledged the shortcomings before his departure. He mentioned that he would not even offer himself another contract, recognizing that the results had not met the standard expected of the once-prominent franchise. The Colts failed to capture a division title, gradually regressed and entered another season without a clear path back to the playoffs. The prolonged drought eroded the trust between the organization and its season-ticket supporters, many of whom waited years for a meaningful turnaround. Coincidentally enough, this week is when season-ticket holders are asked to renew their package deals. Good luck convincing fans to spend more for a comical product. Ballard’s departure leaves Indianapolis facing another significant transition as the franchise searches for leadership capable of restoring its competitive identity. The next general manager will inherit a team in need of a quarterback, receivers, a pass rush, and playable linebackers. Reminder that Indianapolis must find a way to build a roster that can compete consistently without a first round draft pick in 2027. After 10 seasons under Ballard, Colts brass decided that patience is no longer a viable strategy. The challenge shifts to finding the next GM who can change the culture from a decade of mediocrity into a contender.
author: Thomas Butler-Guerrero

title: Rapid Reaction: Colts announce firing of longtime GM Chris Ballard following brutal Week 6 loss

However, he had just two playoff appearances, 1 […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 13: Indianapolis Colts General Manager Chris Ballard during a NFL game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Indianapolis Colts on September 13, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts (2-4), and specifically team owner and CEO Carlie Irsay-Gordon publicly announced on Monday that longtime general manager Chris Ballard has been relieved of his duties: We have relieved Chris Ballard of his duties as General Manager. pic.twitter.com/BleD6bfTsG — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) October 19, 2026 Ballard had compiled a 72-82-1 through a little over 10 seasons with the Colts franchise, having arrived in 2017. However, he had just two playoff appearances, 1 playoff win, and 0 division titles during his lengthy GM tenure. While he initially got off to a hot start following his 2018 NFL Draft Class which included Quenton Nelson, Darius ‘Shaq’ Leonard, and Braden Smith among others, winning PFWA Executive of the Year for that elite draft class, the quality and returns of his subsequent draft classes largely diminished (aside from arguably 2020, which was a solid haul with both Jonathan Taylor and Michael Pittman Jr. in the 2nd round). Never one to seriously spend in free agency, Ballard was notoriously frugal, preferring to re-sign his own players and maintain ample salary cap flexibility, despite glaring starting holes on the Colts roster year-after-year, which weren’t properly addressed. It was a major point of frustration among the Horseshoe Faithful and local talking heads because it just continued to happen on an annual basis. That approach changed during the 2025 offseason, when the Colts signed both safety Cam Bynum and cornerback Charvarius Ward to lucrative, multi-year free agency deals, but by that time, it was too little, and too late. It’s a fair question of whether either one of those signings have dramatically paid off for Indianapolis either. Having had two consecutive 8-9 seasons, and stumbling out of the gates to a 2-4 record, with no playoffs in Indianapolis since 2020 (the COVID-19) year, Sunday’s brutal home loss to one of the league’s worst teams was finally the straw that broke Ballard’s maligned tenure with the Colts. The Tennessee Titans were winless at 0-5 and had an 11-game losing streak in the AFC South, while the Colts were at home and blew a 13-0 lead at halftime—with former franchise legends in the house to honor Adam Vinatieri’s induction into the franchise’s illustrious Ring of Honor. Colts fans had been publicly frustrated with Ballard’s recent results, and coming off an offseason where Irsay-Gordon publicly proclaimed that, “The Stakes had never been higher” for the franchise, she made good on her word, as Ballard was finally shown the door and exits stage left. At a certain point, winning results have to matter, and even though Ballard had a strong personal relationship with the Irsay daughters, the on-the-field product and collective talent of the Colts roster both have only continued to diminish. It was time for a change, and quite frankly, it was long overdue.

title: 3 Numbers to Know From the Jaguars’ Loss to the Texans
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars fell to the Houston Texans in Week 6, moving to 4-2 on the season. Shucks. Here are a few stats that stand out from the loss. 0 That’s how many sacks the Jaguars allowed to Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, and the rest of the Texans’ pass rush. If we made a […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 18: Liam Coen, Head Coach of the Jacksonville Jaguars, reacts from the touchline during the NFL London Series match between Houston Texans and Jacksonville Jaguars at Wembley Stadium on October 18, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Julian Finney/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Jacksonville Jaguars fell to the Houston Texans in Week 6, moving to 4-2 on the season. Shucks. Here are a few stats that stand out from the loss. 0 That’s how many sacks the Jaguars allowed to Will Anderson Jr., Danielle Hunter, and the rest of the Texans’ pass rush. If we made a list of all the reasons Jacksonville lost on Sunday, it’d take a while to get to the offensive line. Who woulda thought? With Anton Harrison placed on injured reserve last week, the Jaguars’ undermanned OL against the Texans’ potent DL was widely seen as a mismatch going into Sunday’s game. Shoutout to the 13% of fans who felt very confident in Walker Little and Cole Van Lanen to step up after Harrison’s injury. According to PFF, rookie left guard Emmanuel Pregnon was the only Jaguar to allow a quarterback hit. Trevor Lawrence was kept clean on 32 of his 44 dropbacks (72.7%). Whenever he bailed from the pocket, it seemed to be because of a lack of open receivers rather than a leak in pass protection. Jacksonville kept Lawrence upright, which is a huge win. He completed 8 of 17 passes for 126 yards and 2 touchdowns against the blitz (111.4 passer rating), per NFL Pro. But I should also point out that Jacksonville couldn’t get C.J. Stroud on the ground. He completed 9 of 13 passes for 93 yards and 1 touchdown against the blitz (115.2 passer rating). Both offensive lines did a better job than anyone expected of giving their quarterback time to attack downfield. 5.7% That’s how much win probability the Jaguars would have added if Liam Coen had gone for it on 4th-and-4 with two minutes left in the game, per ESPN Analytics. Instead, he had Cam Little attempt a 60-yard field goal to tie the game. pic.twitter.com/9evTviO6Qo — Gus Logue (@gus_logue) October 18, 2026 Back to that hypothetical list of reasons why Jacksonville lost to Houston. The defense’s inability to close out games has to be up there — but if we had to point to a specific moment, it’d be Coen’s decision to put the game in the hands of that very defense. Little connected on his third career 60+ yard field goal, which is awesome. The kid isn’t just making some of the longest field goals in the NFL; he’s making some of the most clutch ones. (And shoutout to new long snapper Jacob Bobenmoyer for holding it down (no pun intended) in Ross Matiscik’s absence.) The players did their job… but they should’ve never been put in that position. While I understand Coen trusting his kicker, I don’t get him trusting his defense. Not after the first 58 minutes of Sunday’s contest, anyway. Even if we all believed that Little making the field goal was a sure thing, getting a stop sure wasn’t! Houston was humming all game, and of course, that didn’t stop in the final two minutes. They had three timeouts and didn’t even need ‘em. A busted coverage (far from the first of the game) allowed Woody Marks to scoot for 19 yards on a 3rd-and-2. With a couple of positive run plays, the Texans quickly got in position for a 49-yard game-winning field goal. Coen should’ve trusted his offense to gain four yards and keep the drive alive, rather than trusting his kicker to make a 60-yarder AND his defense to keep Houston out of field goal range. It’s frustrating that he didn’t let his own quarterback decide the fate of the game. Of course, one moment doesn’t decide the entire outcome, but this was a late-game decision Coen probably wants back. 3 That’s the number of NFL players to record a receiving touchdown and an interception in the same game since at least the 1970 merger. The list is Roy Green (Week 3 of 1981), Brian Dawkins (Week 4 of 2002), and Travis Hunter (Week 6 of 2026). Hunter’s performance was the epitome of a silver lining. It’s absolutely a bummer that the Jaguars lost — but did you see the unicorn streaking across the field?! This stat suggests that he’s one of three, but clearly, the dude is one-of-one. If Jacksonville defeated Houston, the only thing we’d be talking about is how it was The Travis Hunter Game. He finished with 4 catches for 59 yards and a touchdown on offense, plus 3 tackles and an interception on defense. Hunter certainly wants back a handful of plays, like the 42-yard catch by Nico Collins on a double move or the “12 men on the field” penalty that gave the Texans offense a fresh set of downs. It was not a perfect game… but dang, was it an exciting one! . @Jaguars @HoustonTexans @TravisHunterJr this is what a 2-way player looks like…scoring TD's and taking them away #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/HDy8pRbc14 — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) October 19, 2026 Hunter has played over 98% of defensive snaps in three straight games — his deployment on that side of the ball shouldn’t change. (He also has a pass breakup in five straight games, the longest active streak in the NFL.) The bigger news is that Hunter played a season-high 9 offensive snaps on Sunday. That may not sound like much, but anyone who watched the game could tell you how much smoother Jacksonville’s operation looked when Hunter was on the field as a receiver. Brian Thomas Jr. played 15 snaps in the first half and 0 snaps in the second half, per ESPN. Hmmmmmmmm. Other numbers to know: 5 : NFL players with 400+ receiving yards and 4+ receiving touchdowns this season. The list is Jaxon Smith-Njigba, CeeDee Lamb, Christian Watson, Davante Adams, and Parker Washington. 4 : Consecutive games with a 20+ yard reception for Brenton Strange, the longest active streak among NFL tight ends. 7 : Interceptions by Jacksonville this season, tied for the most in the NFL. 4 : Redzone takeaways by Jacksonville this season, twice as many as any other NFL defense. full_text: (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2026 NFL regular season’s Week 6 featured the Kansas City Chiefs beating the Los Angeles Chargers to push their unbeaten record to 5-0. Let’s see how the national media tweaked their opinion on the Chiefs over the weekend in this week’s sampling of power rankings: ESPN : 2 (No change) Biggest issue on offense: Offensive tackle health The Chiefs have done an admirable job protecting quarterback Patrick Mahomes, especially since left tackle Josh Simmons, their 2025 first-round pick, has been out because of a bulging disc in his lower back. Coach Andy Reid suggested Simmons won’t be ready for Sunday’s showdown against the Seahawks. Plus, right tackle Jaylon Moore sustained a concussion against the Chargers. Reid might have to continue altering the Chiefs’ playbook if undrafted rookies Kahlil Benson (left tackle) and Joshua Ezeudu (right tackle) are the starters. — Nate Taylor The Athletic : 2 (No change) Fantasy focus: Kenneth Walker III The Chiefs won six games last year. They signed Walker to a three-year, $43 million deal in the offseason. On Sunday, they won their fifth game. Walker is second in the league in fantasy points per game (27.6) after being drafted 16th on average. He had 19 carries for 128 yards against the Chargers and leads the league with 665 rushing yards. — Chad Graff and Josh Kendall Pro Football Talk : 2 (No change) Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III is the NFL MVP so far. — Mike Florio CBSSports.com : 2 (No change) Coming out of the bye, they dominated the Chargers. The same formula worked: Run it with Kenneth Walker and timely throws by Patrick Mahomes, who is doing more and more each week. — Pete Prisco Yahoo! Sports : 2 (No change) It’s hard to believe that an offense with Patrick Mahomes at quarterback has been turned over to another player, but Kenneth Walker III’s impact on the Chiefs can’t be understated. Walker had another 128 yards and two touchdowns on the ground as the Chiefs easily beat the Chargers 22-6. Walker leads the NFL with 665 rushing yards, even though Kansas City has already had its bye. His 133 rushing yards per game puts him on pace for 2,261 rushing yards. Since 1984, Eric Dickerson has held the NFL’s single-season record with 2,105 yards. Walker’s candidacy for MVP will be discussed, but it’s still a long shot because voters have turned it into a quarterback award. Adrian Peterson was the last non-quarterback to win and that came in 2012. The MVP has gone to a quarterback 18 of the last 19 seasons. But if Walker can get to 2,000 yards, it might give him a chance. — Frank Schwab USA Today : 2 (No change) Andy Reid is now 23-5 in the regular season following bye weeks. Sure looks like he might get the opportunity to coach after another bye a few months from now. — Nate Davis Sports Illustrated : 2 (Up from 3) Asking this seriously: Kenneth Walker is the best free agent signing through six weeks of an NFL season since…Peyton Manning and the Denver Broncos? Walker is averaging one hundred and thirty three yards and more than twenty attempts per game. That’s just wild stuff. — Conor Orr Sporting News : 1 (No change) Kenneth Walker III is now averaging 133 rushing yards per game and is up to 6.3 yards per carry with his 8 TDs. He’s on pace 2,261 yards, which should already put him in the MVP discussion as one of the best-ever free-agent pickups. — Vinnie Iyer FOX Sports : 2 (No change) Is it possible that the Chiefs are actually under the radar for most of the NFL? Or maybe we just all take their greatness for granted? But there sure isn’t a lot of chatter or hype about what might be the best team in the league. And Patrick Mahomes , just 10 months removed from tearing his ACL, is quietly on pace for his best season since 2022 — when he won league MVP and the Chiefs won the Super Bowl. Maybe Mahomes belongs in the early MVP conversation, too? The Chiefs play at Seattle and at Denver these next two weeks, so the noise about K.C. is about to get a lot louder. — Ralph Vacchiano

title: The Chiefs’ red-zone offense has to get straightened out
summary: In the Kansas City Chiefs’ 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers, the Chiefs’ offense drove up and down the field against Los Angeles’ defense for 422 yards, the second-most in a single game this season. Kansas City racked up 523 yards in a Week 2 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts. However, Kansas City scored […]
full_text: Credit: William Purnell-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers , the Chiefs’ offense drove up and down the field against Los Angeles’ defense for 422 yards, the second-most in a single game this season. Kansas City racked up 523 yards in a Week 2 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts . However, Kansas City scored a season-low 22 points. It points to an underrated issue so far this season: failed third-and-fourth-down conversions in the red zone. The Chiefs advanced inside the Chargers’ two-yard line three times in Week 6, but managed only seven points. In the second quarter, with a six-point lead, quarterback Patrick Mahomes scrambled away from the line of scrimmage and forced a throw into the back of the end zone. The ball was intercepted, spoiling a third-and-goal opportunity from the two-yard line. Then the Chiefs could have put the game away in the third quarter with fourth-and-goal from the one-yard line. Running back Kenneth Walker was stuffed at the goal line. In his post-game press conference, head coach Andy Reid addressed the red-zone shortcomings that kept a winless Chargers team in the game into the fourth quarter. “We spent time on the short yardage, and we didn’t do very good on it today,” Reid acknowledged at the podium. “So, we’ve got to figure that out and get that straightened out. You’re down in there for a couple more touchdowns, and in the goal-line situations, you’ve got to score on short yardage.” On Mahomes’ interception, his third of the season, Reid said the quarterback was “trying to get it out of the end zone,” but didn’t because he was falling backward. He also noted that the play he called wasn’t set up for that coverage. When asked about the play after Sunday’s game, Mahomes explained his thought process in looking for wide receiver Andrew Armstrong along the back line of the end zone. “Obviously, a ball you can’t throw like that,” Mahomes said at the podium. “The look wasn’t what we wanted, but we had an option, and it was Armstrong, and it happened faster than I expected it, and so instead of just staying with it and throwing it then, I started scrambling, and then I did what you’re not supposed to do. I was trying to throw it away, but at the same time, trying to give him a chance and then getting hit, left it short and so you just can’t do that, especially with how our defense was playing.” On Monday, Reid reiterated that the Chargers had the Chiefs’ number on that specific play. “They got us on the pass one,” Reid clarified. “So that was a good job by them.” When Reid was asked about Walker being stuffed before the scoring line on fourth-and-goal, he was clear with his message about where things could improve. “We gotta be very consistent with our blocking in those areas if we’re going to run the football,” Reid said. “With the slant game going on, we can’t miss a body there; gotta get a body on a body.” A closer look at the failed run play shows left tackle Kahlil Benson failed to “get a body on a body” on the Power run. The Chargers slant away from the run, setting up for down blocks. No. 92 of Los Angeles is too quick off the line, getting past Benson’s down-block attempt and keeping his shoulders square to the line of scrimmage, blowing up the run play and right guard Trey Smith’s pulling attempt. With another injury on the offensive line to consider — right tackle Jaylon Moore entered concussion protocol during the first half against Los Angeles — Reid understands the play-calling needs to keep the personnel on the field in mind, while hinting that the personnel knows it can be better on specific plays. “We have to block better on some, but at the same time, it’s our responsibility to keep with what works,” Reid said. “I’m always going to take the blame on that; we can put the guys in a better position to do their job, but I think if you talk to the guys, I think they’re going to tell you, ‘We have to block it better when we run the football there.’” Mahomes weighed in on seeing runs stuffed, whether against the Chargers or on the Week 3 drive-ending fourth-and-short run against the Miami Dolphins . He also pointed out that running back Kenneth Walker’s 33-yard run came on third-and-one. “Whenever stuff’s not pretty, you’ve got to be able to just push it and get the first down,” Mahomes shared. “I think that’s the biggest thing, and it’s not always going to be pretty. We have the short yardage where we score a long touchdown, and then we have the short yardage where we didn’t get there with the push and stuff like that, and so we’ll continue to work on it.” If the Chiefs need a push, one player it can seemingly get behind is left guard Kingsley Suamataia. After being benched for the Week 4 contest against the Las Vegas Raiders , he came back and was one of Kansas City’s most impactful blockers in Week 6. He paved the way for Walker’s 13-yard run on this play.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Patrick Mahomes has taken to the Chiefs’ under-center offense
summary: When the Kansas City Chiefs selected quarterback Patrick Mahomes with the 10th pick in the 2017 NFL Draft, he watched an offense capable of hosting the NFL’s leading rusher in rookie Kareem Hunt (1,327 yards). When he took the reins in 2018, that offense was gone. Coaches molded it to fit Mahomes, the shotgun gunslinger […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Kansas City Chiefs selected quarterback Patrick Mahomes with the 10th pick in the 2017 NFL Draft, he watched an offense capable of hosting the NFL’s leading rusher in rookie Kareem Hunt (1,327 yards). When he took the reins in 2018, that offense was gone. Coaches molded it to fit Mahomes, the shotgun gunslinger from Texas Tech, and his All-Pro weapons: wide receiver Tyreek Hill and tight end Travis Kelce. Head coach Andy Reid’s West Coast system, now married to Mahomes’ spread-offense tendencies, immediately produced an MVP campaign. Eight years later, the offense is not built around the two-time MVP and three-time Super Bowl champion signal caller. Mahomes captains a unit led by running back Kenneth Walker, the league’s current rushing leader (655 yards), who is on pace for over 2,200 rushing yards by season’s end. The offense’s evolution feels like it happened over one offseason, but it’s been a couple of years in the making. Andy Reid discussed Mahomes’ growth into under-center looks during a video call with local media on Monday. “He came from a primarily shotgun offense,” Reid reflected. “We started slowly getting him used to going under center, then he took to it. He just took it a couple of years ago.” This season, the Chiefs have run 121 under-center plays, averaging roughly 24 snaps per game in such formations. In 2025, Kansas City averaged 11.5 under-center plays per game. Reid added that Mahomes told the coaching staff he liked under-center plays and wanted to mix them in. However, it may have taken the addition of Walker — and the return of offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy — for the offensive identity to make what feels like a necessary shift in retrospect. “He felt really easy with that,” Reid remembered. “It’s worked out well. This year, with the running back situation we’ve got, I think those guys are very good from that home alignment there when Pat’s under.” Not only do the Chiefs lead the NFL in rushing yards per attempt (5.5) this season, but no team has averaged more total yards per game than Kansas City. Out of the bye week, the team put up its second-highest yardage total with 422 yards. Even with injuries at wide receiver, the new-look Chiefs offense has kept things rolling.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs Week 6 snap count analysis: Andrew Armstrong steps up
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs’ snap counts in the 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Jay Biggerstaff-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Let’s take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs ’ snap counts in the 22-6 win over the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 6. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus’ premium stats. Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Andrew Armstrong, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, CB Christian Roland-Wallace, CB Mansoor Delane, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner Did not play: QB Justin Fields Inactive: TE Jared Wiley, QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), DB Jadon Canady, DE Jack Pyburn, OT Diego Pounds, LT Josh Simmons (Back), WR Rashee Rice (Hamstring) The big takeaway: Andrew Armstrong steps up in first career start With wide receiver Rashee Rice (hamstring) ruled out on the final injury report, the Chiefs elevated second-year wideout Andrew Armstrong from the practice squad. He lined up on the opening snap, marking his first career start. It was the first of 42 snaps Armstrong played on offense, starting alongside Xavier Worthy (51) and Jalen Royals (45); he caught a 13-yard pass on one of the two passes thrown his way. Armstrong spent 12 snaps in the slot and 14 snaps on the perimeter of the offense, signaling the use of Armstrong’s blocking near the line of scrimmage on run plays. He lined up for 15 run plays, nearly as much as Worthy (18) and Royals (17). I don’t need a PFF “run-blocking” grade to know Armstrong was an impactful blocker. With an offense built around running back Kenneth Walker gashing defenses, the question becomes whether Armstrong deserves a spot on the active roster, maybe in favor of the return specialist Nikko Remigio. The Offensive takeaway: Joshua Ezeudu plays the whole second half After right tackle Jaylon Moore entered concussion protocol late in the first half, backup Joshua Ezeudu took over on the right edge and stayed there for the rest of the afternoon. He played 30 snaps, 17 of them on pass plays. PFF faulted Ezeudu with one pressure and a hurry, so he kept Mahomes clean in his first time in the lineup for the Chiefs’ offense. After the preseason, he was traded to Kansas City from the New York Giants after spending most of his career at left guard or tackle with Big Blue. It will be interesting to see whether the lineup shifts moving forward, even if left tackle Josh Simmons (back) isn’t ready for Week 7. Also noteworthy is third tight end Jake Briningstool, who played the most snaps (10) he has since Week 1 and made an impactful block to spring running back Kenneth Walker for the 33-yard touchdown run in the first quarter. The Defensive takeaway: Ashton Gillotte ascends in the rotation Second-year defensive end Ashton Gillotte played the fourth-most snaps among the team’s defensive linemen on Sunday, on the field for 52% of the defense’s snaps. In that time, he registered three pressures: a hurry, a quarterback hit and a sack that broke the seal on the Chiefs’ four-sack game. He earned two “Stops,” tackles that count as failures for the offense. It was Gillotte’s biggest timeshare in the Chiefs’ starting lineup this season, and his most impactful performance. He, along with rookie edge rusher R Mason Thomas (five pressures), was constantly in the backfield on Sunday afternoon and is a positive indicator for the pass rush moving forward. title: 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ Week 6 victory over the Chargers
summary: Coming off the bye, the Kansas City Chiefs entered this game looking to go 3-0 against AFC West opponents this season. It was evident from the jump who the better team was. The Chiefs didn’t play a perfect game, and at times it felt like they were coasting, but they dominated all four quarters. Kansas […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Coming off the bye, the Kansas City Chiefs entered this game looking to go 3-0 against AFC West opponents this season. It was evident from the jump who the better team was. The Chiefs didn’t play a perfect game, and at times it felt like they were coasting, but they dominated all four quarters. Kansas City’s pass rushers and standout running back Kenneth Walker III were especially impressive in the Chiefs’ 22-6 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers . Here are five things we learned from the Chiefs stealing the Chargers’ lunch money: 1. K9 is not just the top dog; he’s the NFL MVP Through the first six weeks of the season, this isn’t even up for debate. I know the NFL decided in some nefarious back-channel meeting that the NFL MVP is now a quarterback award. The only exception is when a running back is having a truly transcendent year—well, Kenneth Walker III is doing just that. Over five games, Walker has 665 rushing yards and averages 6.2 yards per carry, with eight total touchdowns. For reference, the last time a non-quarterback won the NFL MVP was in 2012 when Minnesota Vikings running back Adrian Peterson won the award. That season, Peterson rushed for 2,097 yards and 13 total touchdowns, averaging six yards per carry. Before Peterson won the award, you have to go back to 2006 to find the next season a non-quarterback won the MVP. Chargers running back LaDainian Tomlinson won that year. Interestingly, in 2005, Seattle Seahawks running back Shaun Alexander also won MVP. In 2006, Tomlinson ran for 1,815 yards and 31 total touchdowns, averaging 5.2 yards per carry. In 2005, Alexander ran 1,880 yards and 28 total touchdowns, averaging 5.1 yards per carry. It’s still early, and Walker needs to keep up this pace and stay healthy for the rest of the season, but right now, Walker is on pace to rush for 2,260 yards and 27 total touchdowns. Those numbers would not only surpass Peterson’s 2012 MVP campaign, but also beat Los Angeles Rams Eric Dickerson’s all-time single-season rushing record of 2,105 yards that has stood since 1984. Even more impressive. He’s on pace for 2,583 all-purpose yards, which would also beat Tennessee Titans running back Chris Johnson’s 2009 record of 2,509 yards, Walker isn’t just on pace for a great season; he’s on pace for the greatest season of any running back in NFL history. Kenneth Walker III kept rolling with another huge game for Kansas City. 19 CAR, 128 RUSH YDS, 6.7 YPC, 2 TD, 2 REC, 11 REC YDS Walker continues to build a serious OPOY case in his first season with the Chiefs. pic.twitter.com/H7UDopZeHW https://t.co/g2cWBUkgRc — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) October 18, 2026 2. Chiefs are the Kings of the West It feels good to be back on the throne. With this victory over the Chargers, the Chiefs have ensured they will have at least a .500 record against AFC West opponents this season. With the Las Vegas Raiders losing to the Buffalo Bills , the Raiders are 3-3, and the Denver Broncos are the Chiefs’ next closest opponents at 4-2. But let’s be honest: after watching Bo Nix’s ineptitude and the rest of Denver’s offense, do you really think they have what it takes to catch up with the Chiefs? As for the Chargers, they look like the worst team in the NFL. No, they look worse than bad. They look cursed. Sports have a long history of cursed franchises. The reasons a franchise might be cursed range from how fans treat it to trading a legendary player. In the Chargers case, I’m going to jump to an unfounded conclusion and say it’s because they left San Diego. They are being punished from the great beyond by a spirit who is angry they relocated to Los Angeles. San Diego loved that franchise, and they left it for the bright lights of Hollywood. The only question is, whose spirit is responsible for tormenting them? Personally, as a Chiefs fan, I hope it’s Marty Schottenheimer. 3. Nikko Remigio is not as dependable as we were told We were told Nikko Remigio was the Chiefs’ kick and punt returner because he was dependable and does not put the ball on the ground. Well, that changed in this game. He fumbled once and nearly fumbled again, but he was saved because he was down by a hair. The Chiefs also had a block in the back on the play where Remigio fumbled. Harrison Butker missed a point-after attempt and has only made 25% of his attempts from 50+ yards. It doesn’t matter if you can kick the ball a mile if you can’t kick it straight. Not a great day for Harrison Butker. Good from 44, misses wide right from 52, and missed a PAT. — Matt Derrick (@mattderrick) October 18, 2026 4. A bad offensive line makes your pass rush look awesome Chiefs edge rusher George Karlaftis brought his hardhat and lunchpail to work today, and proceeded to abuse the Chargers’ battered offensive line. In fact, nearly everyone joined in on the fun of bullying the human-shaped cutouts the Chargers propped up in front of Justin Herbert. Ashton Gillotte, Peter Woods, and Felix Anudike-Uzomah all hit the quarterback. And just like their last game against the Raiders, when the Chiefs needed somebody to step up and close out the game, the pass rush showed up, with R Mason Thomas beating his man around the edge and hitting Justin Herbert’s arm as he threw. Chiefs edge rushers today: – George Karlaftis: 26.3% pressure rate, 2.33 time to pressure, 1 sack, 2 TFLs – R Mason Thomas: 20.8% pressure rate, 2.31 time to pressure — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) October 19, 2026 5. The Chiefs need Josh Simmons Not because the offensive line played bad today. On the contrary, I thought it was one of their better games this season. But they also took their lumps. Right tackle Jaylon Moore left the game with a concussion. Left guard Suamataia had a calf stinger. Diego Pounds has been inactive all season. But even if fully healthy, the Chiefs didn’t have much depth on the offensive line. Despite playing admirably, I don’t feel great about the Chiefs running out Kahlil Benson and Joshua Ezeudu for a full four quarters against the Seahawks next week. Trying to tackle Kenneth Walker does NOT look fun pic.twitter.com/FtfvsQo2g1 — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) October 4, 2026

title: Chargers Week 6 PFF Grades: Offense hits low point against Chiefs
summary: The Chargers offense is the single most-inefficient group in the entire NFL. They’re 32nd in EPA/play and Sunday loss to the Chiefs was a new low point as they failed to reach the end zone for the first time this season. They scored six points all game, none of which came following any of the […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Cam Hart #20 of the Los Angeles Chargers celebrates after an interception against the Kansas City Chiefs in the second quarter of a game at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers offense is the single most-inefficient group in the entire NFL. They’re 32nd in EPA/play and Sunday loss to the Chiefs was a new low point as they failed to reach the end zone for the first time this season. They scored six points all game, none of which came following any of the Chiefs’ three turnovers. Those three takeaways turned into a pair of punts and a turnover of their own. The Chargers even had the ball at the one-yard line with four downs to score and they still kicked a field goal! Each week this group looks even more helpless than the last and now that they’ve hit their bye week, changes can expected. In what could have been the final game called by Mike McDaniel in LA, here’s how things were graded out for the Chargers. Offense Best WR Ladd McConkey – 70.3 OT Travis Burke – 68.7 C Jake Slaughter – 64.9 WR Derius Davis – 61.3 QB Justin Herbert – 60.5 McConkey returned from miss the last two games to play just eight snaps before exiting with yet another injury, this one to his head. His one catch for 17 yards was almost good enough to lead the team in receiving before Quentin Johnston’s 57-yard reception. Burke continues to be the Chargers’ best healthy offensive lineman. He was steady across the board with a 65.5 in pass blocking and a 68.0 in run blocking. Slaughter had a pair of penalties, including a back-breaking holding call at the one-yard line. He still finished with a pass block grade of 75.6 (first among OL) and a run block grade of 67.7. Worst OG Logan Taylor – 40.5 WR KeAndre Lambert-Smith – 46.7 WR Quentin Johnston – 47.6 RB Keaton Mitchell – 49.3 TE Oronde Gadden II – 49.4 Another rough game for Taylor who is playing out of position at guard. His 47.0 pass block grade was second worst to Alex Harkey while his 37.9 in run blocking was worst among OL. Lambert-Smith had a pair of penalties and lost a fumble on a catch that otherwise would have gone for a first down. Johnston had another drop but ultimately was the recipient of the Chargers’ longest play of the season with a 57-yard grab. Funny enough, it looked like he caught it on accident as it lodged between his arm and shoulder pad as he fell to the ground. Defense Best CB Cam Hart – 89.1 LB Marlowe Wax – 81.5 LB Troy Dye – 76.3 S Tony Jefferson – 73.4 CB Isas Waxter – 72.1 Hart picked off Patrick Mahomes in the end zone for his second interception of the season. He ended with an elite 91.1 coverage grade after allowing one reception for four yards. Wax and Dye combined to play just 15 snaps together but they were both solid with grades above 70.0 in both run defense and tackling. Jefferson had the second-best tackling grade (81.9), the third-best run defense grade (69.3), and the fourth-best coverage grade (69.0). Cam Hart picks off Mahomes in the end zone ‼️ LACvsKC on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/zWLXiWFXZb — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Worst S Genesis Smith – 29.2 LB Del’Shawn Phillips – 29.5 CB Deane Leonard – 33.1 DT Teair Tart – 37.0 EDGE Tuli Tuipulotu – 43.0 Smith continues to have a very up-and-down rookie season. His 95.0 game grade in Week Three is still an enormous outlier compared to his three games with a grade of 35.5 or lower, including two below 30.0. However, he remains a very consistent tackler, posting a 75.2 or higher in that area through the first five games of the season. He only allowed one reception for 12 yards against the Chiefs, but that completion went to Travis Kelce for a first down on third-and-11. Phillips recorded a team-low 29.8 coverage grade after allowing all three targets his way to be completed for 62, almost half of which came after the catch (28). His 26.9 tackling grade was also the worst on the team. Leonard allowed two completions on two targets for 32 yards and was called for a DPI (that honestly should not have been flagged). Tart recorded the team’s lowest run defense grade at 34.0. Tuli finished with a 45.0 run defense grade (second worst) and a 42.7 in coverage (fourth worst). His pass rush grade of 59.3 was fourth best on the team, but not enough to make up for the low marks elsewhere.

title: Los Angeles Chargers news: Will Bolts make changes during the bye?
summary: The Chargers fell 22-6 to the Chiefs on Sunday and at 0-6, it’s time to ask the unsurprising question: Will we see the Chargers make any changes during the bye? For the first time all season, Jim Harbaugh was non-committal to Mike McDaniel’s job security. When asked if play-calling duties would be taken from him, […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - OCTOBER 18: Justin Herbert #10 of the Los Angeles Chargers gets up after a tackle during the third quarter of an NFL football game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chargers fell 22-6 to the Chiefs on Sunday and at 0-6, it’s time to ask the unsurprising question: Will we see the Chargers make any changes during the bye? For the first time all season, Jim Harbaugh was non-committal to Mike McDaniel’s job security. When asked if play-calling duties would be taken from him, Harbaugh simply said, “We’ll look at everything.” It’s not much, but it’s enough to start believing the writing is on the wall for the former Dolphins head coach. Sunday’s loss to the Chiefs was the team’s first game where they did not find the end zone once and their six points were the lowest scoring output of the season thus far, as well. When thinking about the failures of this organization through six weeks, McDaniel’s lack off results is certainly up there, but the failures of this team spread far beyond just his inability to coach and teach this offense even to a serviceable level. So who do we think will be shown the door first? Who will be the first sacrificial lamb of this abysmal season? We want to hear all of your thoughts below! And now for today’s links.
