title: The Miami Dolphins are one step closer to this year’s ultimate prize
summary: Miami Dolphins fans have officially entered the part of the season where we start looking at draft prospects instead of playoff scenarios. At 0-5, the Dolphins are still searching for their first victory coming off of the bye week. Fortunately, they got a little help on Sunday without even putting on their helmets. The Cam […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - OCTOBER 11: Head coach Jeff Hafley of the Miami Dolphins looks on before a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Hard Rock Stadium on October 11, 2026 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Carmen Mandato/Getty Images) | Getty Images Miami Dolphins fans have officially entered the part of the season where we start looking at draft prospects instead of playoff scenarios. At 0-5, the Dolphins are still searching for their first victory coming off of the bye week. Fortunately, they got a little help on Sunday without even putting on their helmets. The Cam Ward led Tennessee Titans finally won a game, beating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 and leaving Miami and the Los Angeles Chargers as the NFL’s only winless teams. And while the Chargers currently hold the top spot in the projected draft order at 0-6, don’t be surprised if Miami eventually overtakes them. In fact, the Dolphins look like the favorites to land the first overall selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. The Chargers have too much talent to stay this bad Let’s start with Los Angeles. The Chargers have Justin Herbert at quarterback, talented young playmakers like Ladd McConkey and Oronde Gadsden Jr. and an established head coach. Despite their miserable start, there’s enough talent on that roster to believe they’ll eventually stumble into a victory or two. Of course, the Chargers are currently 0-6, so apparently stumbling into a victory is easier said than done. They just lost 22-6 to Kansas City, and their Mike McDaniel coached offense couldn’t turn a trip to the Chiefs’ 1-yard line into a touchdown. Man, that sounds famliar… Los Angeles has a stronger foundation than Miami at several key positions. However, the Chargers also face a difficult schedule, which keeps them firmly in the conversation for the first pick. But eventually, talent has to count for something. Right? The Titans already ruined their chances Tennessee entered Week 6 alongside Miami and Los Angeles as one of the National Football League’s three winless teams. Then the Titans ruined a perfectly good tanking party by rallying from a 13-point halftime deficit to beat the Indianapolis Colts. Congratulations, Tennessee fans! Your reward is a 1-5 record and a slightly worse chance at drafting the player who could change your franchise’s future. ( cough, cough… Jeremiah Smith ) The Titans still have plenty of problems, but that victory gives Miami some breathing room in the race for the bottom. Is Tennessee done winning, or can they continue to build momentum and sneak out another victory or two? The Dolphins are built for this Here are the cold, hard facts — the Dolphins simply don’t have enough proven talent to consistently compete with most NFL teams right now. The quarterback situation remains murky. The roster has holes at multiple positions, and as a result, the coaching staff is trying to build something while dealing with the consequences of a difficult transition. Miami could certainly win a game or two, especially since they’ve been playing closer games as of late. The NFL is unpredictable — just ask my betting slips — and even the worst teams occasionally find a way to win. But the Dolphins have a legitimate argument as the league’s least complete team. If Los Angeles eventually gets a few wins from Herbert and his supporting cast, Miami could find themselves alone at the bottom. And for a franchise that desperately needs an infusion of star quality talent, that top selection could be enormously valuable. The race is on Listen, I know… nobody wants to watch their team go winless. But if the playoffs are already out of reach, Miami needs to find a way to make this season count for something. Continue to develop the rookies. Continue to evaluate the young players. Figure out which veterans belong on this team in the future. And, yes, keep an eye on the draft order. It’s not the kind of race any fan wants to win before the season starts. But after five weeks without a victory, Dolphins fans might as well start rooting for the one thing this team can still accomplish — earning the number one pick in the 2027 NFL Draft.

title: Miami Dolphins offense: How to solve a problem like Malik Willis?
summary: Let us start with some stipulations: #1) We assume the Miami Dolphins’ coaching staff knows more about football than we do. As they put it in the U.K., “Is that strictly true?” I have been watching football for at least 55 years. This is how we true Phin fans can tell aurum (Latin for gold) […]
full_text: Dan the Man throwing off his front foot. Look at that beautiful air-to-air missile! | Paul Fields Let us start with some stipulations: #1) We assume the Miami Dolphins’ coaching staff knows more about football than we do. As they put it in the U.K., “Is that strictly true?” I have been watching football for at least 55 years. This is how we true Phin fans can tell aurum (Latin for gold) from pyrite (fool’s gold). We’ve seen the one-year flashes (Gase, Sparano, and McDaniel) all end in first-round WIMPY playoff losses, and not even make it back the second year (except for McDaniel). Wanny won the last playoff game. I was there. Sorry for repeating myself. We all knew these teams were mirages in the Phins’ playoff desert. We see inferior QB play, inferior, untimely defense, inferior play calling, and, most importantly, inferior talent. If we dumbutt fans (who supposedly know zero about football—infinitely less than the all-knowing coaches) can see these flaws, why can’t the GMs and coaches? Why can’t the coaches elevate these players? You may say… Paul: “Maybe they elevated them as far as those players could go?” Hmmm, perhaps. Malik, Malik, Malik – why isn’t he getting better? Stipulation #2) do the coaches really, really want him to get better and maybe win us 3 to 4 games this year(yes, laugh with me, please)? To counter that, under the prior regime with Grier, good draft positions and quantities DID NOT pan out. With Mr. Sullivan making the picks, I do feel much better about us making the safe/prudent pick VERSUS reaching for potential (Dion Jordan, Ryan Tannehill, etc). All that said, I want Malik to work out for us, as a starter or maybe the Don Strock/Earl Morrall role. I will defend Malik for a second: He originally went to Auburn under Gus Malzahn and did NOT develop because he is NOT a Cam Newton or a Nick Marshall (who was born to run Malzahn’s offense). Malzahn’s offense revolves heavily around the run game and DEEP SHOTS (aka receiver go long). The deep shot plays usually revolve around one WR going long. And virtually no check-downs. These are exceptions to everything I am saying right now. This is the OPPOSITE of McDaniel’s timing-and-precision offense (which is why Herbert has had trouble running it). So Malik was corrupted by Malzahn (Michael Silver wrote an entire article on how Malzahn ruined Jarrett Stidham). Anyhoo, Malik ended up at Liberty under Hugh Freeze, who runs similar concepts to Malzahn (they are friends in real life). If you recall Malik’s Liberty highlights, they were long shots were the WR tried to set up post corners to freeze the safety until the WR commits, then pray the WR can split the corner and the safety for long gains. The offense relies on the run game forcing safeties and corners up, then taking deep shots. The problem is you’ve gotta hit the deep shots, and this all goes back to expected probability (I think I mentioned previously that Howard Schnelleberger would routinely spout the average completion percentages of every pass play). Malzahn and Freeze figure that if they get the right defense shown to them, they can call seven deep shots and maybe hit three for 40–60 yards each. That adds up to 120–180 yards per game on the deep shots, plus 220 rushing yards (at a minimum), for 400 yards per game. A normal passing offense throws, let’s say, 25 completed passes for an average of 10 yards, for a total of 250 yards, requiring 20–25 completions on 40 attempts. Malik hit his share of deep shots at Liberty, and those “go” routes made him look like Joe Montana. Not really. Montana is the definition of precision throwing, and Mark Schlereth repeated the mantra this past Sunday: “There is no defense for the perfect throw.” For you younger readers, look up the pass play the 49ers pulled off with Dwight Clark against the Cowboys in the NFC Championship Game. It looked like playground stuff, but it was a play they practiced ad nauseam. Since we don’t know as much as the Phins’ offensive staff about the other stipulations, that leads us to stipulation #3: The coaches ARE probably coaching him, and he is not absorbing it. One of our collaborators in the feed, Gilmiaspr, wrote a beautiful piece about 10 Malik plays from the Bengals game. Well done piece, sir! I would challenge you (if you had time) to look at his feet placement on his throws, and I will wager they are wrong. He has lots of trouble with pocket awareness and premature pocket escapulation (sorry for the obvious pun). You may ask yourself: when Marino had a collapsing pocket, why/how was Marino able to fire passes off almost every time? First, he had an innate sense of how much time he had to throw. Yes, he had a quick release, but that alone doesn’t put the ball generally where it needs to be. He had to know, I am hitting Duper on a crosser, and that takes him 3 seconds to flash in front of me. So if they blitz, I know I can’t wait that long, so I will go for Tony Nathan on the checkdown or throw the ball in the dirt. Or, oftentimes, Marino simply took a step left or right, planted his right foot, and fired his weight forward to drive the ball. I honestly don’t recall Malik planting and firing like that. He runs too quickly, which puts his feet out of position (he ain’t Mahomes-the absolute G.O.A.T. of making precision throws while contorting himself). This is the number one reason his throws are off target. He must plant and fire. This is the step where the coaches need to coach! Give the man a friggin check down. After Nathan retired, Marino had fullback Tony Paige (remember him?) to check down. Paige would torture teams who doubled whatever WRs, or if they copied the Marino kryptonite from the 49ers, and rushed three and dropped eight. He would catch a 3-yard pass and turn it into seven to ten yards. And they would move Paige around like a rook in chess so teams couldn’t get a read on where he would be. ACTION PLAN So to wrap up for now: an action plan that we all know but we must say it loud. Malik, stay in the pocket, and maybe a take sack when YOU are looking downfield. You gotta dive into the deep part of the pool. Yes, it is scary but you make millions of dollars. You gotta lean forward and throw on your front foot. The ball will obey. Photo of #13 as a guide. If you feel the pocket collapsing, step up or to either side. Work on the internal brain clock. You have 4 seconds to throw. Or less. If you run, don’t go all the way back into your drop before making your decision to run. Run then! Many DL don’t even look up until they pushed their guys back a yard or two. This eye discipline is how teams take out Lamar Jackson in the playoffs. IF you take off a couple of times before they push all the way, then you can plant the seed in the DLs mind. Every second that passes in the pocket the LBs can drop back 2.5 yards in their zones which allows them to cover more side-to-side space. Think of a right triangle. I will draw that out soon. Turns out trigonometry applies to football. Who knew? Find you a reliable check down player (Tony Paige, Tony Nathan, Terry Kirby, Troy Stradford, Keith Byars….I love you all) Make then spy you and also make them spy the check down. Reconcile in your mind how the most unathletic physical specimen to ever play QB (I won’t say his name)has 7 Super Bowl rings. Allow me this one indulgence, please! War Damn Eagle! Finally beat the UGA Bulldogs. Reminded me of JJ’s first year with the Phins when we broke the Buffalo streak against us. 16-14 in Miami.

title: Vikings Trade Deadline Targets: Buckner, Taylor, Bynum & More
summary: The Minnesota Vikings are 5-0 and reportedly ready to be aggressive at the trade deadline. Who should they target? That’s the question driving the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, where host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano fired up the brand-new A to Z Sports Trade Simulator to break down every realistic target […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: General manger Nolan Teasley of the Minnesota Vikings looks on before a game against the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings are 5-0 and reportedly ready to be aggressive at the trade deadline. Who should they target? That’s the question driving the latest episode of The Real Forno Show, where host Tyler Forness and producer Dave Stefano fired up the brand-new A to Z Sports Trade Simulator to break down every realistic target — from DeForest Buckner to Saquon Barkley to Cam Bynum. “If the Vikings want to truly make a Super Bowl run they should make a couple of trades and fortify the roster,” Forness said, pointing to past champions like the 2021 Rams adding Odell Beckham Jr. and the Seahawks acquiring Rashid Shaheed as proof that late-season additions matter. GM Nolan Teasley comes from an aggressive organization and has been calling around. “We’ve heard Nolan Teasley’s calling around,” Forness noted. “All the beat reporters like the Vikings are going to add people.” Key points from the episode: DeForest Buckner is the #1 target. “I think the number one player I wanna bring in of anybody that I think could realistically be available is DeForest Buckner,” Forness said. Beyond the playoff push, he sees Buckner as a developmental mentor for rookie Caleb Banks due to their similar builds (6’6″+, 34-35″ arms) and leverage techniques. Likely cost: a third-round pick plus a token sixth. Justin Herbert doesn’t fit. Despite tantalizing arm talent, Forness has major concerns: “I have concerns that he doesn’t fit this offense.” He questioned whether three first-round picks is worth it for a QB thriving in Sean Payton/Joe Lombardi systems, not Kevin O’Connell’s anticipatory West Coast offense. Quenton Nelson is a risky rental. Stefano noted Nelson is “the fourth-ranked guard in PFF right now” and “a Pro Bowl guard,” but Forness pushed back on spending two thirds for a 30-year-old rental when Donovan Jackson is expected back for the playoffs. Jonathan Taylor carries too much tread. With 2,599 carries since college vs. Jordan Mason’s 859, Forness cautioned: “Tread on the tires matters with running backs. It, we don’t want it to, but it does.” Likely cost: a second-round pick. Cam Bynum reunion makes sense. With Theo Jackson struggling, Forness explained: “This is a PhD level defense where rookies don’t often get a lot of playing time.” Bynum already knows Brian Flores’ system, eliminating the learning curve. Proposed deal: a third, a fifth, and Theo Jackson for Bynum and a fourth. Saquon Barkley is within reach. A third-round pick plus a fifth could land the Eagles star, creating a devastating trio with Aaron Jones and Jordan Mason. Pass rush is the priority. “Pass rush, defensive line, I think that should be the priority,” Forness said, noting Jalen Redmond, Andrew Van Ginkel, and Dallas Turner are all playing 80-90% of snaps. Kevin O’Connell isn’t going anywhere. “You are not going to find better as a head coach if you fire him,” Forness said bluntly. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: Whether it’s Buckner anchoring the defensive line, Bynum steadying the secondary, or a surprise running back addition, the Vikings have the capital and urgency to make a Super Bowl push. For the full breakdown with trade simulator point values, salary analysis, and player comparisons, watch The Real Forno Show — a Minnesota Vikings podcast from Vikings 1st & SKOL on the Bleav Network. So here’s a question for you: Which trade target would you prioritize, and would you give up the draft capital to get it done?

summary: The Minnesota Vikings are beginning their preparations for their Week 7 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts at U.S. Bank Stadium, and they could be getting some reinforcements in the backfield. The team has announced that running back Jordan Mason has been designated to return to practice by the team, opening his 21-day window to return […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - SEPTEMBER 13: Jordan Mason #27 of the Minnesota Vikings runs the ball against the Green Bay Packers in the fourth quarter of a game at U.S. Bank Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings are beginning their preparations for their Week 7 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts at U.S. Bank Stadium, and they could be getting some reinforcements in the backfield. The team has announced that running back Jordan Mason has been designated to return to practice by the team, opening his 21-day window to return from injured reserve. Mason was placed on IR by the Vikings the day after their season-opening win over the Green Bay Packers, when he sustained a thumb injury that required him to undergo surgery. Mason led the team in rushing that afternoon with 59 yards and a touchdown on 15 carries. With the Vikings having their bye this past week, he’s now had five full weeks to recover from the injury, so it wouldn’t be out of the question to see the team bring him back in time for this Sunday’s game against the Colts. In Mason’s absence, Aaron Jones has taken on a significant workload in the Vikings’ backfield. Jones has gone over the 100-yard mark twice in the season’s first five games and is currently tenth in the NFL in rushing yardage. If Mason can return and stay on the field, he should be able to form a very solid tandem with Jones and help to keep both of them fresh for the latter part of the season. We’ll be keeping an eye on Jordan Mason’s situation as the Vikings prepare for Sunday’s game, but here’s hoping that we’ll be able to see #27 line up in the Minnesota backfield this weekend for the first time since the regular season opener.

title: Patriots vs. Jets position grades and film review from Week 6
summary: They can’t all be blowouts, can they? Coming off a convincing 45-17 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders, the New England Patriots found themselves in a much more competitive game versus the New York Jets. A big reason for the game’s comparatively close nature was the Patriots’ own inability to play consistent football between turnovers, […]
full_text: They can’t all be blowouts, can they? Coming off a convincing 45-17 victory over the Las Vegas Raiders, the New England Patriots found themselves in a much more competitive game versus the New York Jets. A big reason for the game’s comparatively close nature was the Patriots’ own inability to play consistent football between turnovers, dropped passes and uneven run defense. At the end of the day, they still managed to do enough to secure a 26-19 win and improve to 4-2 on the season. It wasn’t overly pretty, but it was still winning football at the end of the day. Let’s take a look at the film and hand out some grades. Patriots film review from NFL Week 6 Quarterback: The typically blitz-heavy Jets decided to alter their approach against Drake Maye, playing a less aggressive form of defense while simultaneously trying to contain him as best they could. They did a solid job, but at the end of the day New England’s quarterback was simply better. Maye delivered some good throws throughout the day, took what the defense gave him, showed some anticipation (see: 3rd-and-10 throw to Kyle Williams), made sound decisions, and once again played at a consistently high level both when throwing the ball and picking his spots to advance it with his legs. His 0.39 expected points added per play are a reflection of that. | Grade: A Running back: Rhamondre Stevenson averaged only 2.6 yards per carry, but he did what he could: he forced four missed tackles and finished with 36 yards after contact on 36 total rushing yards. He also continued to do some good work as a pass protector, giving up one hurry in 11 reps. TreVeyon Henderson played a limited role after suffering an ankle sprain last week, but he mostly moved well and again showed that he is at his best when operating in space. He did lose a fumble, though, which might have contributed to Corey Kiner seeing some action late . Kiner hit the holes hard and kept the legs churning through contact. | Grade: A- Fantastic rep by #Patriots RB Rhamondre Stevenson in pass pro passing off this stunt with LT Will Campbell and completely eliminating Will McDonald's loop. pic.twitter.com/eUypawhA6E — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) October 19, 2026 Wide receiver: The Patriots’ wide receiver group had a rollercoaster day. Romeo Doubs got open for a 42-yard touchdown on the second snap of the day, but suffered a game-ending shoulder injury along the way. DeMario Douglas led the team with seven catches for 86 yards and a touchdown, but he also lost a fumble when somewhat unnecessarily trying to turn a big play into an even bigger one. Kyle Williams caught just one pass, but it was a big one and showed he can do more than just run go routes. Efton Chism played the second-most snaps among the group but did not finish with any catches while also being uneven as a run blocker. And then, there was A.J. Brown. Making his return from a four-week stint on injured reserve, the veteran was rusty particularly as a finisher: he had two drops and multiple other close calls while catching only three passes for 27 yards. On the bright side, he did manage to get open a lot. Drake Maye targeting Brown 10 times was therefore not a case of force-feeding him; throwing to him was the right read more often than not. | Grade: C+ Tight end: Hunter Henry continues to be one of the most reliable players on the Patriots’ roster, especially as a receiver. He showed good wiggle on a 16-yard catch-and-run on the final drive of the first half, and was able to get wide open on his 7-yard touchdown catch. His run blocking was not quite as consistent (one stuff, one penalty). Eli Raridon also had his ups and downs. He did make a nice adjustment on an 11-yard catch in the third quarter, but could have held onto a touchdown in the late second; he also was at the point of attack on a pair of stuffed runs, but performed well as a move blocker. The same is true for Cameron Latu. | Grade: B+ Offensive line: Even though it lost three starters due to injury during the game, the Patriots offensive line generally played at a high level against a defense that had averaged 3.4 sacks per game coming in. Drake Maye was kept clean for much of the day, with the Jets taking him down not even once. Then, late in the game, the unit — using third-string left guard Walter Rouse and fourth-string right guard Matt Pryor — asserted its will in the run game: the group controlled the line of scrimmage, allowing Corey Kiner to keep advancing the ball on eight straight plays. That said, the performance had its moments but was not consistent, especially on the interior. Run blocking was a concern even before the injuries, and both Rouse and center Jared Wilson had a few bad reps between them down the stretch. On the bright side, Will Campbell played some quality football despite nursing a knee injury, while Caleb Lomu mostly performed well after entering for an injured Morgan Moses. With Campbell and Lomu in the fold, the future seems bright at that position for New England. | Grade: B+ Will Campbell 'influence' vs Enagbare 💪 pic.twitter.com/6SuHgF9JhX — Brandon Thorn (@BrandonThornNFL) October 19, 2026 Defensive line: The Jets were able to create some movement on the line of scrimmage, and exploit New England’s defense for multiple long runs. Looking at the film, however, it appeared to be less of a performance issue and more of New York doing its homework and being able to use Zak Kuhr’s aggressive approach against him and his defense. There were still problems with misplacement and disengagement, but the Patriots’ talent up front also shone through on multiple occasions. That included Milton Williams and Christian Barmore registering back-to-back sacks — the second featuring a dominant bull-rushing rep from Barmore — while rotational backups Cory Durden, DaQuan Jones and Leonard Taylor had some good moments too. The edge trio of Elijah Ponder, Gabe Jacas and Dre’Mont Jones also continued to be disruptive. Jones was at his best setting an edge in the run game, but was a bit more quiet as a pass rusher. Ponder and Jacas flashed their varied skillsets on multiple reps. | Grade: B One of a couple reps where Gabe Jacas swam Jelani Woods into the void Can make TEs look bad with power or finesse pic.twitter.com/QI6FGAHe1A — Taylor Kyles (@tkyles39) October 19, 2026 Linebacker: Robert Spillane continues to be the glue that holds the operation together, and one of the most impactful players on the Patriots roster. His run stuff on 4th-and-2 in the early second quarter against a charging Braelon Allen was an impressive display of his ability to hunker down and hold the line. He also was effective as a run blitzer on multiple occasion. He finished the game with three run stuffs, compared to two by his running mate Christian Elliss. They both had missed tackles as well, and also contributed to the Jets finding success with their turning-the-aggressiveness-against-the-defense plan, but on the whole had a quality outing. | Grade: A – Cornerback: Christian Gonzalez did give up four catches for 45 yards on the day, but only two of those for 20 combined yards came against the Jets’ top receiver. Going up against Garrett Wilson on 17 reps, the Patriots’ No. 1 cornerback more than held his own and forced quarterback Geno Smith to look away from his favorite target repeatedly. Another good outing against a top-tier player. Elsewhere at cornerback, Marcus Jones had a very good day in the office playing both outside and in the slot; he allowed just two passes to be completed to his part of the field. Charles Woods, who again filled in for Carlton Davis as a perimeter corner opposite Gonzalez, looked as good as you would expect a backup to look: there were some hiccups staying with his responsibilities out of bunch formations, but he mostly was well-positioned including on his interception — a play that allowed him to dust off the old receiver skills . | Grade: A Safety: Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson had some good…
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Romeo Doubs injury: Patriots get positive update on star WR
summary: Amid a series of roster moves on Monday, the New England Patriots also decided to place wide receiver Romeo Doubs on injured reserve. As a consequence, the offseason signing will be out for at least the next four games. The absence being much longer than that, however, is not expected. According to a report by […]
full_text: Amid a series of roster moves on Monday, the New England Patriots also decided to place wide receiver Romeo Doubs on injured reserve. As a consequence, the offseason signing will be out for at least the next four games. The absence being much longer than that, however, is not expected. According to a report by Jeremy Fowler of ESPN, Doubs is “hopeful to return after the Week 11 bye” and that the current belief is that his stint on IR will not be a “long-term” affair. Doubs, 26, hurt his shoulder during the Patriots’ 26-19 win over the New York Jets on Sunday. He came down hard after catching a 42-yard touchdown on his team’s second offensive snap of the day, and subsequently exited the contest. Initially deemed questionable to return, he was ruled out for the remainder of the game at the start of the third quarter. On Monday, he was sent to injured reserve. Per NFL rules, Doubs will therefore not be eligible to start practicing until after New England’s Week 10 game versus the Detroit Lions. The timing is favorable for player and club alike, though. With the Patriots on a bye coming out of their cross-Atlantic trip to play the Lions in Germany, Doubs will have an extra week to get up to speed before his team’s next game against the Los Angeles Chargers in Week 12. With Doubs on IR, the Patriots have four receivers remaining on their active roster. A.J. Brown, who himself returned from an ankle injury just last week and made his comeback against the Jets, as well as DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism. Mack Hollins, who has been on injured reserve since Week 5 with a calf issue, will be eligible to return to practice and the 53-man team in Week 9. The Patriots will travel to Chicago this week to face the Bears on Thursday Night Football.

title: Patriots injury analysis after Jets win in Week 6
summary: The New England Patriots have started hitting their strides. Winning three games in a row, they again look like one of the best teams in football and a serious contender for a playoff spot in the AFC. At the same time, however, they continue being followed by some bad injury luck. Their 26-19 win over […]
full_text: The New England Patriots have started hitting their strides. Winning three games in a row, they again look like one of the best teams in football and a serious contender for a playoff spot in the AFC. At the same time, however, they continue being followed by some bad injury luck. Their 26-19 win over the New York Jets on Sunday saw multiple players exit with injury, including one — wide receiver Romeo Doubs — who has since been placed on injured reserve and will therefore be out at least four games. Receiver depth is not the only concern, however, as a look at our weekly injury analysis after rewatching the game shows. Patriots injury analysis: NFL Week 6 WR Romeo Doubs: On the second offensive snap of the day, Doubs was able to get open behind the Jets defense and haul in a 42-yard touchdown pass from Drake Maye. However, he came down hard on his shoulder while completing the catch and remained kneeling in the end zone afterwards. He ultimately did get up, but headed straight into the blue medical tent and later the locker room with a shoulder injury. He never returned. RT Morgan Moses: While most of the initial attention on the unsuccessful deep ball to A.J. Brown in the early second quarter was on the receiver, it quickly shifted to the Patriots’ right tackle. Morgan Moses remained down on the ground. He had pushed Jets pass rusher David Bailey wide, and along the way appears to have awkwardly bended his right foot. The team captain limped off the field and into the medical tent. He later left for the locker room, briefly reemerged, but was ultimately shut down for good. LG Alijah Vera-Tucker: When the Patriots offense took the field with 1:23 left in the first half, Vera-Tucker was not in the lineup. Instead, the left guard had departed for the locker room with what later was announced as a hamstring injury. He did finish the previous drive, but came up hobbled after a Rhamondre Stevenson run for a loss of 2 yards. RG Ben Brown: Lining up at left guard in place of the injured Alijah Vera-Tucker, an unsuspecting Brown was rolled up from behind on a Drake Maye scramble early in the fourth quarter. He remained on the ground, with members of the medical staff and head coach Mike Vrabel tending to him on the field. He later had to be helped off the field by two trainers, and into the blue medical tent. The Patriots quickly ruled him out with a knee injury after that. ED Dre’Mont Jones: Already coming into the game with a shoulder injury, Jones stayed down on the ground after a pass midway through the fourth quarter. He was holding his knee and slow to get up, but did walk off under own power and returned after missing just two plays. What this means for the Patriots As noted above, Romeo Doubs’ shoulder injury has since forced the Patriots to move him to injured reserve — another blow to a wide receiver group that has struggled with stability to start the season. He will be out at least until New England’s Week 12 game at the Chargers. No less concerning is the state of an offensive line that, frankly, is in shambles right now. After already losing starting right guard Mike Onwenu and his replacement Greg Van Roten in back-to-back weeks, it also saw third-stringer Ben Brown go down. Fourth-string guard Matt Pryor, who was signed off the Cardinals’ practice squad in September, finished the game. At left guard, Alijah-Vera Tucker looked good to start his Patriots career but is now a question mark as well. With Brown replacing him and subsequently going down as well, third-stringer Walter Rouse played the final 14 snaps at the position. Then, there is Morgan Moses, who was spotted in a walking boot after the game. First-round rookie Caleb Lomu took his spot in the lineup and for a second straight week looked good in extended action. Lomu, of course, already had to enter the lineup in Week 5 after left tackle Will Campbell had suffered a game-ending knee sprain. It’s not all bad news, though. For starters, Campbell appears to be fine after his prior injury scare. Likewise, Moses was listed as a limited practice participant on Monday’s injury report . Additionally, only Romeo Doubs was moved to IR on Monday; as of Tuesday morning, Brown and Vera-Tucker remain on the 53-man team despite being assigned the non-participant label on the practice report — a potential positive sign for their long-term availability. That said, with the Patriots playing the Bears in Chicago on Thursday night, it would not be a surprise if New England was again forced to adapt its starting O-line one way or another.

title: Patriots playoff picture after Week 6 win over Jets
summary: Their early-season slump firmly in the rear-view mirror, the New England Patriots have started stacking wins. The latest came on Sunday against the New York Jets, a 26-19 victory that improved the team’s record to 4-2 on the year and created some cushion between itself and its rivals. It also helped New England manifest its […]
full_text: Their early-season slump firmly in the rear-view mirror, the New England Patriots have started stacking wins. The latest came on Sunday against the New York Jets, a 26-19 victory that improved the team’s record to 4-2 on the year and created some cushion between itself and its rivals. It also helped New England manifest its position in the standings. Let’s take a look. AFC East standings Buffalo Bills (5-1) New England Patriots (4-2) New York Jets (2-4) Miami Dolphins (0-5) The Bills didn’t quite blow the doors off the Raiders like the Patriots did the previous week, but their 33-30 victory was nonetheless enough to keep them in first place in the AFC East. The Patriots are only one game behind, though, because they currently are in possession of the ever-important head-to-head advantage. They won’t be able to use it to take the division lead this week, though. Even if the Patriots beat the Bears on Thursday night, the Bills will stay ahead while on their bye. The Dolphins will be coming off of theirs this week, and try to get their first win of the season against the Jets. Needless to say, a New York loss would be a major blow to the team’s already faint hopes of making noise in the division and the conference as a whole this year. AFC playoff standings Kansas City Chiefs (5-0) Buffalo Bills (5-1) Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) Cleveland Browns (4-2) New England Patriots (4-2) Denver Broncos (4-2) Pittsburgh Steelers (4-2) On the bubble: 8. Baltimore Ravens (4-2), 9. Cincinnati Bengals (3-2) , 10. Las Vegas Raiders (3-3), 11. New York Jets (2-4), 12. Indianapolis Colts (2-4), 13. Houston Texans (2-4 ), 14. Tennessee Titans (1-5) Not yet eliminated, but let’s be real here: 15. Miami Dolphins (0-5), 16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-6) The Ravens and Jaguars losing their respective games to the Browns and Texans shook up the playoff standings in the AFC. While the Chiefs remain on top while on their own bye, the Bills jumped from fourth to second. Jacksonville fell just one spot, while Baltimore dropped all the way down to eighth. The Patriots, meanwhile, are still the top-ranked among the non-division-leading 4-2 teams. Their 4-1 record in conference games gives them an advantage, they hold the head-to-head edge over the Steelers, and they additionally have the highest strength of victory among all teams in the AFC right now.

Rookie No. 28 overall pick Caleb Lomu went from reporting as an eligible tight end to playing bookend. Count a pair of Patriots cornerbacks among the limited, as well, but not Davis. The veteran starter has missed back-to-back games due to a neck injury, while a rookie fifth-rounder in Prunty has missed back-to-back games due to a hamstring injury. The latter returned for the initial session of the condensed week. As for Henderson, he accounted for 40 yards from scrimmage in the backfield despite being questionable with a high ankle sprain. title: What placing Romeo Doubs on IR means for the Patriots
summary: Romeo Doubs’ sixth game as a member of the New England Patriots was a brief affair. The offseason signing played only two snaps, the second of which a 42-yard touchdown catch that saw him remain down with a shoulder injury. The ailment kept him out of the remainder of the game, and will now sideline […]
full_text: Romeo Doubs’ sixth game as a member of the New England Patriots was a brief affair. The offseason signing played only two snaps, the second of which a 42-yard touchdown catch that saw him remain down with a shoulder injury. The ailment kept him out of the remainder of the game, and will now sideline him for a minimum of four additional contests: as the team announced on Monday, Doubs has been placed on injured reserve . This means the Patriots will be without their high-prized free agency signing against the Chicago Bears, Miami Dolphins, Green Bay Packers and Detroit Lions, if not longer. What else does the move mean for New England? Let’s assess. Momentum stalled Doubs started his Patriots tenure with an underwhelming performance in Seattle, but he has since managed to turn a corner and develop a nice rapport with quarterback Drake Maye. Including his one reception on Sunday against the New York Jets, he now sits at 14 catches that he took for a team-leading 261 yards and three touchdowns. His 18.6 yards per catch rank second behind only Kyle Williams’ 24.5 and his 11 first downs are third, trailing Hunter Henry’s 13 and DeMario Douglas’ 12. For at least the next four games, however, Doubs will not be able to add to those numbers. He also will not be able to continue building his chemistry with Maye, which looked promising in recent weeks. Wide receiver turnover continues The Patriots just activated A.J. Brown off injured reserve after his four-week stint on the list due to a high ankle sprain, but the team’s new-found depth at wide receiver was short-lived. The pair shared just two snaps together before Doubs was lost to injury. The shoulder issue that will keep him out for at least the next four games is the latest blow to New England’s continuity at the position. Two weeks ago, Mack Hollins was also sent to IR due to a calf injury he sustained in the team’s win in Buffalo; he will be eligible to return after the Week 8 game in Miami. And so, for the time being, New England’s receiver group looks like this: 53-man roster (4): A.J. Brown (1), DeMario Douglas (3), Kyle Williams (18 | KR), Efton Chism III (86) Practice squad (4): Kyle Dixon (83), Cameron Dorner (88), Chandler Brayboy (81), Ryan Miller (—) IR (2): Romeo Doubs (87), Mack Hollins (13), Jeremiah Webb (29 | season-ending) The Patriots played one game under similar circumstances so far: in Week 5 against the Raiders, they also only had four wide receivers on their active roster. Back then, the team actually opted not to elevate any extra depth. from the practice squad and instead relied on the tight end position — especially rookie Eli Raridon — to help pick up the slack. New England might use a similar approach in the near future, and at least until Mack Hollins is eligible for a return. Pressure on A.J. Brown A.J. Brown’s first game back from injured reserve was a disappointment. He did catch three passes for 27 yards, but did so on 10 total targets while also dropping two would-be touchdowns. With Doubs now out, the Patriots will need him to be better. While Brown alone won’t have to carry the load offensively, he might be the single most important X-factor when it comes to New England maintaining its current form on that side of the ball. If he can step up, the transition from Doubs to him as WR1 should go rather smoothly, despite the two being different player types; if not, the team could be running into some problems in the very near future. Despite his underwhelming comeback, the Patriots are optimistic. “A.J. has high expectations for himself, and we have high expectations for him as well,” said head coach Mike Vrabel on Sunday. “[I’m] confident that he’ll come back, do a lot of things and help us here the rest of the season.” Bad injury luck continues The Patriots have been decimated by injuries this year, and just six weeks into the season have already been forced to rely on their depth at multiple spots in the lineup. On offense alone, they are currently without fullback Reggie Gilliam, wide receivers Romeo Doubs and Mack Hollins, tight end Julian Hill, and right guard Mike Onwenu, plus his replacement among the starters, Greg Van Roten. They also saw A.J. Brown miss four games, both left tackle Will Campbell and running back TreVeyon Henderson get shaken up a week ago. In addition, there are question marks over three O-linemen — Morgan Moses, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Ben Brown — after they were unable to finish the Jets game on Sunday. In total, the Patriots have now placed 20 different players on injured reserve dating back to Hill’s season-ending injury in the offseason. That does not include Harold Landry and Brenden Schooler spending time on the PUP and NFI lists, respectively, nor others such as Christian Gonzalez or Craig Woodson missing time due to injury. Long story short, it has been a challenging season so far for the Patriots and continues to be just that. Salary cap changes As part of the four-year, $68 million contract he signed with the Patriots in March, Doubs agreed to per-game roster bonuses totaling $1.7 million. At least four installments of those bonuses totaling $400,000 will not be earned now while he is on injured reserve. Considering that those bonuses were classified as likely to be earned after he played all 17 games for the Packers last season, the Patriots are set to receive a credit on their 2027 salary cap. Doubs’ cap number for next season will therefore decrease by $400,000 or more, depending on how much time he will actually end up missing either on IR or as a game-day inactive. Unless there are any adjustments, that number is currently set to be no higher than $18.2 million. Furthermore, Doubs might have some trouble getting his up to $3 million in not-likely-to-be-earned contract incentives for this season . He has $750,000 each on the line for 70 catches, 80 catches, 1,000 receiving yards and 1,200 receiving yards. His currently-projected 2027 cap number will only change in case he does manage to unlock those incentive escalators. Favorable timing It may be the dimmest of silver linings, but the timing of Doubs’ trip to injured reserve actually works out relatively well for the Patriots. With their bye coming up after the Lions game in Germany — i.e. the fourth and theoretically final game he will miss — they would have an extra week to get him up to speed before actually playing another game. Yes, we are grasping at straws here, thanks for asking. Opportunity earned Doubs’ spot on the 53-man roster went to safety Elliott Davison, who was elevated from the practice squad to the game day team each of the last two weeks. With now six safeties on the active roster, this gives New England some extra depth in the secondary and flexibility with nickel and dime packages as well as on special teams: 53-man roster (6): Kevin Byard (31), Craig Woodson (4), Jaylen Reed (23), Brenden Schooler (41), Mike Brown (33), Elliott Davison (27) IR (1): Dell Pettus (24) For Davison, who had one practice squad elevation left, the move also comes with a serious bay pump. After earning a weekly salary of $13,750 on the developmental team, he is now up to $49,166.67 — a 258% increase.

summary: The New England Patriots will be without Romeo Doubs for a minimum of four games. The organization placed the veteran wide receiver on injured reserve amid a series of transactions announced Monday afternoon. Doubs, 26, sustained a shoulder injury while catching a 42-yard touchdown in the first quarter of Sunday’s 26-19 AFC East win at […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - OCTOBER 18: Romeo Doubs #87 of the New England Patriots scores a touchdown against Brandon Stephens #21 of the New York Jets during the first quarter at Gillette Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots will be without Romeo Doubs for a minimum of four games. The organization placed the veteran wide receiver on injured reserve amid a series of transactions announced Monday afternoon. Doubs, 26, sustained a shoulder injury while catching a 42-yard touchdown in the first quarter of Sunday’s 26-19 AFC East win at Gillette Stadium and was downgraded from questionable to out. The March signing stands with 14 receptions for 261 yards and three visits to the end zone this fall for an active depth chart that moves forward with A.J. Brown, DeMario Douglas, Efton Chism III and Kyle Williams. After handling 246 offensive snaps through six games, including two starts, he joins fellow vet target Mack Hollins on injured reserve and will not be eligible to return until the bye week in late November. Entering the NFL in the fourth round of the 2022 draft at No. 132 overall out of Nevada, Doubs spent the previous four campaigns with the Green Bay Packers. The 6-foot-2, 210-pound wideout’s career spans 216 catches for 2,685 yards and 24 touchdowns through 65 appearances. Taking the open spot on the 53-man roster in Foxborough, safety Elliott Davison has been promoted from the practice squad after twice serving as a standard elevation for matchups against the Las Vegas Raiders and New York Jets. Davison, 24, was scheduled to revert on Monday. The 6-foot, 190-pound safety has recorded two tackles and one pass deflection through his consecutive call-ups while playing 10 snaps on defense and 37 snaps on special teams. Signed to the Patriots’ practice squad in September before being released and re-signed , Davison originally entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2025. The former UTSA defensive back spent the duration of his rookie year on the practice squad of the New Orleans Saints. New England also officially signed wide receiver Ryan Miller, center Jacob Rizy and guard Andrew Rupcich to the practice squad on Monday. The club released cornerback D’Shawn Jamison to make room among the 17-man group. Miller, 26, went undrafted out of Furman in 2023. The 6-foot-2, 217-pound wideout spent three seasons between the 53-man roster and practice squad of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers before being claimed off waivers by the New York Giants last December. Awarded to the Miami Dolphins amid training camp and let go last week, Miller has played in 30 NFL games, including six starts, while totaling 17 receptions for 254 yards and four touchdowns. He scored his most recent TD in September from 77 yards away. Rizy, 24, began 2026 on New England’s practice squad after arriving as part of the organization’s undrafted class in May. The 6-foot-5, 306-pound rookie free agent played 155 snaps at center through three preseason games and was waived ahead of the league’s 53-man roster deadline. A former second-team and first-team All-Ivy League selection, Rizy spent three years at Harvard and two years at Florida State. The 27-game starter logged time at center, left guard, right guard and right tackle during his collegiate run. Rupcich, 27, had been waived by the Patriots with an injury settlement in August after reverting to injured reserve. The 6-foot-6, 325-pound Culver-Stockton alum now circles back to an offensive line that saw three starters in Ben Brown, Alijah Vera-Tucker and Morgan Moses ruled out on Sunday. Rupcich first joined New England’s practice squad last September and was retained on a futures contract in February. He entered the NFL with the Tennessee Titans as an undrafted free agent in 2022 and appeared in 12 games while in the AFC South, notching two starts. Jamison, 27, worked out and joined the Patriots’ practice squad last week before becoming a corresponding move amid the attrition. The 5-foot-9, 185-pound cornerback went undrafted out of Texas in 2023 and made his initial NFL stops with the San Francisco 49ers, Carolina Panthers and Pittsburgh Steelers. He spent the first month of the 2026 season on the practice squad of the Arizona Cardinals. Jamison has appeared in 18 games while seeing 107 snaps on defense and 166 snaps on special teams. His career includes 10 tackles, one pass deflection and one start. The Chicago Bears host head coach Mike Vrabel’s 4-2 team at Soldier Field on Thursday. Kickoff is set for 8:15 p.m. ET.
author: Oliver Thomas

title: Patriots vs. Jets: Fan observations from Week 6 win
summary: There’s just something about a Jets Victory Monday that just hits different. I know the rivalry is more or less gone and the Jets haven’t been relevant since Mark Sanchez. But still. These games always serve as a nice reminder for me what my life could have been. I grew up in Connecticut, so I […]
full_text: There’s just something about a Jets Victory Monday that just hits different. I know the rivalry is more or less gone and the Jets haven’t been relevant since Mark Sanchez. But still. These games always serve as a nice reminder for me what my life could have been. I grew up in Connecticut, so I had to choose between Boston and New York at a fairly young age. And while I’d like to think that, had I chosen poorly, I would have least been a Giants fan, you never know. And luckily, I never will. I think what I like most about this win is that it’s a good reminder that the Patriots are legit again. Because objectively, this wasn’t their best showing. Drake Maye was inaccurate at times and missed some reads. The defense gave up big plays and had trouble containing the run. Drops (more on that later) and turnovers cost this team drives and points. But they did enough to win and Mike Vrabel outcoached Aaron Glenn. The Patriots made plays when they needed to and got a fairly ugly divisional win to move to 4-2. And in years past, not too long ago in fact, we all would have been so happy that they actually won a game that we wouldn’t have cared at all how they got there. But we’re now able to separate the ugly wins from the solid ones, which is a nice place to be. The next step is to get the Patriots back to that place where a win like this one would have the Boston media spending the entire week asking if the coach should be fired and if maybe the quarterback’s championship window is closing. Remember those games? Belichick and Brady would squeak by the Jets to move to 8-0 on the year and if you didn’t watch the game and only listened to The Sports Hub you’d think they lost 45-0 and Tommy B literally soiled himself on the 50-yard line. So, while we’re not quite at that level yet, it’s good to see us at a place where we can be happy with the win while also acknowledging that it wasn’t their best game. If there is a heaven, every Patriots game on the 5,000-inch TV in my 50,000-square-foot mansion will take place at 1 p.m. on a beautiful October afternoon where New England defers and gets the ball in the second half. And if there’s a hell, I would imagine you find yourself in a situation where you get drafted by the Jets, finally get out and play elsewhere, but then somehow end back on the Jets. I actually like Geno Smith. He’s a decent QB and will win you some games. And he actually had a fairly decent showing yesterday. But some very questionable play-calling and falling short in situational football…um… situations… ended up being what decided this one. If you follow my writing, you know how strongly I feel about the delayed shotgun draw play on 3rd-and-short. I can’t imagine a worse play call for that situation. Or at least I couldn’t, until I saw the Jets try the same thing on 4th-and-short. On multiple occasions. The Jets had consecutive eight-play drives into New England territory and came away with zero points both times. Overall, I like how the NFL has generally gotten more aggressive with going for it on 4th-and-short. But sometimes, you gotta take the points. Though the Jets are always gonna Jet, aren’t they? Odds are they miss both field goal attempts or botch the snap or a false start knocks them out of range. So what do I know. The game plan on defense seemed to be, from my vantage at least, cede yards on the ground and force long drives, knowing that the Patriots defense is superior to the Jets offense. And other than a busted coverage for a long score, it was effective. That wildly annoying 48-yard touchdown pass to Omar Cooper Jr. was the only time all game the Jets found the end zone, so that means it was a pretty successful day overall. What makes that touchdown so annoying is that it made the game 17-10 instead of 24-3, which is what the score should have been if A.J. Brown had decided to screw his hands on yesterday. That man could spend an entire Spring Break walking naked through the streets of Tijuana and not catch a damn thing. I don’t want to harp too much on Brown’s drops, as I’m very much hoping that he was just really, really, really, really, really rusty after missing 28 days of football. But he was targeted 10 times. He caught three passes. He dropped four passes, two of which would have been touchdowns. The other two would have moved the chains. And then for some unholy reason the Patriots had him out there on the goddam HANDS TEAM and he flubbed the onside kick. If there’s a Patriots receiver who has had a worse game, I don’t know who that is. Sure, Joey Galloway spent his brief Patriots career running the wrong routes… but when Tom Brady threw him the ball, he caught it. And Chad Ochocinco was a ghost, but he didn’t cost the team points. What a disaster of a game from Brown. Live look at Jason Sanders lining up for the onside kick. That might be the first time I ever saw a kicker deliberately aim at a receiver. Though to give him credit, he ran a crossing route that pulled the safety up and completely freed Romeo Doubs on his touchdown catch. So Brown gets the assist there. But by my calculation, one TD assist only cancels out one TD drop. So, he’s still in the red. One other bit of good news: A.J. Brown got 10 targets because he got open so much. So, the foot and the legs are fine. And he’s still able to read a coverage and find the open areas with the best of them. It’s just a matter of whether or not he also broke both of his hands in addition to spraining his ankle. So with the WR3 on IR, the WR2 injured in the first quarter, and the WR1 unable to catch a cold on the first day of preschool, what did Drake Maye do? He went to his WR4 and his TE1, as DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry led the team in receiving. Douglas had one of his best games as a Patriot, although I find it wildly ironic that the one time he didn’t catch a pass, start running forward, and then trip over himself to fall to the ground, the ball gets punched out and he loses it. Whatever chemistry that Henry and Maye were missing earlier in the year, they got it back and then some. The Jets making the bold decision to simply not cover Henry on multiple third downs aside, he knows exactly where he’s supposed to be and knows exactly where he’s supposed to go. Henry has quietly become one of this franchise’s best tight ends of all time. He’s top-5 for sure, and you could even make a case for top-3. One of the better free agency signings of the 2020s. I love playing the “Who The Hell is That Guy?” game in August when the Patriots have three guys all wearing the No. 37 out on the field in the fourth quarter of a meaningless preseason game. I very much hate playing that game in October with the men charged with protecting the quarterback. Thank Tebow that Will Campbell is tough as nails and decided to play yesterday. And another thank you to Tebow that the Patriots chose to go O-line with their first pick in the 2026 draft. Otherwise, we might have seen Milton Williams and Christian Barmore out there pass blocking. That said… what a day from that line. Sometimes a zero-sack day can be a little deceiving, as the QB could spend the afternoon running for his life or just barely get the ball out before he gets decapitated. But not yesterday; Drake Maye had time to throw and only moved when he needed to, all with a line that was 60% third-stringers and rookies. Against a very stout Jets front line, I should add. Has TreVeyon Henderson done anything of note this year? He had a long run for a touchdown against the Steelers, but the hole on that run was so big the entire Klump Family could have walked through it on their way to Old Country Buffet . Kudos to him for playing through an ankle injury, but at the moment the only thing he seems well suited for is running up the gut into a crowded line to set up a 2nd-and-8. Maybe they’re saving some of the more creative receiving packages for him until later in the year. The running game as a whole, though, was exactly what we…

title: ‘Receiver at heart’ Charles Woods keeps coming up big for Patriots
summary: Charles Woods did it all during his final season at Kimball High School in Dallas, including catching the ball 35 times. Nine years later, he got an opportunity to once again put his receiving talent to good use. With the New England Patriots leading 23-13 in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets on […]
full_text: Charles Woods did it all during his final season at Kimball High School in Dallas, including catching the ball 35 times. Nine years later, he got an opportunity to once again put his receiving talent to good use. With the New England Patriots leading 23-13 in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets on Sunday, Woods was responsible for the field side zone on a 1st-and-10. Tight end Kenyon Sadiq’s route took him into precisely that zone, and quarterback Geno Smith — feeling quick pressure from rookie edge Gabe Jacas — decided to go that way. For Woods, this was a gift his entire NFL career in the making. “We were playing in zone. I had great odds. Two defenders broke out on the corner. I didn’t know Geno was going to throw it up, but I made a play,” he said. “In my heart, I still think I play offense. I still think I’m a receiver at heart.” Woods getting the opportunity to catch his first career interception came not just as a result of his personal history, but also the circumstances. New England, after all, has struggled with injuries this season at cornerback; both Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis have missed time, with the latter out on Sunday due to a neck injury . As a result, Woods found himself part of the starting lineup for a second time this season and is now up to 50.7% of defensive snaps — third among all Patriots cornerbacks behind only Marcus Jones and Christian Gonzalez. His high snap total might be the result of him getting bumped up the depth chart due to injury, but he also earned it with some solid play. “He’s been playing good football all year,” said safety Kevin Byard. “He’s a starting corner in this league, so I’m just happy that, when he gets in there and plays, he’s been taking advantage of the opportunity.” “I’m not trying to chase plays these last few weeks,” Woods added. “I’m just letting it come to me and it finally came to me. It’s a blessing. I was excited. I was really excited to see how my teammates were excited for me. Everybody was smiling and happy. That really made me happy.” Woods had every reason to be happy on Sunday. Not only did he catch his first interception since turning pro as a rookie free agent with the Rams in 2024, he also helped the Patriots secure a 26-19 win . In addition, he received a game ball from head coach Mike Vrabel in the postgame locker room. “It’s big for him. Getting an opportunity, never knowing when the opportunity’s going to come. But when the opportunity comes, taking advantage of it,” said defensive tackle Milton Williams after the game. “With Gonzo and CD being out, he never knows where he’s going to be at, how many snaps he’s going to play. But in the right spot, executing when he’s supposed to, and when the ball comes to you, make a play. I was happy for him, proud of him. And we needed it. We needed it bad. So, kudos to him. I hope he enjoys himself tonight.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: A win is a win, but the Saints didn’t exactly inspire confidence
summary: For a moment, it looked like the New Orleans Saints were finally going to give fans a stress-free Sunday. Leading 34-10, the Saints appeared to have everything under control. Then, somehow, they turned a comfortable victory into another fourth-quarter nail-biter. New Orleans surrendered 17 unanswered points and barely escaped with the win. Sure, a win […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Isaiah Likely #9 of the New York Giants is unable to make a catch against the New Orleans Saints during the fourth quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images For a moment, it looked like the New Orleans Saints were finally going to give fans a stress-free Sunday. Leading 34-10, the Saints appeared to have everything under control. Then, somehow, they turned a comfortable victory into another fourth-quarter nail-biter. New Orleans surrendered 17 unanswered points and barely escaped with the win. Sure, a win is a win, but this performance left just as many questions as the last three losses have. The Saints might be one of the hardest teams in the NFL to trust right now, even when they have a commanding lead. And that is on Kellen Moore and his staff. It’s not easy to take a 24-point lead in this league. The offense did enough to put the game seemingly out of reach, and the Saints looked poised to take care of business. But instead of putting the Giants away, New Orleans allowed them to hang around long enough to make things uncomfortable. That’s the frustrating part. This wasn’t a game like we’ve seen recently, where the Saints have to claw their way back after being down considerably. They had the opportunity to control the game after overcoming an early 10 point deficit and nearly threw it away. Of course, nobody in New Orleans is going to complain about getting a win. After all, the standings don’t care how pretty a victory looks. But the way this game unfolded makes it difficult to walk away feeling entirely confident about what this team can accomplish moving forward. The Saints deserve credit for holding on, but they also need to figure out why that even happened in the first place and how to not let it happen again. For now, the Saints will take the win. But if they want to build momentum, they have to learn how to finish what they start.

full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Martin Emerson Jr. #22 of the New Orleans Saints looks on against the Baltimore Ravens during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Martin Emerson Jr. made his presence felt in the New Orleans Saints’ 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, putting together one of the defense’s most impressive individual performances of the season. Emerson finished with seven combined tackles, two interceptions, four passes defensed, one pressure and one tackle. His performance earned him an 88.4 overall defensive grade and a 90.2 coverage grade from Pro Football Focus, highlighting just how effective he was against the Giants. His two interceptions were the biggest difference-makers. Emerson picked off both Jameis Winston and J.J. McCarthy, and was inches away from a third interception late in the fourth quarter. For a Saints defense that’s been lacking consistent playmakers in the secondary, Emerson’s performance was exactly the type of showing that can change the conversation surrounding a unit. The Saints escaped with a seven-point victory after allowing the Giants to erase much of their early deficit. That late-game collapse overshadowed what was otherwise a productive afternoon for several New Orleans players, but Emerson’s performance deserves recognition. If he can build on this performance, Emerson could become an increasingly important piece of the Saints’ secondary moving forward.

title: Game Recap: Saints visit Giants in Week 6 Clash
summary: The New Orleans Saints were finally back on the road when they visited the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The teams exchanged quick punts to begin the game before the hosts found some momentum on their second series. Jameis Winston converted his first […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Devaughn Vele #14 of the New Orleans Saints carries the ball against Andru Phillips #22 of the New York Giants during the first half at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints were finally back on the road when they visited the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Sunday. Here’s a recap of all the action. First Quarter The teams exchanged quick punts to begin the game before the hosts found some momentum on their second series. Jameis Winston converted his first throw of the drive with an 11-yard pass to Isaiah Likely before Darnell Mooney broke off for a 20-yard run. A few plays later, Winston found Likely again for 24 yards as the Giants made their way inside the red zone. He then found Tyrone Tracy Jr for a 17-yard touchdown. Trailing 7-0, New Orleans went three-and-out again before forcing another one out of New York as well. Second Quarter The teams exchanged another pair of punts to open the second quarter, before Tyler Shough and the Saints offense finally began to move the ball as he converted a 3rd-down throw to Bryce Lance. An 18-yard catch by Devaughn Vele moved the drive into Giants territory, but the visitors were soon held to a field goal attempt. Daniel Carlson’s 55-yard attempt missed wide left. Winston connected twice with Malik Nabers as the Giants moved the ball past midfield, and a roughing the passer penalty against Vernon Broughton put them in the red zone. After incompletions from Winston, Dominic Zvada converted a 34-yard field goal for a 10-0 lead. Barion Brown returned the kickoff near midfield for the black and gold, and Shough found Chris Olave for 12 yards to get New Orleans into field goal range. Three straight incompletions meant another field goal attempt. Carlson was good this time from 58 yards. With just over a minute left, Charlie Jones fumbled the kickoff return. Oscar Delp fell on it for the black and gold, giving the Saints a chance to tie the game before the half. Shough scrambled for 25 yards as he looked to do just that. A few plays later, on 4th-and-goal, he found Lance in the end zone with the last play of the half, tying the game at 10-10. Third Quarter CJ Donaldson broke out for a 17-yard run early on the first possession of the second half, before a roughing-the-passer penalty moved the black and gold into Giants territory. Alvin Kamara then ran for 11 yards. Two plays later, Shough found him for a 31-yard touchdown with a vintage Kamara catch-and-run down the sideline giving the Saints a 17-10 lead. New York then went three-and-out with a string of penalties hampering their efforts to find a response. The Saints offense returned and stayed hot after another return to near midfield from Brown, with Kendre Miller running the ball effectively and Shough connecting with Chris Olave and Vele. After Donaldson was marked just short of the goal line, Shough ran it in himself to establish a 24-10 advantage. Winston went 3/4 for 36 yards to begin the ensuing Giants series, before throwing an interception into the hands of Martin Emerson Jr. Despite a 15-yard run from Kamara early in the drive, the Saints were held to a field goal this time. Carlson extended the lead with a 51-yard kick. Fourth Quarter Carl Granderson and Chase Young were able to get to Winston to force another three-and-out from the G-Men, but the Saints proceeded to go three-and-out themselves. Winston couldn’t take advantage, as he was picked off by Julian Blackmon. With a very short field, Shough threw an 18-yard touchdown to Olave to put New Orleans up 34-10. With JJ McCarthy in the game at quarterback for New York, he too threw an interception to Emerson Jr. But Donaldson fumbled on the second play of the Saints ensuing drive. McCarthy threw a 27-yard pass to Nabers before Tracy Jr ran in another touchdown. After a successful two-point attempt, New York cut the lead to two scores at 34-18. New Orleans went three-and-out, and McCarthy began the next possession with a 49-yard throw to Charlie Jones. A play later, he found Likely for a 24-yard touchdown. This time, the two-point conversion was unsuccessful with a pass intended for Nabers. The Saints then went three-and-out yet again. McCarthy continued to move the ball at will, including another 46-yard connection with Nabers. A sack by Colby Wooden helped the black and gold limit New York to a field goal, which put the score at 34-27. It was then another three-and-out for the Saints, giving the Giants a chance to complete the comeback. They almost did, with a pair of passes to Likely and Nabers moving the ball inside the red zone. On 4th-and-1, though, McCarthy’s pass to Likely was incomplete. Shough knelt out the clock to secure the 34-27 victory. The black and gold are in France now, with all attention on Sunday’s international matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers.
author: Sam Mackenzie

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints win against the Giants
summary: The Good: Tyler Shough and takeaways The New Orleans Saints QB fought through a slow start and brought the team back to score 34 straight points. Shough threw two touchdowns in the second half and ran for a third to hold off the Giants 34-27. This was Shough’s first career game with 3+ TDs and […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints scrambles with the ball against the New York Giants during the second quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Good: Tyler Shough and takeaways The New Orleans Saints QB fought through a slow start and brought the team back to score 34 straight points. Shough threw two touchdowns in the second half and ran for a third to hold off the Giants 34-27. This was Shough’s first career game with 3+ TDs and no interceptions, and his second game this year with a rushing TD. There should be no question anymore that the Saints have their QB of the future, as through six games Shough is averaging 240.5 yards, 2 TDs, and fewer than 1 INT per game. He has been a bright spot in a disappointing start to the season, but this week thankfully his play resulted in a win. The defense and special teams supplemented Shough’s solid afternoon by taking the ball away from New York four times. A forced fumble on a kickoff immediately following a scoring drive gave the Saints great field position and allowed them to tie the game before halftime. In the second half the defense intercepted three passes which led to 10 points and built the Saints lead to its largest of the afternoon. This was by far the most takeaways the team had all year, doubling up their previous high of two which came last week against Minnesota. The Bad: Third down conversions The Saints went three and out six times on Sunday and was just 4/15 on third down overall. The Saints actually rank 8th in the NFL in third down conversions this year at 42.5% (it was 45.8% before Sunday), so converting on just 26.6% of their third downs against the Giants was an uncharacteristic performance. Of these 11 missed third downs, only four were on distances of 10 yards or more. This failure to sustain drives got them in trouble early and late in the game and nearly cost them a win. Let’s hope they get back on track next week in Paris. The Ugly: Complacency in the 4th quarter The Saints nearly blew a 24-point 4th quarter lead on Sunday. Once they grabbed a 34-10 lead with 11:31 left in the game, the offense possessed the ball for a little over 4 minutes of the remaining game time despite having four more drives. The Saints fumbled and went three and out three times on their final four drives of the afternoon, which allowed New York to have a chance to tie or win the game on their final drive of the day. On the defensive side they allowed backup QB JJ McCarthy to throw for 243 yards in the final 11 minutes alone and lead three scoring drives in a row to cut the lead to just seven. The Giants had the ball in the red zone on their final drive of the day, but the defense finally made a stand and caused a turnover on downs. The Saints were lucky not to blow this one, as once they got up 24, they took their foot off the gas in a major way, and it was almost their undoing.
author: Hayden Reel

title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Giants
summary: The New Orleans Saints have finally ended their win streak, finding a win over the New York Giants. It didn’t start pretty, and it definitely didn’t end pretty, but New Orleans survived. Up: KR Barion Brown Rookie Barion Brown hasn’t been the difference maker on special teams that New Orleans expected when they drafted him […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - OCTOBER 18: Martin Emerson #22 of the New Orleans Saints celebrates after a play against the New York Giants during the second quarter at MetLife Stadium on October 18, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints have finally ended their win streak, finding a win over the New York Giants. It didn’t start pretty, and it definitely didn’t end pretty, but New Orleans survived. Up: KR Barion Brown Rookie Barion Brown hasn’t been the difference maker on special teams that New Orleans expected when they drafted him to return kicks. But after some highlight plays over the past few weeks, Brown finally had his breakout game against the Giants. Brown had a 41-yard return that helped open scoring for the Saints on the day, resulting in a field goal for Daniel Carlson. Brown would also have a 23-yard punt return in the game, setting the team up in good position. Part of the Saints offensive explosion was their valuable field position, plenty of thanks to Brown. The former LSU wide receiver also recorded his first career reception in the win over New York. Up: CB Martin Emerson Jr. The biggest standout on Sunday is no other than cornerback Martin Emerson Jr. The veteran cornerback logged 7 tackles, all solo, a tackle for loss, 4 passes defended, and most importantly, 2 interceptions. Emerson entered the game after Kool-Aid McKinstry left with what Kellen Moore described as a migraine. Emerson took advantage of the opportunity and became the team’s standout player and a game-changer. With his big game, Emerson has now earned more playtime. It will be interesting to see how the Saints incorporate the veteran cornerback into their defense. Emerson was in a camp battle with Quincy Riley for the CB2 position. Up: Saints’ running game The Saints worked to establish the run, and found success doing so during Sunday’s win. New Orleans rushed for 175 yards on 38 carries, averaging 4.6 yards per carry. Kendre Miller led the team with 70 yards. Three players for the Saints averaged 4.9 yards per carry or better, including quarterback Tyler Shough. Being able to run the ball is all the difference for the Saints offense. Instead of being stuck on third and long, New Orleans faced third and manageable more than not thanks to getting 4 yards on a run on first and second down. The Saints offense has to prove that they can sustain success in the running game, but a strong showing against the Giants proves it’s possible. Down: HC Kellen Moore Weird, after the third quarter ended, I was expecting to put Moore as a positive after Sunday’s game. The Saints were looking pretty with a 34-10 lead after scoring 34 unanswered points. It looked like brilliant resilience by Moore and the Saints offense, who were called out by owner Gayle Benson earlier in the week. Despite another slow start, with the Saints only finding points within the final two minutes of the first half, the Saints’ offensive explosion was brilliant. But of course, Moore has landed as a down for a reason. The Saints absolutely crumbled in the fourth quarter and were one play away from going into overtime despite having a 24-point lead with 10 minutes remaining. This is all too familiar for the Saints, who found a similar way to lose earlier this season to the Las Vegas Raiders. Moore has proved his teams start slow and also can’t finish. It’s rare for a team that starts slow and also finishes slow to win a game, but Moore was lucky enough that his team pulled away with the win. Down: K Daniel Carlson Look, Daniel Carlson finished the day making up for his early mistake, but he hasn’t proven to be the consistent veteran kicker the Saints were hoping for when they hired him. Entering Sunday, Carlson has missed a kick in four straight games, including PATs, and added to that on Sunday with a miss from 55. The veteran kicker quickly made up for it with a 58-yard field goal the very next drive, and another make from 51 yards in the third quarter. Despite his impressive comeback, Carlson needs to prove more to be consistent enough for the Saints’ offense to feel comfortable.
author: Kyle Besson
