full_text: It’s Week 7, and the New Orleans Saints will look to keep their momentum rolling when they face the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, October 25, at Stade de France in Paris. The matchup marks the first time that the NFL will play a regular-season game in France, and the Saints were the obvious choice to help make history especially due to its deep French roots, rich cultural heritage and longstanding connection to France. While the historic setting provides a unique backdrop, the Saints know their trip to Paris is about more than celebrating history. New Orleans is coming off a 34-27 victory over the New York Giants, while Pittsburgh enters following a 26-19 win over Tampa Bay. Both teams will be looking to continue their winning ways as the season approaches its midway point. With history in the making and a chance to get another victory before heading into their bye, the Saints hope to make their trip to the City of Light one to remember. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently point 1.5-point underdogs against the Steelers, with an over/under of 44.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. After gaining just 2 yards on four carries Sunday against the New Orleans Saints, Harris had complained about not being able to get into a rhythm as the Giants were rotating four running backs during the game. full_text: Najee Harris | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants have released running back Najee Harris , a team source confirmed on Tuesday morning. After gaining just 2 yards on four carries Sunday against the New Orleans Saints, Harris had complained about not being able to get into a rhythm as the Giants were rotating four running backs during the game. Head coach John Harbaugh said he understood Harris’s complaint, but his message to all of the backs was to “do something” to “take the job” as the team’s No. 1 running back. Harris won’t be given another opportunity. The 28-year-old Harris had 1,000-yard rushing seasons in each of the first four years of his career, all with the Pittsburgh Steelers. He tore an Achilles tendon early in the 2025 season with the Los Angeles Chargers, and signed with the Giants as a free agent during the preseason. Harris had just 99 yards on 31 carries for New York, an average of just 3.2 yards per attempt. The Giants now have Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary at running back. The Giants also released veteran outside linebacker Jihad Ward on Tuesday. Moves to replace those players on the 53-man roster have not yet been announced.

full_text: Jihad Ward | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The New York Giants have released veteran outside linebacker Jihad Ward just three games after they poached him off the Minnesota Vikings’ practice squad. The news was first reported by NFL Network insider Mike Garafolo . Ward tied his career high with 5.0 sacks last season while playing for the Tennessee Titans, where current Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson had that job. When the Giants needed a replacement on the roster for Brian Burns, out with the season due to a torn ACL, they signed the 32-year-old Ward. He was on the active roster for three games, playing in two. In 41 defensive snaps, Ward had just one tackle. Ward was also a Giant in 2022 and 2023. He was a second-round pick by the Raiders in the 2016 NFL Draft. Releasing Ward could be the precursor to adding outside linebacker Trace Ford to the 53-man roster. Ford, 25, is out of practice squad elevations after playing in the Giants’ last three games. In 49 defensive snaps, Ford has eight tackles. He has also played 78 special teams snaps.

McCarthy. Jameis Winston had just thrown his second interception, and the Giants’ offense was lifeless. McCarthy entered the game and threw an interception on a miscue to Malachi Fields (88): Make that 2️⃣ INTs for Martin Emerson Jr.! NOvsNYG on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/k7IrxOuk0n — NFL (@NFL) October 18, 2026 Fields was pivoting outward—a common route concept used by Matt Nagy—and McCarthy thought the rookie receiver would sit in the vacated window left by Pete Werner (20), who matched Devin Singletary’s flare route to the flat. The ball hit Martin Emerson Jr. (22) in the numbers. The game seemed all but over. Kellen Moore put Spencer Rattler into the game, but Jason Pinnock forced a fumble that was recovered by star rookie Arvell Reese, giving McCarthy the football back at midfield. McCarthy would lead a six-play, 52-yard drive that resulted in a 5-yard Tyrone Tracy Jr. touchdown, followed by a 2-point conversion to Isaiah Likely. This drive made the score 34-18 with seven minutes left in the game. The drive was highlighted by the throw below: Q4, 8:24: First-and-10 via GIPHY The Saints ran quarter, quarter, half ( Cover-6 ) against an 11 personnel clearout concept with a deep post from Fields with two deep crossing patterns from Charlie Jones (89) and Malik Nabers (1), with Tyrone Tracy Jr. (29) and Isaiah Likely (9) releasing to hold the middle hook defenders after helping in protection. The middle quarter defender, Julian Blackmon (23), carried Jones’ cross to the hash before transitioning off to Nabers underneath, but by that point, Blackmon was out-leveraged. The throw was hard and direct — it could have used more touch — and it forced Nabers to make a miraculous adjustment to secure the pass from the far-hash. An ideal throw with touch outside the numbers may have led to a touchdown, given how the Saints reacted to the passing concept. Still, McCarthy recognized the vulnerability and attacked for a 27-yard gain that set up Tracy’s touchdown. McCarthy also had a great pocket. Q4, 5:54 : First-and-10 via GIPHY via GIPHY The Giants forced a three-and-out, giving New York the ball back down 34-18. On the first play of the drive, McCarthy saw the Cover-3 look and gave Jones a chance against deep third defender Quincy Riley (29). New York ran two inside-leaning vertical routes to isolate the outside deep thirds in a one-on-one matchup. Blackmon — the middle-of-the-field-closed safety — followed Nabers over the top on his deep horizontal cross toward Fields, so McCarthy let it rip. McCarthy may not have made this throw in a neutral game script, but it made sense down multiple scores late in the fourth quarter. The ball was underthrown and identified by Riley, but the Saints’ cornerback knocked it into the air, and Jones somehow secured it for a 49-yard gain. Q4, 5:11: Second-and-10 Emerson Jr. almost came away with his third interception of the game on a well-defended play against Fields on first down; the ball hit the turf. McCarthy responded well by trusting his star tight end to make a play: via GIPHY The Giants were in shotgun 2×2, 11-personnel, with Nabers and Likely on the same side. Nabers ran a quick curl, which forced Likely’s defender to cover the deep third, as Jones and Fields ran deep dig routes to hold the center-field safety in place; Likely was isolated against safety Justin Reid (21), who had outside leverage, and the inside help was preoccupied with Jones and Fields, while Emerson was with Nabers on the numbers. McCarthy does an excellent job putting the ball high and inside, away from the defensive leverage, letting the tight end maximize his catch radius and secure the ball. This was a very difficult catch to make, but Likely secures it through contact. Q4, 3:29: First-and-15 via GIPHY via GIPHY J.J. McCarthy stepped into the pocket, set his feet, and fired a 46-yard strike to Malik Nabers pic.twitter.com/yzTHzK0eKq — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 19, 2026 The Giants were in shotgun — 12 personnel — from a 3×1 nub set with Thomas Fidone II (86) as the nub. Likely was the No. 3 to the far side, and he ran a deep horizontal crosser against Cover-4. Nabers ran up the seam to split the deep-fourth safeties, and he did an excellent job turning the hips of Blackmon with an excellent route where he leaned outward and exploded back to the inside. Fields ran a deep dig underneath the clearouts, and McCarthy had his eye on the isolated Nabers. Plays like these are exactly why McCarthy was drafted so high; not only did he step up and avoid the rush, comfortably setting his feet in a clean pocket, but he kept his eyes downfield and delivered an absolute strike that hit Nabers outside and away from Blackmon. The play design ensured that Reid would not be able to get outside his hash to help Blackmon out with the coverage. A great job by Nabers, McCarthy, the offensive line, and the Giants coaching staff to secure 49 yards. Q4, :40: Second-and-10 J.J. McCarthy layering the football over a Saints' defender to Isaiah Likely for a 20-yard gain. pic.twitter.com/rEHWASWahY — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) October 19, 2026 The Giants got the ball back with :57 left in the game, needing a touchdown. McCarthy scrambled for 28 yards, threw an incomplete pass, and then had this 20-yard completion to Likely with :40 left in the game. Again, 12 personnel nub with Likely as the No. 3 and Nabers as the No. 2. Nabers ran a deep corner; Fields on the outside ran a dig to replace what may have been vacated due to Likely’s horizontal crossing route. The Saints were in Cover-6, and Likely’s dig was to the half-field side. McCarthy used touch — something he doesn’t use consistently — to perfectly layer the throw over the middle hook defender. This is a high-level throw, and one that was inches away from being tipped by Werner. McCarthy threw this in a very high-level situation and gave the Giants a realistic shot to pull off the improbable comeback. Final thoughts McCarthy has now sparked questions about when he should be the starting quarterback for the Giants. The velocity and how the ball jumps out of his hand are undeniable. Is he perfect? No. Did he have mistakes? Yes. Would this have happened in a neutral game script? I don’t know! Still, was this an impressive performance? Of course it was! McCarthy will likely start sooner rather than later, and he’ll provide the Giants with an element that Jameis Winston can’t — mobility. McCarthy performed well, but it was just a little too late for the Giants.
author: Nick Falato

title: John Harbaugh to NY Giants RBs: ‘Do something … take the job’
summary: New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has a clear message for the team’s running backs, stuck in a four-way timeshare that is not producing results anyone is happy with. “Do something.” After getting four carries for just 2 yards on Sunday against the New Orleans Saints despite starting the game, Najee Harris expressed his […]
full_text: Najee Harris | Getty Images New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has a clear message for the team’s running backs, stuck in a four-way timeshare that is not producing results anyone is happy with. “Do something.” After getting four carries for just 2 yards on Sunday against the New Orleans Saints despite starting the game, Najee Harris expressed his frustration. “It’s hard to get in a rhythm with one or two plays. The first couple runs will be like, ‘OK, how are they playing it?’ And then the next ones will be, ‘OK, this is how you attack it.’ But if you’re getting a play here and then get taken out for a series, there’s nothing you could do. That’s why I’m saying, ‘I don’t know.’ I’ve never been through none of this before.” At the end of a Monday Zoom call with Harbaugh dominated by the impending decision regarding whether Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy will be the team’s starting quarterback , I asked Harbaugh if he understood Harris’s frustratio and what, if anything, he would do about the backfield timeshare. After the loss yesterday, Najee Harris expressed frustration with the Giants' running back usage approach: "It's hard to get into a rhythm with one or two plays…if you're getting a play here and then get taken out for a series, there's nothing you could do. I've never been… pic.twitter.com/DtA0eNqIcP — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 19, 2026 “Do understand it. Respect it. Also understand that that’s earned,” Harbaugh said. “I would love for us to be in that kind of a circumstance. A (Baltimore Ravens running back) Derrick Henry circumstance or a (Philadelphia Eagles running back) Saquon Barkley circumstance or whatever it might be. That would be great, and we haven’t. Our run game hasn’t earned that yet, and none of those guys have.” Harbaugh had acknowledged on Sunday night that trying to split carries between four backs is not ideal . “Now you can argue that. You can say, well, I don’t like that. I don’t like you divvying up the snaps between four backs. And I can tell you, I don’t like it either,” Harbaugh said. “One of those guys needs to step up. Somebody needs to step up and be the back. And none of those guys have done that yet. And when one of those guys steps up to be the back, then they’ll be the back. That’s your answer.” The Giants are 22nd in the NFL averaging 3.8 yards per carry. Nearly all of their big plays in the run game have come from quarterbacks or wide receivers on jet sweeps or reverses. Cam Skattebo’s 19-yard run is the longest by a Giants’ running back this season. Here are the rushing numbers: Skattebo: 81 carries, 294 yards, 3.6 yards per carry Harris: 31 carries, 99 yards, 3.2 yards per carry Tyrone Tracy: 13 carries, 40 yards, 3.1 yards per carry Devin Singletary: 13 carries, 39 yards, 3.0 yards per carry “My advice would be to any player, and it’s all the guys, we had the same conversation. I’ve had the same conversation with all the running backs, the receivers, it’s no different than any position, but do the most you can with the opportunities you get,” Harbaugh said. “Make the most of those opportunities and you’re sure to get more opportunities. Do something. “So, I get it that you want to get out there and you want to get a rhythm, but that rhythm is earned, too, and it just hasn’t happened yet. Definitely want it to happen. A couple weeks ago, we kind of went that direction and the running game was no different than it was this last game.” Skattebo is the only back with double-digit carries in a game, and he reached that number in every game before being mostly sidelined and never touching the ball in Sunday’s loss to the New Orleans Saints. He has had mixed success, only averaging at least 4 yards per carry in one game without Jaxson Dart at quarterback. His four fumbles in five gamed led Harbaugh to look elsewhere against the Saints. Harbaugh did not take issue with Harris expressing his frustration. “I respect that he said that,” Harbaugh said. “I mean, I get it. Shoot, that’s how we all want it. That’s for sure and I respect that he would want that, too.” Who Harbaugh and the Giants turn to when they hand the ball off on Sunday against the Houston Texans is anybody’s guess. “I do know that each of the guys, because I’ve talked to all those guys, is they want to be that guy. They’re not advocating for the other guy to be that guy. They’re advocating for themself to be that guy,” Harbaugh said. “My advice is go out there and take the job when you get the ball. Take the job.”
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants news: No QB decision yet, running game issues, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as fans await to hear who will be the starting quarterback in Houston this Sunday. The New York Giants can’t keep making this many mistakes and counting on a comeback | The Athletic The New York Giants have trailed by double […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as fans await to hear who will be the starting quarterback in Houston this Sunday. The New York Giants can’t keep making this many mistakes and counting on a comeback | The Athletic The New York Giants have trailed by double digits in four of their six games this season. That’s not a formula for success, and the Giants were burned by digging a deep hole in their 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints on Sunday. The Giants are a flawed team whose degree of difficulty increased when starting quarterback Jaxson Dart was lost seven snaps into their second game with a season-ending knee injury. It was impressive that the Giants overcame an early 14-3 deficit to beat the Cardinals 36-24 in Week 4 and staged a furious comeback to climb out of a fourth-quarter 27-13 hole against the Commanders last week to force a tie. But the Giants’ surprising 3-2-1 start could be derailed if they don’t start playing cleaner football. Nabers nominated for player of the week Vote Malik for FedEx Air & Ground Player of the Week ‼️ https://t.co/RRhnGW7KTA pic.twitter.com/NkLYzLLjOL — New York Giants (@Giants) October 19, 2026 The six things we learned from Giants’ Week 6 loss: The running back plan didn’t make a lot of sense | New York Post At 10-0 late in the second quarter, the Giants were not exactly dominating but they were in control of their game Sunday against the Saints. Allowing a 58-yard field goal should have meant the Giants went in at halftime ahead 10-3. That did not happen. As it turned out — and this was totally, completely unexpected — that long-distance field goal opened the floodgates for 34 consecutive points for the Saints. Miffed Najee Harris: Giants’ multi-back approach ‘extremely frustrating’ | USAToday.com “Of course not,” Harris said when asked if a running back can get into a groove under those conditions. “I don’t think anybody can. This is not anything against the coaching staff. This is just that running backs, like a quarterback, get in a rhythm. It’s hard to get into a rhythm with one or two runs. The first couple runs you’ll be like: OK, how are they playing me? And then the next ones will be like: This is how you attack it. But if you’re getting a play here and you get taken out for a series, there’s nothing you can do. That’s why I’m saying I don’t know. I’ve never been through this before.” Harris described the results as “extremely frustrating” and pointed to blocking issues, saying the Giants have often been “just one block away.” Harbaugh’s response to Harris on Monday After the loss yesterday, Najee Harris expressed frustration with the Giants' running back usage approach: "It's hard to get into a rhythm with one or two plays…if you're getting a play here and then get taken out for a series, there's nothing you could do. I've never been… pic.twitter.com/DtA0eNqIcP — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 19, 2026 NFL Week 6: Big takeaways, questions from Sunday’s games | ESPN.com The Giants continue to fumble — they have at least once in every game this season. They have four lost fumbles in the past three games, including a crusher this week on a kickoff return by Charlie Jones that flipped the game at the end of the first half. The Saints scored 31 unanswered points after the fumble. QB Report Cards for 2026 NFL Week 6 | Bleacher Report The volatility found within Jameis Winston proved too much for New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh. Harbaugh chose to bench Winston after his second interception. Enter JJ McCarthy, who joined the team three weeks ago after a trade with the Minnesota Vikings. McCarthy provided a spark. After the third-year quarterback threw his own interception, he then rallied the Giants to 17 unanswered points and a chance to tie the game during New York’s final possession. Grade: Winston, D-; McCarthy, B NFL Fallout Week 6: The Giants Should Start QB J.J. McCarthy | FOX Sports The New York Giants are not a very good football team. Their 34-27 home loss to the New Orleans Saints on Sunday exposed all of their flaws. They are lucky to be 3-2-1 and in first place in a terrible division. And if they want to stay there and make a real run at the playoffs, they have to give J.J. McCarthy their starting quarterback job. He did what New York’s brass liked about him when they traded for him back in September — at a time when I wrote Winston was the best of the Giants’ terrible options to replace Dart. McCarthy reminded them of Dart. He moved around the pocket. He spun out of trouble and extended plays. And when the Giants got the ball back with just 57 seconds remaining and 71 yards to go, he kickstarted a potential game-tying drive by stepping away from the pass rush and taking off for a career-long 28-yard run. title: Fantasy Football 2026: Waiver Wire, Week 7 edition
summary: Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 7. Week 6 delivered a second straight week with few major injuries – and fantasy managers are thankful for that. However, Week 7 brings a second straight week with four teams on a Bye. One of those teams is the Chargers, but the others have players […]
full_text: Stroud is dealing | Getty Images Welcome to the Fantasy Football Waiver Wire for Week 7. Week 6 delivered a second straight week with few major injuries – and fantasy managers are thankful for that. However, Week 7 brings a second straight week with four teams on a Bye. One of those teams is the Chargers, but the others have players that you actually might want to start in fantasy. Also, there are still lots of players out with injuries from earlier in the season. The waiver wire might not be offering league winners, but that’s OK. It’s still providing much-needed life support to fantasy managers who are simply trying to field competent lineups. It’s like Hogwarts – help will always be given to those who ask for it. The Process : Each week, I try to identify the top Waiver Wire targets and evaluate the short- and long-term prospects of those players. I also do my best to reveal which players who are coming off a big week are fool’s gold. Finally, I look at streamers who might help you in a pinch (this is usually more important during Bye weeks). Some players discussed won’t be available in your league. I try to list players who are available in more than 50% of leagues. But what does that even mean? A 10-team league with six bench spots will have a much larger Free Agent pool than a 14-team league with eight. Most leagues fall somewhere in between. This isn’t “one size fits all.” By way of example, I won’t list Josh Jacobs, Zach Charbonnet, Denzel Boston, Marvin Harrison, Jr. , Keon Coleman, and Brenton Strange , among others who probably aren’t available in any of your leagues. Note that I’m writing this column BEFORE the Week 6 Monday night game (WAS @ SF). WEEK 7 BYES: Bills, Chargers, Commanders, and Jaguars Week 7 Waiver Wire Quarterback: I’ve been pushing C.J. Stroud in this space for several weeks running, and he keeps delivering QB1 finishes. He should be rostered in 1-QB leagues, as he’s averaging 19 fantasy points per game (FPPG), which is just outside the Top-12 and slightly better than Dak Prescott and Matthew Staffford. Houston’s vaunted defense hasn’t shown up this season, so Stroud is being asked to put up points. It’s the exact opposite of the 2025 playoffs. This week’s matchup is the Giants, who just yielded four total TDs to Tyler Shough (QB2 for the week, pending the Monday night game). Aaron Rodgers makes my list for the fourth straight week. He’s putting up good points, on a pass-happy offense, and the schedule is favorable. That’s the explanation, again. Kirk Cousins continues to be more than serviceable as a QB2. We might see Fernando Mendoza sometime in November or December, but for now it’s Captain Kirk’s starship. Need a Week 7 streamer? Kyler Murray is at home against the Colts, who allow the seventh most FPPG to opposing QBs, and he looked a lot better in his last start. Malik Willis and Geno Smith are facing each other, and both should be serviceable if you need them as a second QB in a Superflex format. Running Back: Kendre Miller has been a regular in this column. He’s sharing, and the Saints have struggled to run the ball, but he’s getting ample volume and should be rostered in all formats. Rachaad White will be seeing a lot of volume for as long as “Bill” is out. And he has stand-alone value when the backfield is fully healthy too. Roschon Johnson is getting plenty of run behind D’Andre Swift while Kyle Monangai is out with turf toe, and he scored each of the last two weeks. Since the Bears play Thursday night, there’s a decent chance that Johnson will get one more game as the 1B in Chicago’s proficient rushing attack. Samaje Perine has a role, which has expanded amid Chase Brown’s struggles. He deserves to be rostered. He garnered 14 carries (plus two receptions) in the Bengals’ last game. Tyjae Spears and Nick Singleton are stashes in deeper-bench leagues. It’s a terrible offense, but Tony Pollard is a trade candidate. A few other names to think about, if you’re in need and/or want some depth that could pop later: Tyler Allgeieir , Tyler Goodson , Emmett Johnson, Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy, Jr. (it’s hard to know what’s going on with the Big Blue backfield, but at some point a new lead back may emerge), Brian Robinson, Jr., Kaelon Black , and Mike Washington, Jr. Wide Receiver I’ll mention Tyreek Hill again, although he still hasn’t signed. Another stash I keep listing is Jordyn Tyson , who should be back soon. Now let’s talk about some rookies. I wrote several times in the preseason about how you need to be patient with rookie receivers, who often pop later in the season. Well, the popping is happening. I was ready to put Germie Bernard in my list of “players who probably aren’t available in your league” and then I saw his roster percentages on the major platforms, one of which was around 50%. Doesn’t anyone read my columns? Or every other analyst’s columns? Bernard is a priority add if he’s available in your league. A-Rod trusts him, the Steelers are very banged-up at the position, and he’s good. The last two weeks: 17 catches for 167 yards and a TD, on 21 targets. Ja’Kobi Lane returned in Week 6 and it was encouraging, and it’ll only get better when Lamar Jackson returns. Lane wowed in the preseason and should quickly replace Rashod Bateman as the #2 wideout in Baltimore – in fact that started to happen in the second half on Sunday. More rookies to roster: Omar Cooper, Jr. (103 yards and a TD in Week 6) and K.C. Concepcion . Adonai Mitchell should be back soon for the Jets, and he also should be rostered, but I doubt both he and Cooper will be fantasy-relevant once both are playing. Tre Tucker has two outstanding weekly performances this season, and four forgettable ones. That’s what you’re going to get with him, but he’s the #1 WR in Vegas and should be on rosters (and can be started as needed, just know he’s very boom/bust). Travis Hunter is getting more run on offense, and he took advantage of that this week (4-59-1 on four targets). Both he and Jakobi Meyers are a little tough to trust on a weekly basis, but both should be rostered. Hunter is a cheat code if you’re in an IDP league and he can be started as a defender. We might not see Davante Adams again until December. Both Jordan Whittington and Konata Mumpfield are on the radar. Of the two, I think Mumpfield has more upside. Need depth? I’ll repeat a bunch of names I’ve listed in recent weeks, together with some new ones: Keenan Allen (nine or more targets in three straight games), Malik Washington, Kendrick Bourne, Chris Bell , Antonio Williams , Savion Williams , Brandin Cooks , Cyrus Allen , DeMario Douglas , Jaylin Noel , and Tre Harris . Tight End: It’s hard to trust any of the Rams tight ends (since they rotate so many of them), but Terrance Ferguson could be back the week after next, and he’s the most exciting playmaker of the bunch. He’s worth a flier. Tyler Higbee should also retain relevance with the Adams injury. Others to consider if you need help: Chig Okonkwo , Hunter Henry , and Pat Freiermuth . That’s all I’ve got. Good luck with your waiver claims! ***This column appears each Monday right here at Big Blue View. Each Thursday, my weekly fantasy preview with my rides, fades and sleepers (start/sit) appears here, and on Fridays you can find my weekly Giants Props of the week, also right here. ***
author: David Hartman

title: Las Vegas Raiders release NY Giants draft bust from practice squad
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders have released former New York Giants draft bust Evan Neal from their practice squad. Neal, the No. 7 overall pick by the Giants in the 2022 NFL Draft, was released by the Giants in the cutdown from 90 to 53 players at the end of the preseason. The Raiders added the […]
full_text: Evan Neal | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Las Vegas Raiders have released former New York Giants draft bust Evan Neal from their practice squad. Neal, the No. 7 overall pick by the Giants in the 2022 NFL Draft, was released by the Giants in the cutdown from 90 to 53 players at the end of the preseason. The Raiders added the 26-year-old to their practice squad on Sept. 4. Neal never appeared in a game for Las Vegas. Neal did not appear in a game for the Giants last season. He played in only 29 of 51 potential regular-season games over his first three seasons as injuries took a toll. New head coach John Harbaugh gave Neal an opportunity this offseason, but Neal did not make the roster. The Raiders also released former Giants tight end Chris Myarick from the practice squad. One of the players they added, offensive lineman Darian Kinnard, spent some time on the Giants’ practice squad earlier this season. Defensive linemen work out The Giants had two defensive linemen in for workouts on Monday, according to the league’s transactions wire. Taki Taimani is a 6-foot-1, 324-pound 27-year-old who played nine games over the 2024 and 2025 seasons with the Minnesota Vikings. He was waived due to injury late last month. Jamheer Carter is a 6-foot-2, 311-pound rookie out of Virginia who went undrafted. He signed with the Los Angeles Chargers and was briefly on their practice squad.

title: NY Giants ‘working through’ quarterback decision, won’t make one yet
summary: New York Giants coach John Harbaugh said on Monday afternoon that the Giants have not yet made a decision who their starting starting quarterback will be on Sunday against the Houston Texans. “We’re working through that now. Honing in on a decision,” Harbaugh said via Zoom. The Giants, of course, have a decision to make […]
full_text: Jameis Winston and J.J McCarthy | Getty Images New York Giants coach John Harbaugh said on Monday afternoon that the Giants have not yet made a decision who their starting starting quarterback will be on Sunday against the Houston Texans. “We’re working through that now. Honing in on a decision,” Harbaugh said via Zoom. The Giants, of course, have a decision to make after J.J. McCarthy threw for 243 yards and led the Giants from a34-10 deficit to the brink of a stunning comeback on Sunday in a 34-27 loss to the New Orleans Saints. What will the decision be based on? “Absolutely like every other personnel decision we make what gives us the best chance to win the football game at this given time or what combination of players and schemes and things like that give us the best chance to, in this case, move the ball, score points, protect the football, etc.,” Harbaugh said. “The things that help us win. Whatever it is that furthers us and helps us. That’s what we want to do.” The Giants are without starting quarterback Jaxson Dart after he suffered a season-ending knee injury in Week 2. Winston took over as the starter in Week 3, and has gone 2-1-1. McCarthy was acquired Sept. 28 from the Minnesota Vikings in exchange for a fifth-round pick. “Jameis has done a great job in so many ways. I just admire him and respect him for it,” Harbaugh said. “He’s helped us win games. Did what he had to do to win games, and that’s something you value very much. “J.J. just got here a couple weeks ago. Where do we stand? We’re trying to put an offense together that he’s got a feel for and those kind of things. All those things are things you factor in.” Harbaugh admitted that being without Dart is an ongoing adjustment. “When we lost Jaxson that made it tough for us to be what we said we wanted to be,” Harbaugh said. “That changed everything. We were trying to find ourselves for a few weeks. We still have been, honestly. “The thing that’s important to remember — we are a work in progress. We are most definitely a work in progress … it’s a long season and we are in the midst of it. We are in position. It’s our responsibility now to find ourselves and put together the type of football team and go get what we want. It’s all right there for us.” Harbaugh just isn’t ready to let the world know which quarterback will try to take the Giants where they want to go.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Grades and advanced stats from the Giants’ loss to the Saints
summary: When you fall behind 34-10 at home to a previously 1-4 team, you can’t expect the reviews to be good, even when you make a desperate comeback in the final quarter to almost erase the deficit you created by stinking up the joint in the middle two quarters. The Pro Football Focus grades reflect both […]
full_text: When you fall behind 34-10 at home to a previously 1-4 team, you can’t expect the reviews to be good, even when you make a desperate comeback in the final quarter to almost erase the deficit you created by stinking up the joint in the middle two quarters. The Pro Football Focus grades reflect both the rotten middle and the much better beginning and ending of this frustrating game. Let’s see who they felt the responsible parties were, both good and bad. PFF grades: Offense To be blunt, Sunday we got mostly Bad Jameis and not enough of Good Jameis, as is reflected in his second lowest grade among Giants offensive players, by far his worst of the season. He did some good things early in the game, but one TD and two INTs is a poor game in anyone’s eyes. It wasn’t the pass rush – Winston was pressured on only six of his 30 dropbacks. His touchdown pass came on a play he was pressured, and his interceptions came on plays he was kept clean. How about J.J. McCarthy? Surely his fantastic 243-yard fourth quarter, including a TD and almost another one to get the Giants to overtime, qualify as an outstanding performance? Well, not quite. McCarthy was only 11 of 21, barely above 50%, and in addition to his one TD he also had an interception. PFF grades relative to what is expected of a player. Completing passes is expected of a quarterback. Interceptions are the opposite of what is expected. So, even though his 243 yards and TD count for something, the turnover counts a lot in the opposite direction and the missed throws bring his score down as well. The result: a passing grade in the “Average” range, although his overall offense grade ranked very good because of his 28 yard run. Malik Nabers was the highest-graded Giant on offense. His grade was just short of the “Elite” 80s, though. On the one hand, he got open a lot and caught many throws. On the other hand, all his catches were on short to intermediate throws and his 52 YAC was less than one-third of his total receiving yards. Isaiah Likely was the second highest-graded Giant on offense. He’s not spectacular, but he catches a bunch of balls every week, some of them TDs. Likely leads all NFL TEs in receiving yards (383) and TDs (5). He has graded near or in the 70s or higher in every game he has played as a Giant except for the rainy, windy Tennessee game, giving him a season receiving grade of 81.1. What a great free agent signing – his $13.3M AAV contract looks like much better value than it did to me when he was signed. The third-highest graded Giant on offense was Charlie Jones. What? The guy whose fumble turned the game around for New Orleans? Yes, but the grade you see above is his offense grade – he caught two balls in three targets, one of them for 49 yards and one a contested catch. Jones got a very bad 41.7 special teams grade for his kickoff fumble. Other than that, most of the offensive grades were in the 50s-60s average to slightly below average range, as befits an offense that was MIA for the middle half of the game. You will note that only one Giants running back, Tyrone Tracy, even managed to grade “Average.” Cam Skattebo got a 58.9 participation trophy because he did get on the field to block for a few plays. We need to talk about the offensive line. Andrew Thomas continues to play injured but gallantly, managing an above average grade on 52 of the 77 offensive snaps to lead all Giants’ offensive linemen. Thomas gave up just one hurry, but he did have a penalty. J.C. Davis saw his first action, replacing Thomas for 25 snaps, compiling a very good grade as well, with no pressures surrendered. The rest of the OL was less successful. Marcus Mbow, replacing the injured Jermaine Eluemunor, and Jon Runyan graded slightly below average. Bryan Hudson, though, followed up his successful debut as starting center with a poor John Michael Schmitz-like performance. Sisi Mauigoa, however, had his third consecutive poor game, especially in pass blocking. The defining feature of the offensive line as a whole, though, is that every single lineman except Andrew Thomas was below average in run blocking (Davis only marginally so). The Giants running backs aren’t playing well, but they’re not getting help from their blockers. PFF grades: Defense You wouldn’t think it for a team that allowed its opponent to jump out to a 34-10 lead, but a number of Giants played well on defense against the Saints. The clear leader was D.J. Reader with a spectacular 89.2 overall defense grade, his third time above 80.0 in his six games and the fifth time in five games that he has graded at least very good. Although he missed one tackle, he made 7 tackles, all of them “stops” (unsuccessful runs for the offense – you know, like the ones the Giants’ running backs make). Shelby Harris got an average grade for his two tackles and two assists. Darius Alexander was slightly below average and Bobby Jamison-Travis well below average in his first NFL action. Tyler Nubin’s days as a starter, or at least a major part of the rotation, may be numbered. Ar’Darius Washington graded an elite 81.4 and Jason Pinnock a very good 78.1 at safety (despite giving up a 31-yard TD) yesterday. Jevon Holland was barely average. The other very good grades went to the Giants primary edge rushers. No one sacked Tyler Shough, but Abdul Carter (73.6) had a hit and three hurries, while Kayvon Thibodeaux (73.5) had a hit and two hurries. Jihad Ward and Trace Ford graded below average. More on Thibodeaux later. At linebacker, Arvell Reese and Tremaine Edmunds had mixed results. Reese had four tackles (all of them stops) and two assists but missed two tackles. Edmunds had six tackles (two stops) and three assists but also missed a tackle. Both played every snap. Finally, the cornerback room did not have its best day, as befits a defense that gave up 34 points in a little more than half the game. Not a single one even graded average, although Deonte Banks (56.8) came close. Dru Phillips (49.5) and Nic Jones (44.7) played poorly, each surrendering a TD. With Paulson Adebo and Colton Hood out, and now Greg Newsome injured as well, the Giants’ cornerback room is in dire straits, getting money for nothing. Advanced stats Aaron Schatz’s (formerly of Football Outsiders, now FTN Fantasy) defense-adjusted value over average (DVOA) metric is considered one of the best overall indicators of team quality, taking into account not just how efficiently your team is playing but how good the guys on the other side of the ball you’re playing against are. The news isn’t exactly great for the Giants: The New York Giants have the third-lowest DVOA ever for a team that is either 3-2-1 or 4-2. Lower: 2017 Dolphins (4-2, finished 6-10) 2022 Colts (3-2-1, finished 4-12-1) — Aaron Schatz 🏈 (@ASchatzNFL) October 19, 2026 They rank 30th in offense, 22nd in defense, and 10th in special teams. Not surprisingly, Schatz’s DAVE metric, which combines DVOA with his pre-season projection for each team with decreasing weight for the latter as the season progresses and more in-season evidence is gathered, still sees the Giants as the least likely NFC East team to make the playoffs: The good news is that maybe the Giants’ offensive coaches are geniuses anyway, at least compared to one supposed quarterback guru: Fun fact: JJ McCarthy had more passing yards in 11 minutes than the Vikings have had in any game all season. — Connor Stalions (@cpstalions) October 19, 2026 My name is Kevin O’Connell and I have no playoff wins and every qb I let leave looks way better on their next team. I’m known as a QB guru — Kaleb Davison (@nephworldwide) October 18, 2026 Completions on passes thrown 40+ yards downfield this season: JJ McCarthy: 2 (on 19 dropbacks) Vikings: 2 (on 169 dropbacks) — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) October 19, 2026 OK, just kidding, Kevin O’Connell is a good coach. He does have his team at 5-0, even though Brian Flores deserves a lot of the credit. Getting serious, McCarthy’s play, despite his INT, was…
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: What’s wrong with the NY Giants’ run game?
summary: The New York Giants run game could best be described, in a word, as “bad”. A desire to run the ball has been woven into the very DNA of the Giants’ offense. A strong running game has been John Harbaugh’s signature for as long as he’s been a head coach, and he brought in long-time […]
full_text: New York Giants running back Najee Harris takes the hand-off. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants run game could best be described, in a word, as “bad”. A desire to run the ball has been woven into the very DNA of the Giants’ offense. A strong running game has been John Harbaugh’s signature for as long as he’s been a head coach, and he brought in long-time run game guru Greg Roman to design the Giants’ rushing attack. Harbaugh also brought fullback Patrick Ricard over from Baltimore in free agency and the Giants made a point of drafting the powerful offensive lineman Sisi Mauigoa. The Giants also drafted Malachi Fields, a big-bodied wide receiver with significant blocking upside. The Giants’ final roster roster is a departure from NFL norms and featured four running backs, four tight ends, a fullback, and just four wide receivers, one of whom has primarily been a returner. Despite wanting to be a smash-mouth, run-heavy offense with an emphasis on the power run game, the Giants’ run game has degraded with each passing week. They’ve been plagued by turnovers and largely been ineffective on the ground. In Week 4, the Giants’ backs carried the ball 28 times (Cam Skattebo: 18, Najee Harris 9, Tyrone Tracy 1), and averaged a combined 3.1 yards per carry with a fumble. In Week 5, the three backs carried the ball 21 times (Skattebo: 13, Harris: 5, Tracy: 3) and averaged 3.5 yards per carry. That, however drops down to just 2.55 yards per carry if we subtract Skattebo’s 19-yard carry at the end of the game as an outlier. The Giants’ running game reached a new low in the loss to the New Orleans Saints. Harris got the start while Skattebo was (effectively) benched after he fumbled away the game against the Cardinals, getting just six offensive snaps and zero touches. “I didn’t expect to have zero, but I mean, I was expecting to not play as much just like I did,” Skattebo said after the game. “And the message is keep your head down and keep going, you know. They understand the type of player I am and I just got to continue to do my job and do it to the best of my ability.” “It sucks, but I can’t put the blame on anybody else but myself,” he added. “I did it to myself. So their consequences leave me on the sidelines, keep me there, and I understand why, like I said. And, I’m going to continue to go out there and give it everything I have for the New York Giants and continue to work hard.” The Giants running backs carried the ball just 14 times (Tracy: 6, Singletary: 4, Harris: 4) and picked up a total of 34 yards on the ground, for an average of 2.4 yards per carry. Tracy, though, did score the Giants’ first rushing touchdown since Week 1. After the game, Harbaugh blamed the flow of the game both for the lack of touches as well as Skattebo’s absence. And it is true that the Giants were forced away from the run game once the wheels fell off the offense and defense in the third quarter. However, that also doesn’t explain why the run game was so ineffective when the game was still close or after the Giants had closed the gap. The problem is multifaceted, with problems in the blocking, the runners, and in the structure of the offense. Blocking woes The Giants have struggled to block their run plays. There have been both poor blocks allowing penetration into the backfield as well as free runners that might have been missed blocks or oversights in the blocking scheme. Harris’ first run of the afternoon might be one such play. The Giants run a counter play outside zone to the offensive right, while having Darnell Mooney pull to the play-side as a misdirection along with Isaiah Likely from an H-back alignment. The offensive line does a pretty good job of washing most of the Saints’ front to the side and creating an initial lane for Harris. However, Andrew Thomas doesn’t get to the second level, leaving a linebacker to tackle Harris. At the same time, while Chase Young is frozen by Mooney and Likely’s motion, he’s completely unblocked on the back side of the play. If the Giants intended the motion to freeze the back-side defender long enough for the runner to get to the second level, that would be an issue with the play design. However, if one of Likely and Mooney was supposed to chip Young (which should be Likely), that would be a missed assignment. On the second play, the Giants call an off-tackle run to the right using outside-zone blocking. Again, it’s initially blocked up well, however the key block falls to tight end Thomas Fidone II, who’s asked to pull from the left edge all the way around to the right side. Fidone does a good job of getting in position, but misses the block. Harris does a better job than anticipated of getting to the edge, and the Giants had blockers in place at the second level. Both right tackle Marcus Mbow and right guard Sisi Mauigoa did a good job of getting into space and staying ahead of the play. They were in position to block Harris up for a nice run along the right sideline. However, the player Fidone missed was able to torpedo Harris and trip him up for a gain of just 2 yards. The first play of the very next drive featured an even worse non-block (again from Runyan Jr.). The Giants once again seek to start the drive with a run, showing a heavy look with both Patrick Rickard at H-back and Isaiah Likely at fullback. Harris takes the handoff, however Runyan is beaten badly by the defensive tackle and driven deep into the backfield and into Harris. The defensive tackle not only takes half-man leverage, but Runyan pops upright out of his stance and never manages to establish any kind of leverage himself. So instead of being able to redirect or re-anchor, he is put on skates. The running backs In addition to the blocking issues, the Giants’ backs were also inefficient, and both Harris and Tracy potentially left significant yardage on the field. “Nobody has really taken the bull by the horns,” Harbaugh said after the game. “Motor (RB Devin Singletary) really hasn’t had a chance to take the bull by the horns. So, we thought we’d get him in the mix, too. So, we put four guys up and see if we can get something going with the running game. That was the idea. “You can say, well, I don’t like that. I don’t like you divvying up the snaps between four backs. And I can tell you, I don’t like it either,” he added. “One of those guys needs to step up. Somebody needs to step up and be the back. And none of those guys have done that yet. And when one of those guys steps up to be the back, then they’ll be the back. That’s your answer. And that’s as honest as I can be about it. And they know that, too. And believe me, they’re all hungry. They want to step up. One of those guys wants to step up. Somebody’s going to step up and take that job. We’re going to see who it is.” That was born out in NextGenStats GPS tracking tacking data after the game. The Giants RBs were expected to earn more yards than actual at the time of the handoff, per NGS tracking data: Singletary: 0 yards over expected (14 -> 14) Harris: -14 (2 -> 16) Tracy: -17 (18 -> 35) Skattebo: 0 carries — Doug Analytics (@Doug_Analytics) October 18, 2026 Part of the issue goes back to blocking and their teammates not sustaining their blocks after the handoff. However, the Giants’ backs also showed some lack of patience behind the line of scrimmage. None of the Giants’ backs had enough carries to qualify for NextGenStats rushing leaders stats. However, we do know that Skattebo was sixth in the NFL in “efficiency” last week, and second in time behind the line of scrimmage. Based on those numbers, it seems likely that the Giants’ primary backs have been trying to hit the holes as hard and fast as possible. However, a modicum of patience could help the Giants realize their missing yardage. Patience and vision are two of the most important traits among running backs, perhaps even more important than raw speed and explosiveness. While none of the Giants’ backs are true home run…

title: Jets vs. Patriots: The duality of Jets
summary: There are genuinely positive signs about the direction of the New York Jets franchise. The 2026 New York Jets are a bad football team. I would argue that both of those statements are true, and this team’s 26-19 loss to the Patriots in Week 6 proves it. This season is not only about wins and […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - OCTOBER 18: Charles Woods #22 of the New England Patriots celebrates with teammates after an interception against the New York Jets during the fourth quarter at Gillette Stadium on October 18, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Jaiden Tripi/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are genuinely positive signs about the direction of the New York Jets franchise. The 2026 New York Jets are a bad football team. I would argue that both of those statements are true, and this team’s 26-19 loss to the Patriots in Week 6 proves it. This season is not only about wins and losses for the Jets. That statement has been uttered so often that it’s practically a cliche, but there is truth to it. Wins and losses aren’t irrelevant for this team, but there are major implications for this team’s future that go beyond where the Jets finish in the standings this season. The most important is the success of the rookie class from the 2026 NFL Draft. The success or failure of a rebuild largely depends on Draft classes being successful. It’s too early to make definitive statements, but we have seen positive signs from all three picks this team made in this year’s first round. They look like they belong. We can’t declare anybody a star yet, and the class has shown some degree of inconsistency. Still, none has looked overmatched on an NFL field. More than that, we have seen a monster Kenyon Sadiq game and a monster David Bailey game. Now we have a monster Omar Cooper game. The rookie, playing the first full game of his career, had 6 catches for 103 yards and a touchdown and had a second touchdown taken off the board on a suspect penalty call in the first quarter. Bad teams come in all shapes and sizes in this league. The 2024 Jets were a team full of overpaid big name players who were past their prime, had massive egos, and didn’t play together. The 2025 Jets were a team that was just completely overmatched from a talent perspective most weeks. The 2026 Jets don’t resemble either of those squads. There aren’t many big names on this roster, and they no longer look incapable of competing. Still, while the talent level has improved, this is still a team with a below average base of it. In a league with a salary cap of $301.2 million, the 2026 Jets have an astounding $116.6 million in dead money. Yes, the Jets are being charged over 38 percent of the Jets’ salary cap dollars to players who are no longer with the team. They don’t tell you about that in the fine print when you decided to go “all in” around a 40 year old quarterback. Despite their improvements, the Jets remain the less talented team most weeks when they take the field. They have to be due to their cap situation. There was no way to build a top notch football team in 2026. Teams like the Jets can still win games, but they have a lower margin for error. They need to play smart and opportunistic football. They can’t afford to overcome errors. Much of that comes back to coaching. It’s difficult to say where the responsibility for players ends and where it begins for coaching when we discuss a team’s success or failure. When it comes to evaluating coaching, I ask myself a simple question. Are the coaches making this team more likely or less likely to have success? One test I have is whether you see a team understand how to play situational football. When you’re in a two minute drill or at the end of a quarter, things are moving too quickly for there to be instruction from the sideline. Either the coaching staff has drilled into players what must be done and what cannot be done or it hasn’t. The Jets were outscored 10-0 in the final two minutes of the first half in this loss, which led Zack Rosenblatt of The Athletic to dig up a truly incredible stat. The Jets have been outscored 100-6 in the final two minutes in the second quarter since Aaron Glenn was hired, according to TruMedia. Have seen a few figures out there but that seems to be the accurate one. That’s zero TDs and two FGs for the Jets with 11 TDs and eight FGs… — Zack Rosenblatt (@ZackBlatt) October 19, 2026 Keep in mind that these scenarios take up only two minutes of each game. That stat has been accumulated over 46 minutes of game time, just a little over three quarters of football. I don’t even know how it’s possible to get outscored 100-6 in 46 minutes of NFL action under any circumstances. But we have seen firsthand the lack of situational football training from the Jets at the end of the half in four of six games. Three times the clock has expired on the offense driving with the ball. In yesterday’s game, a quick three and out that lasted only 23 seconds gave the Patriots the ball back with a chance to get another score before halftime. In those situations, the smartest teams in the league strike a good balance between trying to score and running out the clock to prevent the other team from having enough time to score in the event of a punt. In yesterday’s game, the Jets didn’t even run the ball once. The Patriots were only forced to use a single timeout on the drive. They ended up scoring a touchdown with 14 seconds left on the clock and no timeouts. I understand that you need to throw more than you run in a two minute drill, but it’s standard practice to run the ball once to melt the clock as a hedge against the other team having too much time if the event of a quick three and out. What made this more confounding is the Jets spent the bulk of the first half showing an unwillingness to do anything other than run the ball. Three of the first four Jets drives on offense stalled when Frank Reich called four consecutive runs, and the fourth run netted either 1 or 0 yards. It’s always easy to get on playcalling when it doesn’t work, but an essential part of play calling means staying ahead of the defense. When an offense keeps stalling because it won’t stop running and is eventually stopped, it’s pretty clear there’s a degree of stubborness at play that is hurting the offense. I could go on about the coaching. There is plenty to discuss. We could talk about players not being aware of an obvious hard count situation as the clock is expiring at the end of the quarter or some shaky calls on the other side of the ball. The bottom line is that the Jets show many signs of a poorly coached football team. While their talent level is better than in the past, they aren’t yet good enough to bad execution and poor situational coaching. Few Jets fans are going to leave that game feeling very happy. It was an ugly loss. When it comes to the overall trajectory of the 2026 season, though, it’s perfectly fine to feel a tad conflicted. The Jets are showing some real positives, namely this rookie class. For the first time in four years, it looks like this team is on the verge of hitting a Draft class in a big way. Still, much work remains. This team is losing more than it’s winning. And its coaching is part of that story.
author: John B

title: It’s getting harder to see how the Eagles’ Jalen Hurts marriage ends well
summary: Without having all the facts at our disposal, the impression left by the fiasco surrounding Jalen Hurts’ blood clots, his ill-fated trip to London and the confusing and ever-changing circumstances surrounding it all certainly leads one to believe that the Eagles might have messed this whole thing up. While the narrative around how much sleep […]
full_text: Without having all the facts at our disposal, the impression left by the fiasco surrounding Jalen Hurts’ blood clots, his ill-fated trip to London and the confusing and ever-changing circumstances surrounding it all certainly leads one to believe that the Eagles might have messed this whole thing up. While the narrative around how much sleep Jalen Hurts received prior to taking the field in England is changing by the hour (he did not play the game on no sleep, but reportedly did get a few hours just prior to the game ), it still has the appearance of a less-than-ideal situation. Hurts was obviously not at his most rested, and in my mind, the decision to play him in that game remains a highly questionable one. Also, these international games are awful. They need to stop. Playing football is dangerous and exhausting enough without having to force players to fly over an ocean for 5-6 hours, re-acclimate their body clocks, and then risk their health. If a player suffers an injury serious enough that requires a hospital stay, they have to do it in a foreign country where it may not be safe for them to make a trans-continental flight for a few days. That’s probably what should have happened with Hurts, but that will be a matter for the league and the NFLPA to sort out. Nevertheless, here we all are, six weeks into a disastrous 2026 season that is over. There will be no playoffs and, even if the Eagles somehow win the NFC East with a losing record, anothe title is out of the question. Fans are watching the remnants of a Super Bowl championship roster crumbling before their very eyes, and it feels as though we’re witnessing the end of an era. The offensive line as we know it is gone. The wide receiving room is missing that game-breaking superstar, even with DeVonta Smith in the lineup. Saquon Barkley can’t run behind this line, and can’t stay healthy. They’re down to RB4. There is one tight end. The offensive coordinator looks overmatched. The defensive side of the ball is healthier, but not healthy. Vic Fangio is probably retiring after this season, and who could blame him? What becomes of the defense after he leaves? It would be hard to imagine any head coach being able to sustain a winning record with all these injuries and an incomplete roster, and maybe that has bought Nick Sirianni some time. Or, maybe it will be an excuse for Howie Roseman and Jeffrey Lurie to tear it all down and hire a head coach that can also be the team’s offensive coordinator and play caller. These are all fascinating questions that will be revealed in due course, but the biggest one of all is Jalen Hurts. And after this incident with the blood clots, it’s getting harder to see a future with him under center in 2027. It’s not because Hurts is a bad quarterback, because he clearly isn’t. But even when things looked their most optimistic, there were questions about whether the Eagles would hitch their wagons to Hurts long term after this season. Hurts’ contract extension only guarantees him $22 million following the 2026 season, and serves as an off-ramp for the team to change directions at that position if they want to. The 2026 season was supposed to determine whether Hurts would be able to play well enough to continue on in Sean Mannion’s offense. Unfortunately, we only saw five weeks of uneven play, with Hurts at times struggling to string together drives with an injury-plagued roster and a new offensive coordinator that is still getting his feet wet. And, Hurts also played one of those games on four hours’ sleep in another country after spending the previous night in the hospital because of concerns about blood clots. It’s virtually impossible to judge anything about Hurts’ future based on what’s happened on the field, so Roseman and Lurie will have to make a determination about Hurts’ future based on the circumstances the team is facing as well as the money involved. With Tanner McKee under center the rest of the way, it’s likely the Eagles are going to finish with a top-10 pick. Roseman is likely to start selling veterans at the NFL trade deadline to pile up more picks. In a way, the Hurts situation will make Roseman’s decision at the trade deadline much easier than it otherwise would have been. Saquon Barkley, Riq Woolen, Dallas Goedert, Landon Dickerson and Nolan Smith all should be dealt. The Eagles could pile up enough draft capital in this year’s and next year’s drafts to do whatever they want next April. It’s also perceived to be a solid draft class at quarterback. The opportunity for Roseman to grab a cost-controlled signal caller that can function better in the type of offense the Eagles want to run may be too good an opportunity to pass up. But first, the Eagles have to decide what they want to be. Do they want their offense to look like a Sean McVay/Kyle Shanahan type offense? If so, do they believe Mannion and Sirianni are a good combination to construct an offense like that? Is it too difficult to get someone to create and run an offense with Sirianni as the CEO head coach? That certainly seemed to be an issue last off-season as multiple experienced offensive coordinators turned down the Eagles’ job. The simplest and cleanest way to get the Eagles back on track just may be to get rid of everyone, strip the coaching staff and the roster down, and retool. With a ton of draft picks, the Eagles could rebuild their lines and get a new QB pretty quickly. A new head coach/offensive coordinator would be able to identify the QB he believes would be best suited to run his offense and work on building a new program, starting in 2027. Unfortunately, that would mean Jalen Hurts is traded this off-season. Make no mistake, Hurts is the best quarterback in franchise history . It would be very interesting to see how things would work out if Sirianni was gone and an offensive-minded head coach was brought in who would tailor an offense around Hurts’ strengths. But it would also require Hurts to run the ball more often than he has, and if he’s decided he’s not a running QB anymore, then Hurts’ value as a franchise player decreases tremendously. One also has to wonder if Hurts has lost trust in the organization and how they handled things in London. Sirianni was left hanging out to dry by Roseman and Lurie in his Monday press conference, forced to dance around questions concerning the process that took place. It was bad PR and made Sirianni look like the team was hiding information, although one would assume the ambiguity was done to avoid making statements that could be used against the team in a potential lawsuit and also to protect Hurts’ rights to medical privacy. So we’re left to speculate and guess, and it would appear from the outside that this was handled very badly. It has the appearance of the team prioritizing getting Hurts back on the field as opposed to being conservative and making his personal health the No. 1 priority. Again, that is speculation, but that is the appearance. And if that is all true, does Hurts even want to be an Eagle moving forward? There are so many decisions that will need to be made after these next 11 games are completed. Do the Eagles get rid of all the coaches and start over with a coaching structure that makes more sense? Does Fangio return and, if not, what does that mean for the defense? Which players will be dealt at the trade deadline? But the most important will be … is Jalen Hurts still the franchise quarterback of the Philadelphia Eagles? Right now, it’s getting harder to see how that will be the case in Week 1 of 2027.

title: Eagles News: Jalen Hurts situation “shakes the foundation of what we think we know about how the team operates”
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! As the great Zach Berman has said, people will speculate in the absence of information. And the Eagles might not enjoy that speculation. But if the Eagles have permission from Jalen Hurts to share more about the specifics of his situation, […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - OCTOBER 04: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts #1 looks on during the game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Philadelphia Eagles on October 4, 2026 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA.(Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! As the great Zach Berman has said, people will speculate in the absence of information. And the Eagles might not enjoy that speculation. But if the Eagles have permission from Jalen Hurts to share more about the specifics of his situation, it sure seems like they should. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Bowen: We still don’t know enough about Jalen Hurts’ situation, but we know the Eagles organization is reeling & looks incompetent – PHLY Eagles It’s irritating when coaches do this, because they know very well the medical staff is not available to answer anything. As one Sirianni questioner pointed out, Sirianni is the team spokesman here. It would be reasonable to expect him to be briefed by the medical staff before going out to answer questions. In fact, this was an occasion on which we might have expected to hear from Howie Roseman or even Jeffrey Lurie. Instead we got Sirianni repeating himself, starting multiple answers with “again,” as if all of this was just so repetitive and tiresome for him, hours after we learned the extent of the problem. “We put out a detailed statement for you guys to hear and to understand,” Sirianni said. The only thing Sirianni really made clear is that it wasn’t his decision, to play Hurts or to fly him home. He might get fired this season because of losing, but from what we know right now, I wouldn’t expect this matter to directly lead to Sirianni’s departure. (It could certainly do so indirectly, by exacerbating the losing.) Someone, maybe multiple someones on the team’s medical staff surely will have to have to answer for this, though. […] But it’s bad enough to cast doubt on Hurts’ future here, and by extension, on Sirianni’s future. The organization hasn’t been at a crossroads like this since Carson Wentz demanded to be traded. Even then, though, the Eagles had Hurts. I don’t see Tanner McKee taking the team to any Super Bowls. Overall, this is a shocking failure from an organization that prides itself on its professional standards. It shakes the foundation of what we think we know about how the team operates. Is there a trust issue between Jalen Hurts and the Eagles? – BGN One thing is for certain, some close to Hurts were not happy with how the Eagles dealt with the blood clot situation. They also felt Hurts should have been treated far better by the team this offseason by offering another contract extension. The Eagles never budged. With the perception of how the Eagles dealt with Hurts’ situation, coupled with the looming contract extension, it may not help the relationship. The Eagles Somehow Made the Jalen Hurts Situation Even Worse on Monday – SI This is purely my opinion: I am not sure what the Eagles would have ultimately gained by sneaking Hurts onto the field knowing he was suffering through a dire medical condition and then parking the franchise quarterback on an airplane to let the condition worsen. Again, doing this knowingly would be one of the most significant medical controversies in NFL history and would require firing an entire medical staff. As Mike Florio of Pro Football Talk noted, demand a reexamination of everything when it comes to the way we treat players. Certainly, there have been high-profile stories of team medical professionals acting negligently, and I am not naive to the fact that a doctor can make a horrible mistake. However, this would represent a multiperson, department-wide breakdown for which I don’t have a reference point. But if this were the case, wouldn’t Hurts’s agent be publicly warring against the Eagles on behalf of her client instead of collaborating on a statement with them? There are so many details about the nuances of the treatment, what was known at the time in London, what kind of testing equipment was available to the Eagles in another country before the team made a decision to play Hurts, and what, ultimately, was passed along to the person or people deciding it was O.K. for Hurts to play. We cannot have this narrative both ways: The Eagles seemed to be preparing for a rebuild and, weeks ago, traded one of their best remaining offensive linemen after the Johnson retirement. They also needed to win a game in the absolute destitute swampland that is the NFC East so badly that they would put a quarterback in a life-threatening situation? The Biggest Questions About Jalen Hurts’s Health, and Where the Eagles Go From Here – The Ringer What does this mean for Hurts’s future with the Eagles? Hurts was likely going to be one of the main characters of the 2027 offseason even before this blood clot issue. He’s under contract through 2028, but the bulk of the guaranteed money from the deal he signed in 2023 has already been paid out, and the team could get out of his contract after next season for just a $54.5 million dead cap hit. It’s also possible that Hurts could have been a trade candidate next spring, if the Eagles were interested in moving on, or, if this season had gone well, they might have considered extending him early, before the QB market explodes. Lamar Jackson, C.J. Stroud, and Bryce Young will be among the passers looking for new deals next offseason, just as the quarterbacks from the 2024 draft class—including Caleb Williams and Drake Maye—become eligible for second contracts. The Eagles often try to be ahead of the market—that was the case in 2023 when they got Hurts’s last extension done before Jackson’s new deal with Baltimore. Now, though, it’s not simply a question of timing or cost to keep Hurts, but Philadelphia needing to decide if he’s even still their long-term quarterback. The Eagles are currently on their third offensive coordinator/play caller in the last three years; the most recent change, from Kevin Patullo to Sean Mannion, a Matt LaFleur protege, brought an entirely new scheme for Hurts, one with increased time under center and more frequent use of play-action. The early results haven’t been great—though the injuries, particularly Barkley’s, and personnel changes along the offensive line have made it difficult to give the system a true evaluation. Siranni signed a contract extension in 2025 within months of the Eagles’ most recent Super Bowl title, but it’s hard to imagine that his job is super secure as yet another season spirals away. Playing the rest of this year without Hurts just makes all of those offseason questions more difficult to answer. Eagles QB Jalen Hurts’ blood clot diagnosis explained – ESPN Hurts was originally diagnosed with having a superficial blood clot, according to a team statement released on Oct. 15, which was discovered following an ultrasound in London before the Eagles’ Week 5 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars. It was deemed that mobility was important and Hurts could safely play in the game, per the statement. A follow-up ultrasound last Wednesday showed the blood clot had moved, the team said. Hurts was subsequently ruled out of Sunday’s Week 6 game against the Carolina Panthers and has since been put on injured reserve. ESPN spoke with Dr. Jordan K. Schaefer, associate professor of internal medicine at the University of Michigan specializing in disorders of hemostasis and thrombosis, for a better understanding of causes, treatments, and outlook for those with blood clots. Dr. Schaefer has not treated Hurts and is not involved with the Eagles. The conversation has been edited for brevity and clarity. Jalen Hurts is out for the season. Where do the spiraling Eagles go from here? – The Athletic The problem with this conversation? The worse the Eagles finish, the worse it is for…

title: Eagles-Panthers snap counts
summary: The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 6 loss to the Carolina Panthers are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE DEFENSE SPECIAL TEAMS DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Cole Payton, Jaydon Blue, Drew Kendall INACTIVE: Marquise Brown, Joe Milton III, Saquon Barkley, Michael Carter II, A.J. Epenesa, Jalyx Hunt, […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Darius Cooper #80 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs against the Carolina Panthers during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The official snap counts from the Philadelphia Eagles’ Week 6 loss to the Carolina Panthers are in. Let’s take a look and run through some analysis. OFFENSE Jordan Mailata is the only player on offense who’s played 100% of the Eagles’ offensive snaps this season. He’s also played 11.32% of the Eagles’ special teams snaps. Well, the Eagles did have offensive line continuity in this game with the same lineup from last week and none of the starters getting hurt in this game. Not that it really made a difference for the offense. Tanner McKee posted a 77.5 passer rating in his first career start in a game where the Eagles weren’t resting starters. He wasn’t good and neither was his support system (coaching and talent combined). With Carson Steele suffering a shoulder injury, Dameon Pierce nearly had to play the entire game. The Eagles dressed Jaydon Blue, who was called up from the practice squad, but clearly did not trust him to play. Pierce has logged 10 targets combined over the last two games. Makai Lemon has logged the highest snap count percentages of his rookie season in back-to-back games. He saw the third-most targets on Sunday with six. They resulted in three catches for 19 yards. DeVonta Smith clearly wasn’t 100% while playing through a hamstring injury. Despite seeing more limited snaps than usual, he led the Eagles with 14 targets, which produced seven receptions for 75 yards and a touchdown. Dontayvion Wicks was also not 100% while playing through a hamstring injury. He saw the fifth-most targets on the team. There have been calls for Darius Cooper to play more. And not just from me! He’s the team’s best blocking receiver and he was coming off a career receiving performance in Week 5. And how was he rewarded? With the fifth-most snaps of any pass-catcher and just two targets, the same amount as Elijah Moore and Carson Steele. And this despite the fact that McKee and Cooper have worked well together in the past! Not to mention Smith and Wick playing through injuries. Just seems like the coaching staff could’ve done a better job of trying to get one of their more inspiring offensive options at the moment more involved. “[The Eagles] can't be taking Darius Cooper off the field. Darius Cooper, I would argue, might be their second-most important receiver for the way they want to play." — @FDuffyNFL pic.twitter.com/01198zpjpg — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) October 12, 2026 PHLY’s Bo Wulf pointed out that Johnny Mundt leads the NFL in holding penalties at his position. Hasn’t exactly been a great addition to the tight end room. Elijah Moore logged his first touch in an Eagles uniform; a single reception for four yards. DEFENSE Yet another game where the defense had to be on the field a lot because the offense simply can’t sustain drives. The Eagles’ defense has faced the third-most snaps in the NFL this season and they’re not very far behind the teams ahead of them. This was Jalen Carter’s second-highest snap count percentage of the season, only behind Week 1. This jibes with the sentiment that he’s getting healthier. Though it’s not really ideal to be playing him this much. He played 36 more snaps than the next-closest defensive tackle! With Jalyx Hunt unable to play in this game, Nolan Smith getting hurt early on, and Jonathan Greenard clearly playing through injury, Arnold Ebiketie was the Eagles’ top edge rusher. Keyshawn James-Newby went from being a temporary practice squad elevation to the Eagles’ No. 2 edge rusher in this game due to all of the injuries at that position. Kenny Moore, not Marcus Epps, was the safety next to Andrew Mukuba in nickel packages. Jihaad Campbell and Jeremiah Trotter Jr. rotated at off-ball linebacker but it wasn’t exactly a 50-50 split. Jordan Davis logged his second-highest snap count of the season and that was with him getting injured in the fourth quarter. He was credited with half of a sack, which gives him half of a sack on the season. Byron Young playing the same amount of snaps as Moro Ojomo? Not really what you want to see. But Ojomo did get banged up. Again, Greenard was clearly limited coming into this game. Ty Robinson played more often than usual and actually logged a pressure on just five pass rush snaps! Perhaps he warrants some more playing time. SPECIAL TEAMS Making his NFL regular season debut, rookie safety Cole Wisniewski was limited to special teams duty after being temporarily elevated from the practice squad. Marcus Epps was limited to special teams duty in his first game back from injury. This after beginning the season as the safety next to Mukuba in nickel packages. DID NOT PLAY ACTIVE: Cole Payton, Jaydon Blue, Drew Kendall INACTIVE: Marquise Brown, Joe Milton III, Saquon Barkley, Michael Carter II, A.J. Epenesa, Jalyx Hunt, Lane Johnson Payton served as QB2 behind McKee. A little curious to have Blue active but not use him at all to spell Pierce. Blue is relatively newer to the team but he’s been in Philly since the last day of August. Kendall was active on an emergency depth basis. Perhaps he’ll be healthy enough to replace Jake Majors in Week 7. Hollywood Brown missed three games due to injury and then was a healthy scratch behind six active receivers. I can’t imagine he’s on this roster for much longer? Can’t imagine he has much trade value but maybe Howie Roseman tries to hold out hope on that front? And then maybe cuts him after the trade deadline, if not sooner? Milton III was designated as the emergency third quarterback after only joining the Eagles on Friday. Barkley, MC2, Epenesa, and Hunt all missed the game due to injury. There seems to be hope that Barkley might be able to play in Week 7. As a reminder, Johnson is set to remain on the Eagles’ roster until June 2027 , even though he retired.
