title: 49ers struggled against a one-win team, but they won and improved to 6-0; today was a good day
summary: With both the Seattle Seahawks and the Los Angeles Rams losing in Week 6, the San Francisco 49ers had themselves an opportunity to add another game to their lead in this NFC West thing. I don’t know about you, but I knew it wasn’t going to be easy. And it wasn’t in their 23-17 win over the […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 19: Malik Mustapha #6 of the San Francisco 49ers reacts during the fourth quarter against the Washington Commanders at Levi's Stadium on October 19, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images With both the Seattle Seahawks and the Los Angeles Rams losing in Week 6, the San Francisco 49ers had themselves an opportunity to add another game to their lead in this NFC West thing. I don’t know about you, but I knew it wasn’t going to be easy. And it wasn’t in their 23-17 win over the Washington Commanders, given how wide open the NFC East is and how the 49ers are dealing with their own issues; this wasn’t going to be a cakewalk like the 7.5 points indicated. Even knowing it wasn’t going to be a boat race, I certainly didn’t expect THAT. I didn’t feel good when the half ended, thinking there was a window for the Commanders to come back, and that’s exactly what they did. But the 49ers pulled out the win, and the defense, despite falling apart in the second half, made it right at the very end. They also picked up the offense when they sputtered out in the same half. That means we play the oldies but goodies. Ice Cube, what kind of a day is it? And because Fooch didn’t give me my pony in the game thread. Here’s the pony: View Link The 49ers struggled in this game, but good teams find a way to win; bad teams find a way to lose . While the victory is nice, it shows the 49ers need to get healthy if they want to make it back and finally win a Super Bowl. All of our gripes, annoyances, rolled eyes, whatever we did to cope with this frustrating game, come back to that: They won. Something should be said for them being 6-0 despite all these injuries. This week we’re going to hear about how the 49ers are “beatable,” and maybe Brock Purdy isn’t MVP. Whatever. The 49ers are a 6-0 team but still beatable, while Brock Purdy is now the NFL’s all-time passing leader; I’ll take that. He can get back into the MVP conversation later. The 49ers won, the rest of the NFC West lost. But again, as Fooch always said: a win is a win is a win. I don’t prefer this type of win to be against a 1-win Commanders team, but their backs were against the wall. They had to make right for that (dumb) tie they had last week. Many of you noticed how I grabbed a clear shot of Mike Evans’ jersey number 5 in the 5-0 headline I had on the site. Well, how adequate is it that the 49ers are 6-0 thanks to one number 6, Malik Mustapha? Mustapha delivered that hit to stop a Commanders run and then jarred the ball loose on a possible touchdown to save the day. And here are those amazing plays in order: MALIK MUSTAPHA SAYS NO! 🚫🙅‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/bX0a1k24ej — 95.7 The Game (@957thegame) October 20, 2026 ANOTHER INCREDIBLE PLAY BY MALIK MUSTAPHA 49ERS FOOTBALL #PMSMNFonESPN2 pic.twitter.com/qo7invtGRt — Pat McAfee (@PatMcAfeeShow) October 20, 2026 If trends continue, that means if the 49ers go to 7-0, De’Zhaun Stribling did something to help the win. Don’t get too excited; I doubt Stribling will be back in a week, when we were looking like later in November/early December. So I guess the player contributing to the undefeated streak will end… I would be saying that if there wasn’t a number 70, and that jersey belongs to Romello Height. And I think next week we’ll get another big game from him after this one. This game? Height led the team in pressures. That’s a good draft pick, I’ll say. So if current trends continue, we may see Romello Height’s photo featured front and center. Speaking of Height, the defensive line is getting it. They got gassed (and gashed) late, but Height and Gracen Halton both showed us that once they get Nick Bosa back, this line has a chance to be filthy. Along with those two, Mykel Williams played maybe his best game as a pro. The 49ers have some youngsters on the defensive line that are developing nicely. I also want to call out the officiating: it was trash for both sides. That officiating crew looked way over their heads during that game with their calls (including letting Fred Warner get away with that hit). That illegal contact penalty towards the end was absolute garbage—and predictable before the ball was snapped—only highlighted more by how long it took them to figure out what the penalty was. But good teams overcome bad officiating. Still, you know it’s ridiculous when you can predict something stupid like this is coming on fourth down: Refs call illegal contact on the Niners on this 4th and 8 attempt by the Commanders… Not a lot of contact here pic.twitter.com/LKSqrBBA7f — Rate the Refs (@Rate_the_Refs) October 20, 2026 Again, the 49ers and the Commanders both got hosed by the officiating crew. It was near-embarrassing. Hopefully the 49ers get Nick Bosa back next week. They have the Atlanta Falcons, then a much-needed bye. And then add more pieces and just. stay. healthy! But we don’t need to worry about that right now. Right now, the 49ers are undefeated at 6-0, have a three-game lead in the NFC West, and are doing this not healthy. This team is only going to get better.
author: Patrick Holloway

title: Kyle Shanahan on Mike Evans’ injury: ‘We don’t think it’s a long-term thing’
summary: The San Francisco 49ers lost multiple players during their victory over the Washington Commanders: WR Mike Evans (Achilles)LB Luke Gifford (groin)CB Upton Stout (shoulder) When asked about the severity of Evans’ Achilles injury, Kyle Shanahan said, “Just the same thing that was bothering him all week. Just acted up during the game; couldn’t go. We’ll […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers lost multiple players during their victory over the Washington Commanders: WR Mike Evans (Achilles) LB Luke Gifford (groin) CB Upton Stout (shoulder) When asked about the severity of Evans’ Achilles injury, Kyle Shanahan said, “Just the same thing that was bothering him all week. Just acted up during the game; couldn’t go. We’ll see how he feels this week.” Shanahan said he didn’t think Evans would need further Achilles testing, which is a good sign. Jennifer Lee Chan tweeted that she’s hearing Evans’ Achilles is intact. Shanahan added that “it was a pretty close call” whether Evans would play in this game. The two talked leading up to the game, and Evans said he’d dealt with it during his career and felt confident he’d be good to go for Week 6. When asked about his level of concern about Evans, Shanahan said, “It’s something that’s bothered him before, and something that has bothered him throughout the week. When you have Achilles tendinitis like he does, it kind of is what it is. It flared up tonight. I hope he recovers throughout the week. But we don’t think it’s a long-term thing. Right now, it almost cost him this game. It cost him two quarters. Hopefully, he’ll be able to play next week. But if not, we’ll have to have the rest of the group step up and hopefully get him healed up after the bye week. Shanahan said, “That was the confidence he gave me, but we knew he might not be able to last.” Christian Kirk is a “possibility” for Week 7 against the Falcons. “He had two good practices in. It’s just his first two practices of the year. We were down on wideouts, so it’s still something we discussed. But we decided to give it another week.” Per Shanahan, Demarcus Robinson will not be ready this week. Shanahan acknowledged that “it’s tough” at wide receiver with all of the injuries: “That’s what you got practice squad guys for. We’ll see how all of our guys heal up. I’ll be surprised if we got Deebo or D-Rob back until most likely after the bye week. We’ve got enough guys in our building. We’ll put a plan together and see how it goes.”
author: Kyle Posey

title: 49ers escape Week 6 with a win over the Commanders after a second-half letdown
summary: Jordan James took the opening kickoff to the 36-yard line for the San Francisco 49ers. Jordan Watkins started at wide receiver opposite Mike Evans. Jacob Cowing came in on the first third down. Evans caught a 25-yard pass on the first play. Kaelon Black converted on 3rd-and-1. The offense quickly got into the red zone. […]
full_text: (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jordan James took the opening kickoff to the 36-yard line for the San Francisco 49ers. Jordan Watkins started at wide receiver opposite Mike Evans. Jacob Cowing came in on the first third down. Evans caught a 25-yard pass on the first play. Kaelon Black converted on 3rd-and-1. The offense quickly got into the red zone. Brock Purdy’s first target to George Kittle went for a touchdown, giving the 49ers a 7-0 lead. It was the third time the Niners began the game with a touchdown drive this season. Purdy went 5-for-6 on a 9-play, four-minute drive. Jayden Daniels found Terry McLaurin on what looked like a busted coverage to begin Washington’s first drive for 27 yards. But their drive stalled after Luke Gifford limited Daniels’ scramble to three yards, and Malik Mustapha spooked Stefon Diggs into a drop. That meant the Commanders would settle for a 51-yard field goal to make it 7-3. So much for any Achilles injury or soreness, Evans gained 54 yards to start the Niners’ second drive. Once again, they were in the red zone. But Christian McCaffrey lost three yards on a screen pass, and Connor Colby’s false start gave the Niners 3rd and long. The offense stayed on the field for 4th and 3. Purdy looked right, didn’t see anything that he liked, so scrambled for the first down. On third-and-goal from the one-yard line, Christian McCaffrey punched it in to give the Niners their second consecutive scoring drive. This drive took a little under five minutes on 8 plays. Eddy Pineiro missed another extra point, making it 13-3. It is the kind of miss you can’t turn a blind eye to, as they add up. Luke Farrell was flagged for a facemask on the kickoff, gifting Washington great field position. A Daniels scramble was negated after Romello Height drew a holding flag. Daniels fled the pocket because Gracen Halton won. On third and 9, Osa Odighizuwa sacked Daniels, forcing the punt. Raheem Morris’s blitz gave everybody a 1-on-1, and Odighizuwa rewarded him with a sack. On the same play, the cart came out for McLaurin, which is the last thing you want to see. Jacob Cowing inexplicably fielded a punt, then muffed it, giving the Commanders a 58-yard gain in field position. Evans was held on one play. He couldn’t hold on to a third-down target, and the 49ers punted on their third drive. Washington had another bust on its third drive. Two players were guarding one, leaving Chig Okonkwo open 35 yards downfield. He stepped out of bounds six yards earlier, for a 29-yard gain. Nonetheless, Washington was knocking on the door once more. Daniels was stopped short of the sticks on third down, forcing a 4th-and-2. But Daniels threw it away, and the Niners forced a red-zone stop. Purdy found Jordan Watkins for a gain of 22. Then Brandin Cooks for 13 on a now slant. As the 49ers were driving, McCaffrey fumbled for the first time this season and gave the ball right back to Washington. But Gracen Halton drew a holding call and sacked Daniels, so all was forgiven. That holding penalty was the most by a 49ers defensive tackle since DeForest Buckner was on the roster. It’s another way to quantify impact. Farrell had another penalty; this one was costly. Instead of 1st and goal from the seven, it was third and long. But Purdy scrambled his way out of trouble once more. He picked up a first down on 3rd and 11. He ran right by Sonny Styles. Trent Williams was flagged for holding right after, putting the offense back behind the sticks. After Evans picked up a first down, he limped off the field and into the locker room. During the timeout, Evans looked like he was stretching his Achilles. He left the game with 94 yards. Purdy kept the ball on fourth down to pick up a first down. McCaffrey finished it off, giving the 49ers a commanding 20-3 lead. It was a 14-play drive that took over six minutes off the clock without giving Washington another possession. The 49ers had 17 first downs compared to the 16 total plays run by Washington. Washington received the ball to begin the third quarter. They got their third first down of the game after Treylon Burks caught an 18-yard pass. Romello Height drew a holding call. Keion White forced a false start. The defense got the Commanders into another third-and-long situation. On 3rd and 8, Daniels ran into Mykel Williams, his first sack of the season. The Commanders were 0-for on third down after they picked up their third sack of the evening. The offensive line picked up Washington’s 6-man pressure, allowing Purdy to find Kittle for a gain of 35. A third-down pass was tipped, and the offense had a rare trip into the red zone that didn’t result in a touchdown. Pineiro’s 33-yard try was good, making it 23-3. Washington answered with an 11-play drive that took over five minutes. Jayden Daniels kept the drive alive on a 4th-and-five to Diggs before finding him in the end zone. That made it 23-10. Brock Purdy ran into trouble to end the third quarter, and the Niners offense would face another second-and-forever. Purdy navigated the pocket well on third down, but Kittle had the pass poked away, leaving it to Corliss Waitman’s second punt. It looked like another McCaffrey fumble, but Christian’s brother didn’t touch the ball on replay, and the Commanders retained possession. The 49ers were fortunate to avoid a helmet-to-helmet penalty on Fred Warner. On 3rd and 4, Mykel Williams tipped Daniels’ pass to force another punt. However, Malik Mustapha was flagged for illegal contact, giving the Commanders a fresh set of downs. The call went against Mustapha, but the replay showed it was against Renardo Green. Washington converted its first third down of the game in the fourth quarter. A late hit by Odighizuwa tacked on 15 yards. And just like that, it was 1st-and-goal from the nine. Daniels hooked up with Raachad White, who had a step on Deommodore Lenoir, for another touchdown. That made it 23-17. The 49ers got sloppy. After the drive, they committed eight penalties for 63 yards. Daniels was 22-for-27 with a passer rating of 124.8. Their offense was clicking. Could the offense answer back? Purdy couldn’t avoid a free rusher and took a sack on a second-and-long. He sailed a throw on third down. The Niners went three-and-out on back-to-back drives. It’s no coincidence they struggled without Evans. Raheem Morris had enough of Upton Stout. Ashtyn Davis came in at nickel for Stout. Davis gave up a 30-yard completion. Washington scored on the next play, but a penalty negated a 31-yard touchdown run. On 4th-and-8, Washington used a valuable timeout. Romello Height sacked Daniels, but a flag in the secondary once again gifted Washington a fresh set of downs. The flag was on Davis. Height made a great rush. The game would come down to 4th and 3 after a big hit by Mustapha on third down. Mustapha came through again by jarring loose a target at the goal line. The 49ers don’t win this game without his performance. The Commanders had two timeouts. We’ve seen the 49ers be aggressive in these situations, but that was with Evans on the field. On 3rd and 8, the Niners ran the ball and drained the clock. A conservative call that gave Washington the ball back with a minute remaining and a chance to win. It was the offense’s third straight three-and-out. Siran Neal was flagged for kick-catch interference. That put Washington around midfield with 52 seconds remaining. Instead of Stout or Davis, Lenoir moved into the slot with Jack Jones replacing him outside. This follows Davis’s struggles on the previous two drives. Daviels took an intentional grounding penalty after Romello Height got pressure once again. It was costly, as the 10-second run-off left only six seconds remaining. Height and White sacked Daniels on a three-man rush, helping the 49ers escape.

title: 3 keys to a 49ers win over the Commanders: Can Raheem Morris contain Jayden Daniels?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have a chance to go 6-0 on Monday night when they host the Washington Commanders at Levi’s Stadium in primetime. Heading into the game, the 49ers are 7.5-point favorites on a hefty 51.5 point total. San Francisco has been on a heater to start the year, and they’ve had success over […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Brock Purdy #13 of the San Francisco 49ers in action during the game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Alika Jenner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have a chance to go 6-0 on Monday night when they host the Washington Commanders at Levi’s Stadium in primetime. Heading into the game, the 49ers are 7.5-point favorites on a hefty 51.5 point total. San Francisco has been on a heater to start the year, and they’ve had success over some quality opponents so far. The Niners have blown out the Los Angeles Rams and Miami Dolphins. They beat the Arizona Cardinals, who have looked more competitive than expected this year. And they’ve beaten the Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos, who were both in their respective conference championship games last year. They’re taking on a Commanders team coming off an embarrassing loss, as a last-second blunder by quarterback by quarterback Jayden Daniels forced them into a tie with the New York Giants last weekend. San Francisco does have some injury news going into the game, as receiver Mike Evans is expected to play despite missing the entire week of practice. How can they pull off the win on Monday night? Here are three keys to a Niners win in Week 6. Maintain third down efficiency The 49ers have been the second-most efficient offense in the NFL through Week 6, ranking only behind the Buffalo Bills in EPA per play. A big part of that has been winning on early downs. They’re by far the most efficient offense on the league by EPA per play on first and second downs. As a result, they don’t get to third downs that often, ranking 32nd in the NFL in third downs per game. The Commanders have actually been quite a solid early-down defense, ranking eighth in the NFL in EPA allowed per play on first and second downs. However, when you get to third downs, it’s a different story. Washington is 28th in the NFL on third downs by EPA allowed per play. They struggle to get off the field, ranking 24th in the NFL in third down conversion rate allowed (43.2 percent). The 49ers have regularly been an elite third-down conversion team under Kyle Shanahan, and they lead the NFL in conversion rate this year, while ranking second in success rate on third downs. This is setting up to be a strong environment for the 49ers offense, and the total indicates so. The numbers are on their side here in this matchup with both early down, and especially third-down success. Contain the quarterback Washington’s offensive line has been better than expected this year, and the Commanders have shown they want to run the ball as well. The issue? They’ve been inefficient in doing so. But with Jayden Daniels back, Washington’s run game saw a boost last weekend, with the quarterback going for over 100 yards and two touchdowns on the ground alone. The 49ers will be in a good spot if they can continue stopping the run on Monday. But a big part of the equation is accounting for Daniels’s feet too, which is what makes the passing game more dangerous as well with the scramble drills. Raheem Morris has been creative getting pressure on the quarterback this year. This could be more of a contain game for the 49ers’ defensive line, and stopping the run on early downs will also help mitigate the threat of Daniels and force Washington into unfavorable situations. Get off to a strong start The 49ers have had a couple of impressive finishes to games this season, thanks to some clutch play from Brock Purdy. The MVP candidate engineered some fourth-quarter scoring drives to win games against both Denver and Seattle, and the 49ers are 6-0 as a result. He also helped shutdown Arizona’s late comeback effort in Week 3, leading to the 36-30 win. San Francisco has shown they can win early. But getting off to a strong start here feels like a big key. One, we just mentioned Washington’s struggles running the ball. Playing from behind for a large portion of the game would only make them even more one-dimensional. Two, the Niners remain banged up at receiver, and Mike Evans is clearly hurt coming into this one. Even against a shoddy Commanders pass defense, it would be ideal if the 49ers didn’t have to rely as much on Evans and his banged-up self in a game where they’re favored by 7.5 points. We also saw the run game start coming to life against Seattle. Remaining balance feels like the way to solve this Commanders defense, and the 49ers have been highly efficient this season when they’ve been able to. The Niners are at home here as big favorites. The matchup plays into their favor, and it feels like a spot where they should take care of business, rather than letting things linger against a dangerous quarterback.

title: 5 best Titans players in thrilling Week 6 win over Colts
summary: The Tennessee Titans executed a shocking comeback victory, beating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 in Week 6. They trailed 13-0 at halftime and overturned a multi-score deficit in the second half by making splash plays on offense, defense, and special teams. We’ve identified the Titans’ five best performances from Sunday’s triumph. Jeffery Simmons, DT Jeffery Simmons […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - OCTOBER 18: Tennessee Titans wide receiver Carnell Tate (14) makes the catch for a touchdown in the second half of play during and NFL game between the Tennessee Titans and the Indianapolis Colts on October 18, 2026 at Lucas Oil Stadium at Indianapolis, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Tennessee Titans executed a shocking comeback victory , beating the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 in Week 6 . They trailed 13-0 at halftime and overturned a multi-score deficit in the second half by making splash plays on offense, defense, and special teams. We’ve identified the Titans’ five best performances from Sunday’s triumph. Jeffery Simmons, DT Jeffery Simmons kickstarted the Titans’ comeback effort by stripping (and recovering) Colts RB Jonathan Taylor of the football. The multi-time Pro Bowler was also credited with two sacks. Simmons was his usual unblockable self against the Colts. Carnell Tate, WR The offense ran through rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate in Week 6. He scored his first career touchdown on a well-designed pass by Cam Ward to tie the game 13-13. Tate finished with six receptions for 70 yards and a TD. He continues to look like a legitimate WR1. Joey Slye, K Kicker Joey Slye made four second-half field goal attempts to help lead the Titans’ comeback win. That included makes from 56 and 49. Slye even made a 48-yard extra point after a penalty pushed the try-after attempt backwards. He’s so consistent with a big leg. Jacob Martin, EDGE Titans veteran EDGE Jacob Martin had a sack and applied consistent pressure on Colts QB Daniel Jones. It’s not saying much, but he’s definitely been the Titans’ most consistent edge rusher. Martin also missed a few tackles, but he was generally quite good. Amani Hooker, S Veteran safety Amani Hooker generated the first of four turnovers. The savvy ballhawk tip-toed the sideline expertly to haul in a tipped pass while keeping his feet in-bounds and securing the ball without juggling it, ensuring the refs couldn’t overturn the call. Hooker is having an underrated season for this Titans defensive backfield. Honorable mentions: Cor’Dale Flott (CB), Tony Adams (S), Jermaine Johnson II (DE), Anthony Hill Jr. (LB), Femi Oladejo (DE), James Williams Sr. (LB), Julius Chestnut (RB).

I hoped they would keep him forever. Ballard didn’t just get fired because he sent two first-round picks to the New York Jets for CB Sauce Gardner, but that certainly didn’t help. If you are going to trade two first-round picks for a player, especially a defensive player, that player better be a game wrecker. Gardner is a really good player, but that was a huge overpay. title: What Commanders’ Dan Quinn said about crucial 4th-down play vs. 49ers
summary: So, we’ve all seen it. And it was weird.   The video on the ESPN broadcast feed from Monday night’s game between the Commanders and 49ers showed what looked like Washington head coach Dan Quinn saying something that amounts to the fact he was unsure of what down it was.   That’s a rough look […]
full_text: So, we’ve all seen it. And it was weird. The video on the ESPN broadcast feed from Monday night’s game between the Commanders and 49ers showed what looked like Washington head coach Dan Quinn saying something that amounts to the fact he was unsure of what down it was. That’s a rough look after the game management nightmare that resulted in a tie with the New York Giants in Week 5. Quinn couldn’t afford one in Week 6. One was (apparently) was caught on camera. Or maybe not. Either way, it looked, well, not great. The Commanders head coach says this is much ado about nothing , but let’s rewind. Washington had a fourth-and-2 with roughly 13 minutes left in the second quarter. Jayden Daniels rolled to his right and then a flag fell down, though the play was allowed to complete. The quarterback inexplicably threw the ball out of bounds and to no one. Did Jayden Daniels just throw the ball away on 4th down??? #NFL #Commanders #RaiseHail #49ers #FTTB #WASvsSF pic.twitter.com/WzU2IxfkeF — Dom (@ZeroChillSports) October 20, 2026 That’s a curious decision in itself, to say the least. Why wouldn’t you put the ball in play and try to convert? Even more trouble was this the video you’ll view below, where it looks like Dan Quinn didn’t know what down it was. Here’s his explanation of that issue , as told to on-site reporters during his Monday postgame press conference . "I definitely knew it was 4th down." Commanders HC Dan Quinn on the 4th down play that Jayden Daniels threw the ball away in the second quarter. pic.twitter.com/SiBP2SIClg — ESPN (@espn) October 20, 2026 “I definitely knew it was fourth down,” Quinn said. “We were going for it. And, what I think you’re referring to, with the illegal shift there’s not a penalty to go for a field goal. It’s a turnover on downs.” After the game-management kerfuffle from a week ago, that’s a good thing. And it still wasn’t a great look. The 49ers declined the flag, negating that point, and locking in a turnover on downs. No matter what actually happened on the headset, the result was a major disappointment considering the ball was on the 49ers 13-yard line. The Commanders simply must’ve come up with a score there and they didn’t. That led to trouble at the end of the game that the Commanders ultimately lost. Success on the play we’re talking about could’ve changed the game. There's no way Dan Quinn's saying "Aww, that was 4th down" like people are suggesting? There's no way, right? I refuse to believe that. pic.twitter.com/37ZoU64cFK — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) October 20, 2026 The Commanders ultimately fell just short, and all these little moment matter. Do you think Dan Quinn knew it was fourth down? Let us know in the article comments below. It’s 2:30 a.m. when I’m writing this. I’m very tired. Please excuse the typos that are most certainly in this story. — SB

title: Commanders report card: Team grades in NFL Week 6 loss to 49ers
summary: Here we are again, following up another Commanders loss. Yeah, Washington had a shot at the end and could’ve beaten a more talented 49ers team on Monday night. But they didn’t. Keeping it close doesn’t get a half point in the win column.   Horseshoes and hand grenades and all that. So here we are, […]
full_text: Here we are again, following up another Commanders loss. Yeah, Washington had a shot at the end and could’ve beaten a more talented 49ers team on Monday night. But they didn’t. Keeping it close doesn’t get a half point in the win column. Horseshoes and hand grenades and all that. So here we are, dissecting a 23-17 loss to San Francisco at Levi’s Stadium that dropped the Commanders to 1-4-1 . Yeah, we know the early-season schedule was rough, but that ain’t gonna cut it. There were several reasons why that happened, none more prevalent that a just-plain-awful first half where the Commanders couldn’t do anything right. A valiant second-half comeback attempt might’ve just saved Dan Quinn’s job (for now), but it couldn’t prevent another loss. While we won’t make this a first-half-vs-second-half report card (that would just be too confusing), it might help some grades. So, get ready for some middle-of-the-road stuff in this Week 6 report card. Rushing offense The Commanders had just two handoffs in the first half. I mean, how, as a play caller, is that possible, even with a decreased play count? The Commanders ended up with 13 carries to running backs – a beauty by Jeremy McNichols was called back by penalty – for 43 yards. That’s a 3.3-yards-per-carry average . Not great. We can concede the blocking wasn’t ideal and the 49ers were getting after it, but the run designs and the commitment to the run game were lacking overall. Grade: D Passing offense Jayden Daniels’ stat line doesn’t look too shabby. He completed 29-of-40 passes for 300 yards , two touchdowns and no picks. Daniels heated up in the second half and nearly brought the Commanders back from the brink. The pass protection remains suspect, but the Commanders still worked the ball down the field despite a brutal Terry McLaurin injury that will have a lasting effect. Stefon Diggs is a dawg (up, I spelled that right) and Treylon Burks is surely the No. 2 receiver moving forward. The air attack got better as the game progressed, but couldn’t finish the job. Grade: B Rushing defense K’Lavon Chaisson punched the ball free from Christian McCaffrey’s grasp – Frankie Luvu recovered it — and the 49ers running back was pissed. He executed some on-field revenge in the first half, with 10 carries for 44 yards and two touchdowns. He had just 20 yards after that. See why these grades are tough? The front seven tightened up but still wasn’t great, allowing 4.3 yards per carry. Grade: C Passing defense Welcome, my friends to another tale of two halves. Brock Purdy exploited the Commanders in the first two quarters, to the tune of 9.7 yards per attempt. He was using George Kittle and Mike Evans to great effect, but things toned down when Daronte Jones started blitzing more and Evans was lost to injury. Nick Cross had a real impact on this one, as did the pass rush once it kicked up. It was, however, too little and too late to get a win for Washington. Grade: C Special teams Luke McCaffrey should count his lucky stars that punt didn’t touch him, cause it sure looked like he was trying to catch the punt and bailed out way too late. Drew Stevens was just fine and Tress Way was a boss as always. No big returns gained, no big returns allowed. Grade: B Coaching We don’t believe in moral victories around here. Yes, the Commanders fought back in the second half. That’s a plus for head coach Dan Quinn. The defense flipped the script in the second half with three points allowed after giving up 20 in the first. That’s a plus for defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. It’s hard to find pluses for offensive coordinator David Blough after watching the game live. All that said, a loss is a loss. The coaching wasn’t good enough. And, are we suuuure we buy DQ’s explanation on that fourth-down disaster in the first half? Grade: F How would you grade the Commanders after that loss to the 49ers? Let us know in the comments below.

title: Key takeaways from Washington Commanders loss  to San Francisco 49ers
summary: BOX SCORE We all know what happened in Week 5. We don’t have to go over that debacle against the Giants for the 1,000th time. Washington said all the right things, took accountability for that mess and maintained a unified front while vowing to be better moving forward.   Head coach Dan Quinn even turned […]
full_text: BOX SCORE We all know what happened in Week 5. We don’t have to go over that debacle against the Giants for the 1,000 th time. Washington said all the right things, took accountability for that mess and maintained a unified front while vowing to be better moving forward. Head coach Dan Quinn even turned his hat around. While seemingly silly, it was a symbol that he and the Commanders were ditching the relaxed vibe and taking things more seriously. Proving that they were better and had rebounded well was a tough task, however, considering they had to fly across the country to play the unbeaten San Francisco 49ers on Monday night. The 49ers were more talented at most every spot, even with San Francisco beset by with injuries. Leaving with a win was always considered tough – it would’ve been huge considering the dismal state of the NFC East – but remaining competitive seemed necessary. Despite an awful first half, the Commanders certainly were. And wouldn’t ya know it, this game also came down to a last-second scenario, with the Commanders pushing to win the game with no timeouts and less than a minute left. Could the Commanders handle this late-game scenario? The game management wasn’t the issue here, but the result wasn’t any better. The game was in the balance, with the Commanders pushing hard for a score with less that an minute left. In the decisive play, Daniels was called for an intentional grounding call that generated a loss of down and a 10 second runoff, setting up a presumptive last-second chuck into the end zone. Jayden Daniels ’ final pass never left his hand, leaving this comeback attempt just short of a miracle finish. Jayden Daniels gets sacked as time expires. 49ers win 23-17 pic.twitter.com/7NMR0apwfI — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) October 20, 2026 The Commanders lost this one 23-17 , a heartbreaker that drops the Commanders to 1-4-1 on the season heading into their bye. Here are some key takeaways from this Week 6 defeat: Dan Quinn’s seat cools a bit The Commanders attempted to convert a fourth down in the first half that went completely wrong. They were flagged for an illegal shift on the play, but quarterback Jayden Daniels threw the ball away over working to complete a pass that would earn a first down. It was a messy play that has become all too common. Then a video clip from the broadcast went viral, where Quinn seemed to look confused about what down it was. This is a very tough look for Dan Quinn. Looks like he thought the 4th down play was 3rd down. Very tough especially after last week pic.twitter.com/KUU8D2S81d — JP Finlay (@JPFinlayNBCS) October 20, 2026 UPDATE (10/20, 12:27.a.m.): Dan Quinn said in his postgame press conference that he knew what down it was, and that he was addressing a question on the headset. Here’s his answer: Dan Quinn explains what he was actually saying on that fourth down … pic.twitter.com/t3x5L9EKWG — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) October 20, 2026 Back to what we discussed in the intro, Quinn needed a solid performance and signs of hope for better following what happened in Week 5. Netflix/The Ringer reporter Tom Pelissero stated that owner Josh Harris preferred to not make an in-season change but would be following Monday night’s game closely and barring signs the team had given up or blowout losses, he preferred to let Quinn try and turn things around. With that in mind, will Harris admire the Commanders fight in the second half? They were within one possession late against a super-talented 49ers team and it was clear late in this game that the Commanders showed fight. The Commanders cut a once massive deficit to one possession with a Jayden Daniels pass to Rachaad White, one of many plays by the star quarterback that got Washington back in the game. . @Chaad_1 in the endzone ‼️ 📺 #WASvsSF on ESPN pic.twitter.com/2wABqdIg3B — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 20, 2026 The Commanders were driving for a go-ahead score inside of two minutes, but a fourth-and-3 was not converted and put the Commanders in a bind. Bottom line: The Commanders showed fight. That’s a data point Harris will consider as he evaluates what comes next. Daronte Jones flips the script The Commanders entered Week 6 allowing red-zone touchdowns on 83.33% of the time. Yeah. You read that right. That’s obviously worst in the league, and the Commanders didn’t do a lot better. The 49ers kept on scoring from inside Washington’s 20-yard line, facing little resistance on the way past the goal line. The Commanders had been getting beat often when their heavy blitz rate didn’t produce pressure early on, and Jones brought the heat far less often against the 49ers and a quarterback in Brock Purdy who knows how to exploit it. The first half stats were wild, with San Francisco averaging 7.4 yards per play. The Commanders looked wiped and at a complete loss for how to attack the 49ers. After allowing 20 points in the first half, the Commanders gave up just three in the second half. What a freaking turn. Jones started to blitz a lot more in the second half and to great effect, including this Odafe Oweh sack, generated by an interior blitz, that gave the Commanders a chance. Defense forces a three-and-out 🙌 📺 #WASvsSF on ESPN pic.twitter.com/8Pu2T3vA5g — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) October 20, 2026 The Commanders got consecutive three-and-outs in the fourth quarter to allow for a real comeback attempt, which was alive with 52 seconds to go. It fell short, but the Commanders defense got better as the game went on. There’s still plenty to work on, but the second half was an encouraging sign after the disaster that was the first half. Losing Terry McLaurin a nightmare scenario Commanders star receiver Terry McLaurin suffered a knee injury in the first quarter that, well, did not look good. Per the broadcast feed, McLaurin’s knee seemed to buckle as if structurally unsound. Terry goes down and immediately grabs his left knee pic.twitter.com/7EtIvcTsmM — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) October 20, 2026 He tried to get off the field but eventually went to the ground. He was treated there by trainers, with teammates all around him. An air cast was placed on his leg and he was carted off the field. Terry McLaurin wearing a large air cast on his left leg as he hobbles onto the cart. pic.twitter.com/am35L8NF3b — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) October 20, 2026 We won’t know the exact nature of the injury until later Monday or Tuesday, but there should be a high level of concern that he’ll miss extended time. That would be a nightmare scenario for a team left reeling after a rough start to the season. McLaurin is a locker-room leader and the team’s most talented catcher, someone who draws defensive attention and makes life easier on others. While the Commanders have a deep receiver room, his loss would be immeasurable for a team that needs as many talented players as possible. We don’t want to speculate about the length of his absence or even the exact injury diagnosis, but it’s fair to say his loss had a negative impact on this game – he had Washington’s only explosive play of the first half – and was a somber note on a rough night in the Bay Area. What are your takeaways from another heartbreaker? Let us know in the comments below:

title: Commanders GM Adam Peters talks Dan Quinn, NFC East, trade deadline
summary: Commanders general manager Adam Peters held his weekly interview with the Sports Junkies on 106.7-FM The Fan a few days later than normal, considering some travel conflicts and the later Monday night start to Washington’s Week 6 contest against the San Francisco 49ers.   So, hopefullly, this was the last Commanders interview focused on what […]
full_text: Commanders general manager Adam Peters held his weekly interview with the Sports Junkies on 106.7-FM The Fan a few days later than normal, considering some travel conflicts and the later Monday night start to Washington’s Week 6 contest against the San Francisco 49ers. So, hopefullly, this was the last Commanders interview focused on what happened against the New York Giants . Fan fatigue has set in — we’ve heard you in the comments — and now all bases have been covered. Peters was largely forward thinking in that regard during his weekly set, and focused on Dan Quinn the culture builder – that has been evident during the practice week, with complete player buy-in – the NFC East , the trade deadline and more. Here are the highlights from that Monday morning interview: Dan Quinn as a culture builder “He did a really good job with that. Presenting to the team, ‘This is what happened, this won’t happen again; what are we’re going to do to fix it and how can we beat the Niners?’ I think he created that culture. I have been on teams where things have fractured and people start pointing fingers and there are whispers in the building and the doors are closed and guys are having conversations. We aren’t even close to that. That’s a testament to his leadership and leadership in the building with the coaches and veterans on the team have done a great job of that, too.” Aftermath of Giants tie “It showed a lot of leadership and growth that everyone took accountability. That’s the sign of a well-coached, good team that no one’s pointing fingers. Then it’s just about looking at what we have in front of us. And it’s everything. We still have 12 games, 70% of the season and the division’s still open. It was about, ‘what are we going to do to beat the 49ers?’ That’s the approach we took, and it was really impressive to see from the group.” Communication on final drive vs. Giants “There’s communication throughout the drive, with how many timeouts we have. I think everybody was aware of that. It obviously didn’t pan out that way. It didn’t look that way and, certainly, the result that we didn’t execute it well enough. I think the communication there was good, not as good as we needed it to be in that instance. After we did the postmortem on that and figured, ‘where did we miss this and how can we make sure this doesn’t happen again,’ — I wasn’t on the headset. I wasn’t able to hear any of that. I was on the sideline watching like you guys all were. Getting the rundown, we figured out where the miscommunications were and it won’t happen again.” Issues with second-half defense “We can be a dominating defense at times, really good against the run and attacking the ball and making plays on the ball. We had an interception that was taken off the board …We’re getting our hands on the ball, making plays on the ball, but in the second half we haven’t been as effective and consistent. Those are things we’re looking at. What do we need to do? Is it our calls, our execution, our stamina? What are the things that are holding us back from us being a 60-minute defense?” Division falling back to Commanders “Everything is in front of us. That’s 12 games, 70% of our season, and we’re still right in that. Hopefully, we’ll be in that until the end. If we win this game, we’re right back in that even closer.” Trade deadline “At this time, we’re actively making calls. Teams are calling us and we’re assessing the market right now. If there’s something that makes sense for us, we’re certainly going to take action. … I wouldn’t categorize us as either (buyers or sellers) right now, as we get closer that will crystalize a little bit more but, certainly, the give up part, that ain’t happening.” Listen to 106.7-FM’s entire interview right here:

title: Commanders News: Is Dan Quinn’s job (really) in jeopardy?
summary: The Daily Slop Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles ESPN Is Commanders coach Dan Quinn’s job […]
full_text: The Daily Slop Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles ESP N Is Commanders coach Dan Quinn’s job in jeopardy after tie with Giants? Washington Commanders coach Dan Quinn sat at a table deep inside Northwest Stadium, trying to make sense of a moment that made none. A coach known for wearing his hat backward instead wore a look of disbelief. For the next 10 minutes, he tried to get comfortable. He folded his arms, then put them at his side, then put them back on the table. There was no comfort, not with what he had to address. He took a quick deep breath after the first two questions, then readied for more. And more would come. There was no getting around what happened: a botched final sequence in his team’s Week 5 matchup with the New York Giants prevented a game-winning field goal attempt on the final play, resulting in a 27-27 tie. “Feels like a loss,” Quinn said. Inside the hushed locker room afterward, receiver Terry McLaurin stood against a burgundy cement wall. He looked upset; he looked drained; he looked bewildered. McLaurin, in his eighth season with the franchise, thought he’d seen it all in Washington — but last Sunday brought something new. “Unacceptable,” McLaurin said. With 50 seconds remaining in overtime, the Commanders had the ball at the Giants’ 24-yard line with no timeouts. Then, all hell broke loose. They didn’t snap the ball until there were 12 seconds to play. On the play, quarterback Jayden Daniels dropped back to pass and then quickly looked to scramble. He started upfield, then was tackled with nine seconds left. He did not get off the ground for another four seconds and there was little urgency by his teammates. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE The Athletic The Commanders are on the brink. They’re also in primetime. Get the popcorn The nature of playing on “Monday Night Football” means that — by the time the pregame show arrives — the developments from the previous Sunday of wall-to-wall pigskin has been parsed and dissected, and all that remains to talk about are the two opponents that night and any recent developments around them. This particular Monday night, that leaves only the undefeated San Francisco 49ers and the visiting Washington Commanders. The topic, then, has to be what might be the most examined sack-for-no-yards-lost in NFL history: the final play of the Commanders’ confounding 27-27 tie against the New York Giants, in which quarterback Jayden Daniels, with no timeouts, took a snap with a dozen seconds left, was tackled with eight ticks remaining — and never got another snap off. “Ultimately, it’s on me at the end,” Daniels said last week. “It’s my responsibility, point blank,” coach Dan Quinn said. “It falls on me,” offensive coordinator David Blough said. Whoever takes the largest slice of the blame pie remains open for debate as Washington heads into its MNF kickoff with the 49ers. What’s not up for discussion: Just as the Commanders proved they’re not ready for a nation’s eyes to be on them, they enter a stretch in which four of their next five games stand alone in primetime. Anyone who wants to be watching football will be watching the Commanders, whether they are deserving of that distinction or not. This is a franchise that has a decidedly tumultuous relationship with primetime football, and one that will spend the next month-and-a-half either proving it is worthy of the country’s attention or fading into oblivion once again. Nothing short of the professional futures of the people who run this team hang in the balance, and football fans who care deeply about or are indifferent to the Commanders will get to examine it all in real time. title: NFL Power Rankings: How all 32 teams stack up for Week 7, plus offensive issues
summary: How does every NFL team stack up heading into Week 7? We made our 1-32 list and picked the biggest offensive problem for every team.
full_text:
Week 6 of the 2026 NFL season featured some troubling performances from offenses around the league. The Cardinals went 0-for-5 in the red zone, yet still defeated the Rams, who lost a fumble and turned the ball over on downs twice. Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert had an interception for the sixth straight game, helping lead to a sixth straight loss. And Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr . was sacked five times against the Bears.

 Why did these offenses struggle so much? In addition to our updated 1-32 rankings, we asked our NFL Nation reporters to pick out the biggest offensive issue for each team. From ineffective run games to a lack of red zone efficiency, what is causing each team to falter this season?

 To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another. Here are a few highlights from this week's rankings:

 
 The Texans are slowly climbing up our list after a shocking 0-4 start to the season. After defeating the Titans in Week 5, Houston got another win over a divisional opponent in the Jaguars. The London matchup was also the Texans debut of wide receiver  Marvin Harrison Jr ., who had three receptions for 34 yards after being traded from the Cardinals last week. 
 The Rams are out of the top 10 in our rankings for the first time this season after their second straight loss Sunday . They are the fifth team in the past 50 seasons to enter a season as the outright Super Bowl favorite and lose at least four of their first six games, per ESPN Research. None of the previous four teams made the conference title game (2015 Seahawks, 2002 Rams, 1999 Vikings and 1987 Giants). 
 The NFC East is off to a rocky start, becoming the first division in NFL history to be winless in consecutive weeks in which every team in the division played a game, per ESPN Research. That struggle has been illustrated in our list. Compared with last week's rankings, the Cowboys are down six spots, the Eagles are down five, the Giants fell four and the Commanders were lowered one spot. Dallas is the only one of those teams to not play a backup QB this season. 
 
 Let's get into the full list, starting with the same No. 1 team from last week .

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. San Francisco 49ers (6-0) 
 Week 6 result: Beat the Commanders 23-17 
 Week 6 ranking: 1 

 Biggest issue on offense: Wide receiver injuries

 

 The Niners haven't had many problems in terms of production, but they have had a significant amount of attrition at wideout. Ricky Pearsall ( knee ), De'Zhaun Stribling ( ankle ), Christian Kirk (calf) and Demarcus Robinson ( ankle ) were supposed to be four of the team's top five receivers and all landed on IR before Week 3. That doesn't account for Deebo Samuel Sr .'s multiweek hamstring injury  or the various bumps and bruises  Mike Evans  played through before departing Monday night's game with Achilles tendinitis . The good news? Most of them are expected back this season, but the 49ers have had to scramble in the meantime. -- Nick Wagoner 

 
 

 

 2. Kansas City Chiefs (5-0) 
 Week 6 result: Beat the Chargers 22-6 
 Week 6 ranking: 2 

 Biggest issue on offense: Offensive tackle health

 

 The Chiefs have done an admirable job protecting quarterback Patrick Mahomes , especially since left tackle Josh Simmons , their 2025 first-round pick, has been out because of a bulging disk in his lower back . Coach Andy Reid suggested Simmons won't be ready for Sunday's showdown against the Seahawks . Plus, right tackle Jaylon Moore sustained a concussion against the Chargers. Reid might have to continue altering the Chiefs' playbook if undrafted rookies Kahlil Benson (left tackle) and Joshua Ezeudu (right tackle) are the starters. -- Nate Taylor 

 
 

 3. Buffalo Bills (5-1) 
 Week 6 result: Beat the Raiders 33-30 
 Week 6 ranking: 3 

 Biggest issue on offense: Putting the ball on the ground

 

 Any criticism of an offense that leads the league in scoring and ranks top three in total offense and yards per play might seem like a nitpick. But running back James Cook III and quarterback Josh Allen have coughed up a few too many fumbles to start the season. Just imagine what this offense would look like if it weren't for five lost fumbles, including three in opposing territory. The Bills did show improvement against the Raiders on Sunday, though, committing zero turnovers. -- Nick Suss 

 
 

 4. Minnesota Vikings (5-0) 
 Week 6 result: Bye 
 Week 6 ranking: 6 

 Biggest issue on offense: Injuries across the board

 

 The Vikings spent the five games before their bye searching for smooth air offensively. There were plenty of reasons for that, but the biggest was simply health-related personnel turnover. Players who have missed at least one game include quarterback Kyler Murray ( concussion ), receivers Justin Jefferson ( ankle ) and Jordan Addison ( hamstring ), running back Jordan Mason ( finger ), left tackle Christian Darrisaw ( concussion ), left guard Donovan Jackson (knee), and tight ends T.J. Hockenson ( concussion ) and Josh Oliver (biceps). All but Jackson and Oliver are expected to return next week. -- Kevin Seifert 

 
 

 5. Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2) 
 Week 6 result: Lost to the Texans 34-31 
 Week 6 ranking: 5 

 Biggest issue on offense: Penalties

 

 Penalties have cost the Jaguars three touchdowns, including a pair of 3-yard touchdown runs by running back  Bhayshul Tuten . It happened again in Sunday's loss, with a questionable holding call on tight end  Brenton Strange . The Jaguars didn't get points on that possession because QB Trevor Lawrence threw an end zone interception two plays later. Jacksonville did score touchdowns after the other two penalties, against New England and Cincinnati, but it finally caught up to them in a three-point loss to the Texans. -- Michael DiRocco 

 
 

 6. Seattle Seahawks (3-3) 
 Week 6 result: Lost to the Broncos 17-14 
 Week 6 ranking: 4 

 Biggest issue on offense: Turnovers

 

 The Seahawks' run game has been underwhelming and their pass protection has been problematic, but no issue is holding first-year coordinator Brian Fleury's unit back like turnovers. It has committed 12 of them, third most of any offense so far. While  Sam Darnold 's struggles go beyond his interceptions, he has thrown seven picks in four games since returning from a glute injury . Seattle has also lost five fumbles. How costly have those giveaways been? Ten of the Seahawks' turnovers have come in their three losses, which were by a combined eight points. The opponents in those losses scored 44 points off those takeaways. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 7. New England Patriots (4-2) 
 Week 6 result: Beat the Jets 26-19 
 Week 6 ranking: 9 

 Biggest issue on offense: Offensive line health

 

 The Patriots had three starters -- right tackle Morgan Moses (ankle), left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker (hamstring) and right guard  Ben Brown  (knee) --  get knocked out of Sunday's game . And the only reason Brown was in the lineup was because opening-day starter Mike Onwenu ( ankle ) and his replacement Greg Van Roten ( hip ) were put on IR earlier in the season. The Patriots have started three different OL combinations in their first six games, and there will likely be a fourth Thursday in Chicago. -- Mike Reiss 

 
 

 8. Baltimore Ravens (4-2) 
 Week 6 result: Lost to the Browns 13-10 
 Week 6 ranking: 7 

 Biggest issue on offense: Penalties

 

 Baltimore's offense has been flagged an NFL-worst 31 times, with a bulk of the penalties coming from false starts (13) and holding (13). On Sunday, the Ravens were called for delay of game three times with backup quarterback Tyler Huntley , which led to a season-low 10 points. title: 49ers WR Mike Evans reps Bay Area with Curry jersey, leads NFL Week 6's arrivals
summary: NFL stars continue to turn game-day arrivals into their own weekly fashion showcase.
full_text:
Fall fashion is finding its footing as the NFL enters Week 6.

 With October in full swing, players are navigating a mix of crisp temperatures and lingering warmth as they make their pregame arrivals.

 The Seattle Seahawks and Denver Broncos kicked off the week Thursday night with temperatures around 50 degrees in Denver, setting the stage for layered looks. Sunday's slate offered a similar fall feel in Cleveland, Foxborough and Philadelphia, where temperatures are expected to hover in the 50s. Meanwhile, warmer conditions in Tampa Bay and Los Angeles gave players more room to experiment with lighter ensembles.

 From all black leather fits like Tennessee Titans defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons to fur coats like Houston Texans QB C.J. Stroud wore in London, here are Week 6's most fashionable fits that caught our eye:

 

 Primetime arrivals 
Bay Area basketball pride met bold fall style ahead of the San Francisco 49ers ' "Monday Night Football" matchup against the Washington Commanders . Wide receiver Mike Evans paid homage to Stephen Curry in a black Golden State Warriors No. 30 jersey, paired with black cargo pants and sneakers. Defensive lineman Osa Odighizuwa took a dressier approach, layering a fuzzy green-and-white cardigan over a white shirt and black tie. Brown corduroy pants, a black beret and amber-tinted glasses rounded out his look.
 
 
Ahead of "Sunday Night Football" against the Dallas Cowboys , Green Bay Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin leaned into fall style with a burgundy leather jacket and matching pants over a black shirt. He accessorized with tinted shades, patterned shoes and an oversized "Z" pendant.
 
 Sunday's best 
No player quantifies pound-for-pound among the best in the game quite like the 170-pound Philadelphia Eagles receiver DeVonta Smith on the field and with his gameday tunnel fit.
 
This week, Smith returned from injury to the Eagles lineup with a European style look blending a clean stone mélange Bottega Veneta wool jacket with a classic but fly dress shirt, tie and tailored trousers. Smith's shiny Black tabi loafer work well with this combo.
 
And don't forget about the accessories -- Smith's Louis Vuitton Porte-Documents Voyage PM briefcase and Saint Laurent sunglasses complete the fit.
 
The extremely competitive A.J. Brown once said "nobody in this league is touching Smitty when it comes to dressing with suits" referencing the unique, sleek custom pieces that Smith wears often courtesy his primary bespoke haberdasher Brian Alexander.
 
But fashion means versatility, and this look from Smith shows his range.

title: How active NFL players continue to redefine all-time sack list
summary: Myles Garrett's torrid pace up the all-time sack list paces active players making their moves among the greats.
full_text:
Last season, defensive end Myles Garrett won his second Defensive Player of the Year award after setting the NFL's single-season record with 23 sacks with the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 This season, he'll continue his climb up the NFL's all-time sack list as a member of the Los Angeles Rams  after a blockbuster trade  in June -- making the Rams favorites to win the Super Bowl, according to DraftKings Sportsbook, heading into the season. 
 
 Garrett entered the season with 125.5 career sacks, which was tied for 20th in NFL history and third among the other six active players --  Von Miller  (No. 9), Cameron Jordan  (No. 17), Calais Campbell  (No. 25), T.J. Watt  (No. 26), Danielle Hunter  (tied for No. 27) and Khalil Mack  (T-29th) -- in the top 30.  
 
 Joining the top 30 soon could be  Aaron Donald ,  who unretired  to join Garrett on the Rams' defensive line. Donald's 111 sacks currently sits two behind 30th.  
 
 As for Garrett, he entered his 10th season in the NFL averaging approximately 14 sacks per season. If he were to replicate that production, he would tie Pro Football Hall of Famer Jason Taylor, who currently sits at No. 7. If Garrett were to have another historic season, he would surpass Michael Strahan (No. 6) and approach career top-five territory. 
 
 
 
 Miller, who signed with the  Dallas Cowboys  in August, can also pass Strahan in his 15th season -- as he sits only three sacks behind him.   
 
 But Garrett's 125.5 career sacks heading into the season was 10.5 more than any other player since his rookie season in 2017, according to ESPN Research. The pass rusher recorded at least 14 sacks in each of the past five seasons, the longest such streak by any player since 1982. 
 
 If Garrett has 18.5 or more sacks this season, he will hold the record for the most over a two-season span since 1982, according to ESPN Research, and his current ascension up the career list ranks as the second-fastest pace among the top five all time behind only Reggie White's.  
 
As we look at how the sack list is redefined this season, we'll highlight milestones across the NFL landscape 
 We will update this file as the active players move up, and we'll add nuggets and milestones throughout the season. 
 

 

 Week 6 update 

 With Garrett still out, it was another quiet week on the sack front. Of the active leaders, it was the oldest that recorded the lone sack of the week in Campbell. He moved back in front of Hunter. 

 Week 5 update 

 Hunter was the only player among the active leaders to record a sack this week, moving him ahead of Campbell to No. 26 all-time. Hunter now has three sacks through five games. 

 Week 4 update 

 Watt kicked off things in Week 4 on "Thursday Night Football" in an impactful way. He had one sack, one forced fumble and a fumble recovery to move his total to 4.5 sacks on the season. Other than that, there wasn't much activity with Garrett continuing to be on IR. 

 Week 3 update 

 There wasn't much movement on the list this week with only Mack (1) and Hunter (.5) recording sacks. Watt, Campbell, Hunter and Mack (in that order) now make up 25 to 28 on the all-time list. Along with Campbell, the three top active leaders -- Miller, Jordan and Garrett -- have yet to record a sack this season.  

 Week 2 update 

 The second week of the season saw little movement near the top of the career list, but Watt's hot start continues, with the defensive end recording 1.5 sacks to now put him at 3.5 through two weeks (No. 2 in the NFL this season) and break a tie with Campbell to move to 25th. 

 Hunter (27th) and Mack (29th) also recorded one sack apiece over the weekend to break ties and move up one spot on the list. 

 Donald (33rd) made his  season debut on "Monday Night Football" against the Giants after taking two years off. He finished with three tackles, one for a loss, but did not record a sack. 

 

 

 Week 1 update 

 Of all the active sack leaders, Watt was the only one to record a sack, finishing the game with two to move to a tie with Campbell for 25th. 

 And while Donald was held out of the Rams' Week 1 game, Garrett will be out for at least the next four after failing to record a tackle in Australia and landing on injured reserve after having to have arthroscopic surgery on his knee.

 After the Rams' opening loss, Garrett said this was " the worst version of myself that I've put out there."

title: 'It's Groundhog Day': Why Ravens lead the NFL in blown double-digit leads
summary: Here is a look at the trends in the Ravens failing to hold double-digit leads.
full_text:
CLEVELAND -- All of the Baltimore Ravens ' confidence built up from their clutch play the past three weeks disappeared by the end of Sunday's 13-10 loss to the Cleveland Browns . 
 
 As Andre Szmyt's  37-yard game-winning field goal sailed through the uprights as time expired, the Ravens lamented another loss they felt they should have won. Even Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton , who is one of the most insightful players in this locker room, hit his breaking point when he didn't have an answer for how to solve another late-game collapse. 
 
 "I'm not going to sound like a broken record," Hamilton said. "It's 'Groundhog Day' with this question. I don't know. I'm not going to give you an answer. I really don't know. So, sorry, that's the best I can give you, but we've had this conversation so many times. I don't even feel like addressing it again." 
 
 Hamilton is referring to Baltimore's 16th blown double-digit lead since 2020, which is the most in the NFL in that span. It's three more than any other team (the Los Angeles Chargers are second with 13). 
 
 On Sunday, fill-in starting quarterback Tyler Huntley led the Ravens to a 10-0 lead after two drives. The Baltimore defense, meanwhile, didn't look like it was going to allow the Browns to score, recording as many sacks (three) as completions by halftime. 
 
 Then, all-too-familiar mistakes -- Derrick Henry 's fumble, Tyler Loop 's missed field goal and the secondary's lapses in coverage -- helped Cleveland score the final 13 points of the game. 
 
 "That's a type of game where I think [in] all three phases, you have chances to create more separation," coach Jesse Minter said. 
 
 
 The Ravens acknowledged their frustration because they had believed they had moved past these types of meltdowns. Baltimore's last three wins came in the final moments from Loop's game-winning field goal against the Dallas Cowboys in Brazil, Malaki Starks ' leaping catch of an onside kick against the Tennessee Titans and Hamilton's interception in overtime at Atlanta. 
 
 There is hope that quarterback Lamar Jackson will come back this week after missing the last two games with an ankle injury. It would be a timely return for the Ravens (4-2) considering the next three games are against the Cincinnati Bengals (3-2), who are considered Baltimore's biggest threat to the AFC North title, and two division leaders in the Buffalo Bills (5-1) and Jacksonville Jaguars (4-2). 
 
 "We just didn't make the plays that we wanted to make this game," defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike said. "One thing I know about this team [is that] we are going to learn from this, we are going to grow from this, and we are going to get better. We are going to have our eyes moving forward to the next opponent."' 
 
 Here is a look at the trends in the Ravens failing to hold double-digit leads: 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 Turnovers on offense 
 
 
 The momentum shifted Sunday when Henry fumbled in the fourth quarter, giving the ball to the Browns at the Ravens' 35-yard line with 12:36 left. Seven plays later, Cleveland running back Audric Estime rushed for a 2-yard touchdown to tie the game at 10. 
 
 After the loss, Henry told his teammates in the locker room: "Put this one on me." 
 
 "I got to take care of the ball," Henry said. "There's no excuses for that. I got to be better. I put the team's in harm's way. I sound like a broken record with this, but I got to go back to work on it. Can't put the team in that situation." 
 
 
 
 This was Henry's NFL-worst third lost fumble in the fourth quarter since the start of the 2025 season, but there's plenty of blame to go around. In those 16 blown double-digit leads, Baltimore has totaled 15 turnovers in the fourth quarter with seven interceptions and eight fumbles. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Missed field goals 
 
 
 Early in the fourth quarter Sunday, Baltimore could have made it a two-score game. But Loop's 49-yard field goal veered wide left to keep the Ravens' lead at 10-3. 
 
 "I just did not strike it the way I needed to," Loop said. "[I] didn't hit the ball clean. It ended up having some bad rotation, and [it] just slid out to the left." 
 
 
 
 
 Loop has made some huge kicks recently from the winning 56-yarder as time expired in Brazil to the 64-yarder against the Titans to the pair of 51-yarders at the Falcons. But three of his seven career misses came in the second half of collapses against the New England Patriots (Week 16 of last season), Pittsburgh Steelers (Week 18 of last season) and Sunday at the Browns. 
 
 "There is a confidence level for how Tyler prepares and how he practices and how he operates and how he strikes the ball, but at the same time, that position itself is completely results-driven," Minter said. "So, we'll continue to work with him and continue to try to put him in position, but we need to make second-half kicks. You could argue that second-half missed field goals are no different than turning the ball over in those situations. So, [that's] definitely something we want to keep striving to be better at." 
 
 
 
 
 
 Struggles in the secondary 
 
 
 Like so many times in these devastating defeats, the Ravens unraveled late against the Browns. 
 
 In the first three quarters, Baltimore held quarterback Deshaun Watson  to 8-of-14 passing for 70 yards. In the fourth quarter, the Ravens allowed Watson to complete eight of 12 passes for 94 yards. 
 
 "Being a member of the secondary, it seems like whenever we are losing these games, the ball is in the air," cornerback Marlon Humphrey said. "Obviously, we played a decent game before that, but when it counts, how can you win the game? I feel like that's usually won in the back end, and we just weren't able to do that today." 
 
 In the 16 blown double-digit leads, the secondary has struggled in the fourth quarter where quarterbacks have averaged 111.6 yards passing, throwing 17 touchdowns and no interceptions. 
 
 "It's pretty frustrating," Humphrey said. "I think we feel that we are better, we feel that we're equipped, [and] we feel that we're ready for these moments. We just [have] got to consistently do it. We [have] got to consistently believe that you trust the guy next to you. I think it all starts with communication. Someone has to end the game for us. I think that's the biggest thing. Are all 11 guys thinking, 'I'm going to be the one to end the game.' That's where it starts, and that's where it ends."

title: Inside NFL's field-stitching process from Rio to Paris
summary: How does the NFL install new fields in stadiums not made for them? The man known as Papa Turf walked us through it.
full_text:
Papa Turf had seen Copacabana Beach only from his hotel room. He had spent more time managing a rehab effort at the stadium than sleeping. But when Tyler Loop's walk-off 56-yard field goal -- kicked from the edge of the NFL logo -- snuck inside the left upright to give the Baltimore Ravens a last-second victory over the Dallas Cowboys in Rio de Janeiro last month, it wasn't just the Ravens who were happy with the result.

 "Honestly, [I was] feeling like that was a perfect way to end an exciting game," said Nick Pappas, the NFL's field director, who was hoping "field czar" would stick as a moniker instead of the "Papa Turf" sobriquet bestowed upon him by a league executive. Pappas was watching Loop from the far end zone, not caring which team won, only that nobody would have to talk about the grass afterward. "To see it end on a play where the cleat-to-surface interaction is so critical, on a long, important kick, was added validation that my decisions and efforts throughout the process were the right ones."

 That kick ended a weekslong odyssey through once-in-a-generation rain during what was supposed to be the dry season, the busy local soccer schedule, cargo flights from the Netherlands, hurried processing through Brazilian customs, a crash course in agronomy for the media and a round-the-clock, maddeningly slow stitching of the field by Zamboni-like sewing machines to render the field a nonfactor. Loop's sure footing on the final kick came on the part of the field that was at the heart of the frenzied repair.

 "I thought overall the field held up well," Ravens coach Jesse Minter said after the game. "I didn't see a bunch of plays where guys were falling down or anything like that."

 The NFL did it all again for next Sunday's game in Paris, albeit without the late-night drama and transcontinental logistics.

 

 Pappas and the NFL had the benefit of time to get the Stade de France field ready for the Saints and Steelers, an important difference from Brazil, where Pappas had to cut off the field-sewing process to leave enough time to paint the yard markings and team logos. Grass maintenance is such a niche discipline that very few understood just how unusual and aggressive a decision it was to stitch up a field with a game just days away.

 "Probably only people who are in the turf industry would maybe have the insight to say, 'You're stitching on a game week, huh? That's interesting,'" said Pappas, who oversees all the NFL's playing surfaces.

 The challenges for Rio and Paris were both climate related: historic rain in Rio and record heat during the European summer, when the field for Paris was being grown at a farm in Italy. The solution was the same -- a decades-old technology that involves stitching synthetic fibers into a grass field, creating a hybrid field that provides better footing for players.

 That Rio would need extra management was not a surprise to Pappas or the NFL. Rio's famed Maracanã is used heavily by local soccer clubs. In 2024, when the NFL first played in Sao Paolo, slipping was an issue.

 It's not unusual in the United States for stadiums to be resodded after a rainy game or heavy usage that causes damage. But in Brazil, the sod farm that could supply a new field for Maracanã was also in the rainy zone, so the grass that would have been needed to resod was also sopping wet. Resodding was out.

 "I never felt like the field in Rio was like a disaster. I never felt it was going to fail. I didn't think that we were ever going to have to have the conversation of, can we play there." Pappas said.

 The NFL has canceled games because of poor field conditions -- in 2016, the Hall of Fame game was canceled and a 2018 Monday night game was moved out of Mexico City to Los Angeles -- but those were considered black eyes, Pappas said, to be avoided at all costs. The NFL declined to provide a precise figure on its investment in the field preparation process, stressing that its focus is on getting it right.

 The situation was less dire for Paris' Stade de France. The NFL had intended to put down a hybrid field that was being grown at a farm in Milan, Italy. But that field -- a synthetic carpet with soil and seed added, so that the natural grass grows into the carpet -- wasn't flourishing because of the extraordinary heat in Europe. So, in early September, Pappas pivoted. The NFL had a natural grass plot from that same Milan farm laid in the stadium. Last week, it was stitched to reinforce it. There have been just a handful of soccer matches on the field in the last few weeks.

 

 The relatively light use of the Stade de France made the process easier because there were breaks in the stadium usage that allowed the NFL to install its field. In Rio, Pappas made the decision to stitch the field about 12 days before the Sept. 27 game, but the NFL didn't have control of the field until a week before the game.

 "There's not a whole lot any of us can do," Dr. John Sorochan, the NFLPA's field consultant, said. "The actual triaging doesn't happen until right after they take over control."

 The union would prefer the league get control of stadiums earlier, to maximize how much the fields are managed. It is an issue the NFLPA could raise during negotiations with the league as the NFL seeks to expand its slate of international games. As is, the NFL negotiates directly with the stadiums for game and field-control timing. Pappas must also navigate local federations who have their own concerns about what kind of field will be left behind after the NFL leaves. In Melbourne, for instance, the stadium replaced the field after the Rams and 49ers played, in anticipation of a big Australian rules football match.

 Eleven days before the Rio game, the hulking stitching machines used for the project were loaded onto a cargo plane in the Netherlands, bound for Rio. Stitching fields is not new -- the technology has existed since the late 1990s -- although it is more common in European soccer leagues than in the United States. One example of a stateside reinforced natural grass surface: Green Bay's Lambeau Field.

 
 O Maracanã iniciou nesta segunda-feira o processo de troca do gramado. A primeira etapa consiste na raspagem do campo para a retirada do gramado atual. Na sequência, serão instalados os novos rolos de grama da Bermuda Celebration. O processo de renovação está sendo realizado de forma programada, e o campo estará preparado para receber as próximas partidas da temporada.

 �� Daniel Brasil / Maracanã

- Maracanã (@maracana) September 28, 2026 
 
 The machines landed in Rio on Sunday, a week out from the game. By Wednesday afternoon, they were through customs in Brazil -- "Maybe the fastest anything has ever gone through customs legally in Brazil," Pappas said -- and they were at the stadium by 9:30 p.m. Wednesday night. By midnight, stitching had begun, with little more than three days to go until game day.

 The overgrown sewing machines have bobbins of fibrous yarn. A needle drives the thread directly into the ground, creating a hybrid field from a grass field. The goal is to drive the fiber below the height of the grass. In spots where the grass is worn away, the fiber is visible. It might be unsightly, but those fibers protect the existing grass and create additional traction. For players, the field still feels and plays like fully natural grass.

 Stitching a field is numbingly methodical. The needles are driven into the ground, and then the machines move up 2 centimeters and repeat the process, over and over. It takes about two hours to go 100 yards. In Rio, there were two machines and four operators -- one per machine, working in two 12-hour shifts. With the very limited time available in Rio, Pappas decided to stitch the middle of the field, which was the most worn. The area from the top of the numbers on one side of the field to the top of the numbers on the other side, a bit outside the hash marks, was stitched, so that the NFL's…
